How Town was born

But now it’s caught on, and it automatically scans everything for me. It reads my emails all the time. This is a situation where my firm is kind enough to provide me with an executive assistant. There are many people who don’t have one. You might say the market for executive assistants is pretty small because most people don’t have them. But if you can build one with silicon, the market becomes quite large. Then you find people saying, “I’m going to let someone read my email all the time,” something I would never do for privacy reasons. It’s a double Jevons paradox—a Jevons paradox of privacy.

For those who don’t know, the Jevons paradox is that when the steam engine became more efficient—when James Watt made a more efficient steam engine—the assumption was that demand for coal would drop. What used to take a pound of coal would now take an ounce. But demand actually increased a thousandfold, because now you had something that could do the job very efficiently. It seems like this probably applies to the assistant market as well.

But I’m curious: how do you define your market? Is it some kind of assistant? That seems like too narrow a definition.

Town as a token-allocation machine

Jean-Denis Greze

I think of this market as an attempt to create a product that works with people to find more and more opportunities to use AI to do their jobs better. In some cases, I think of our product as a token distribution machine. We try to give people options for where they can apply the tokens, and then they can choose whether they want the outcome.

As tokens get cheaper, there are more and more places where you could apply them that you wouldn’t use them for with today’s expensive tokens, and certainly wouldn’t use people for. The simplest example is writing preparatory notes for every meeting you go to. Even if you have a personal assistant, they won’t take the time to write perfect preparation notes for every 30-minute meeting. That’s an irrational use of time. But an LLM can do it for pennies.

Suddenly, it’s possible for everyone to have prep notes for every meeting, including research on who else is in the meeting and whether they’ve said anything on X in the last week that might be relevant. All this niche research now makes sense because it’s much cheaper. Our job is to find more and more of these things and ask you, as the user, “Hey, do you want us to do this for you?”

I’ll give you another example I’ve been really into lately. If you’re a small business owner running a restaurant in America, your wholesalers—the people you buy ingredients and other things from—probably email you an Excel spreadsheet or PDF with prices for their entire range once a month, or maybe once a quarter. These are thousands, if not tens of thousands, of products, and prices are constantly changing. If you own a restaurant and have a part-time finance person, that person should check once a quarter how prices have changed, to see if you can order something from other wholesalers or if you’re being overcharged because the price of something has gone up 20% or 30%.

Mostly, you don’t do that. It’s a rare occurrence, and while it could save you money, it’s a hassle, it’s not part of your operating activities, and you don’t have a full-time employee to do it. With AI, you can set up a process to run once a month and perform an analysis. You can literally create a tool like this for yourself in five minutes with a prompt. If it doesn’t find anything worthwhile for 11 out of 12 months, it’ll cost you about $1 a month. But the interesting thing is that in the one month a year when it finds something, it’ll save you hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars.

Now what may or may not have been worth the effort is worth doing at least once a month. You should do this every time there’s a change. It might be worth doing every day if your wholesaler changed prices every day, but that’s not the case. Our job is to show this opportunity to the restaurant owner. It’s not that they’re not smart or don’t understand their business well; they do. They just won’t find this valuable unless we show them. So we’re saying, “Hey, listen. Do you want me to make sure your wholesalers don’t change prices in a way that hurts your business?” The answer is, “Of course, do it.”

You don’t really care how often it runs. You care that every now and then you get an email saying, “Hey, you should probably move these things to another wholesaler. They’re offering a discount, or this place is really raising prices on these items, and it’s getting a little too expensive. Maybe you should take those items off the menu.” It’s not high math. But you need a product that tells you this is possible and does it for you.

Alex Rampell

Well, the interesting thing about this example is that if you went to a restaurant owner and said, “Do you want a personal assistant?”—

Jean-Denis Greze

He wouldn’t have any idea.

Alex Rampell

He wouldn’t have any idea. Yeah, yeah. Whereas if you said, “Do you want to save money?” It’s like GEICO, right? “Want to save 15% on your car insurance?” Or, “Want to save on iceberg lettuce? I can save you $500 a year for $50 a year.” The answer is yes. But how do you know? It’s a question or a challenge for product marketing.

How have you thought about horizontal versus vertical?

What I hope I’m conveying correctly is that we’re going to start as horizontally as possible because we don’t want to be limited to something narrow. We don’t want to be siloed and have a brand as “the company that saves you money on iceberg lettuce.” We want to do that, and we’re going to learn. This is my pitch to your candidates right now, by the way, so I hope I’m getting this right. We’re going to learn from thousands, tens of thousands of companies and people using our product. We wouldn’t know about it until someone downloads Town and uses it, and we learn from their experience. Then we can understand what vertical it could be. How do you think about vertical versus horizontal?

Horizontal vs vertical

Jean-Denis Greze

I think most AI products today will have very similar capabilities. Most of the tools in the work context will be able to do the same things. So the differentiator—the thing that has been the main thing in Silicon Valley for a long time, having product features that are ahead of the market—is going to be harder and harder to sustain as an advantage.

We can put that aside and have an interesting conversation about the fact that I think the unit of value in software has shifted from the app to the computer. But what that really means is that it’s going from the app to everything a human can do, and a human can do almost everything with a computer. So we’re completely abstracting away from the app level, and I think the value at the app level is going to go down.

If the capabilities are the same, how do you build a successful company? Our view is that, as AI gets better, it will be able to tailor the product to each user’s needs much more specifically. If you’re an electrician who signs up at Town, the things we recommend you automate during onboarding will be very specific to electricians. If you’re a venture capitalist, they’ll be very specific to venture capitalists. If you’re an executive assistant, they’ll be specific to EAs in that industry, and so on.

How do you do that? The models aren’t sophisticated enough yet that, if you just ask a model, “Hey, recommend things Alex, who’s a venture capitalist, could automate with Town,” you’ll get more than pretty good surface-level suggestions. You won’t get anything really deep. And we don’t look at user data, because part of being ready to work with enterprise customers is that you can’t look at user data. So we look at the overall metrics for who our most active users are on the platform, and then we go talk to them. When we talk to them, they tell us what they’ve automated.

We can talk to 10 power users who run restaurants. In those conversations, we might notice that there are 5 things they all do in common. Then we sit down as a team and prototype automations, which we call “routines,” for restaurant owners—things we think are really useful, like one that deals with wholesale suppliers. We use those as a foundation. When someone comes on board, we look at their email and inbox and say, “It looks like you’re a restaurant owner.” Then we offer them templates of problems and potential solutions for restaurant owners that we think are really good, based on what we’ve extracted from those interviews.

You sign up and start using the product. Then the AI gets better, and we talk to more restaurant owners. Now we don’t have 5 things we can do for restaurant owners; we have 15. It’s still a little manual, but it can be sped up. You can automatically schedule interviews, offer restaurant owners a free Amazon gift card, and interview them with AI to see what they’re doing with your software. So you’re not working at human speed anymore; you’re working at AI speed. That library gets better, and the models get better. The recommendations then rely less on the library, and we think that over time, with this approach, we’ll be able to offer 80/20, highly personalized software for people.

People in the future won’t just have one role. You might be a restaurant owner, but you also manage your restaurant’s finances because you don’t have a separate person for that. You might also have a vacation rental property. You want your Townie to be good at all 3 things. And you have 2 kids in school, and it can help you plan their summer classes. This is completely custom software, and we believe you can use AI to build it.

Another strategy you’re seeing in the market, and what I think the labs are doing, is the FDE approach. That’s a completely different thing. With FDE, a person comes into your business, learns how it works, and then builds custom software using AI from the labs to serve you better. If you’re a company willing to spend about $5 million a year paying OpenAI for FDE, that looks pretty good right now. But I think that over time, as the models get better, the FDE approach will actually get a lot worse, while our approach—using automation and AI to build custom software—will scale a lot better.

We’re betting on starting with PLG: small and medium-sized businesses that are very tech-savvy, because our approach scales really well there. We’re going to let others compete in the enterprise sector with this more hands-on software. Our bet is that the knowledge we gain from the flywheel of development will make us more successful in the long run than these more individual approaches.

Jean-Denis Greze

The short answer, although it’s not the best one, is that we have a very different vision for the user experience of email and calendar. For some reason, other players haven’t focused on that. There’s a lot of complexity in email and calendaring, which makes our product much, much better at it. But that’s the short answer, because someone at OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google could wake up and decide to do the same thing.

The better answer is to think about our customers and what they want. When we talk to midsize businesses—companies with 500 to 1,000 employees—we ask them, “Listen, do you know who’s going to be the best model provider in the next 3 to 5 years? What’s your opinion?” They don’t know. They really don’t know. So we say, “If you buy an OpenAI product, it will always have OpenAI models in it. What if OpenAI isn’t the best provider, or doesn’t have the best intelligence for you, in the next 3 to 5 years? As AI does more and more for you, you may find yourself at a competitive disadvantage.”

Will they raise the price? Yes, all of that. The first thing we say is, “Look, we’re a neutral app. We’ll use the provider we believe is best for you at this time.” This is a significant part of our strategy. It’s not just about general intelligence, but also about who’s better at working with voice, video, or slides. We consider it our duty to determine what’s right for your business among all the possibilities in AI: frontier models and open-source models. I think you can not only save money, but also avoid the risks associated with choosing the wrong partner.

There are companies that chose OpenAI about 2 years ago, and then Anthropic got better at coding over the course of 12 months. Those companies had to use both because they realized that, to be competitive, they needed Claude. Then they needed those exact models. If you’re a smart business, you really think about the neutrality of who’s providing you with the intelligence and who’s doing the routing. So that’s one reason.

The second reason, which is very important, is our position that, as a business, you truly own the data, memories, and contacts that are created in Town. In the old world, before computers, businesses had different assets: physical assets, and maybe human assets. Now, increasingly, people might call it context, but there’s a set of assets—everything AI knows about your business to help you run it effectively. I believe you should own that entire set. You should own it to the point where, if there were ever a better solution than Town, switching to another solution would take a day. That’s what I’m selling: the idea that you want to own this asset.

If you look at people who hire developers to build software for them, they’re actually trying to make it harder for you to switch to someone else. So that’s the second reason. First, you want neutral intelligence, but you also want an application layer above the intelligence that allows you to switch easily. In the new world, it’s about having that level of context and having someone who makes it available to you.

The risk I’m taking with Town is that the cost of switching is lower for my customers. But that is my advantage. If I can’t have the best product on the market, that’s okay; it just means I lose. That’s my competitive position against the labs.

The third part for me is just learning. If you’re a big enough company, the labs won’t be training on you. But if the way you do business ever gets into the hands of someone who resells it to others, you’re effectively selling what makes your business successful to someone else.

And you definitely don’t want to do that. We don’t train on your data; it’s just not part of our business philosophy.

One last thing about competition: we have a different view of the world and of the relationship between humans and AI. We’re probably more forward-thinking than even the labs themselves. In Town’s Teams product, there’s a mode for creating an internal CRM where we trust agents to decide what corporate information is available to other employees.

Here’s an example: you’re in Town and ask, “Does anyone know anyone in the finance department of this prospect?” Town can reach out to other employees’ agents to find someone connected to the lead you need. It’s a very powerful tool, but from a privacy perspective, it needs to be designed with the utmost care.

I think about it this way: we’re focused on getting people to work at the speed of AI, not the speed of humans. The human version of my question would be to write in Slack or Microsoft Teams, “Does anyone know anyone on that team?” Then everyone in the company has to read the message and think about it, and you might get a notification in a day or so.

Alex Rampell

That’s right. People are slow routers.

Jean-Denis Greze

That’s right. With us, you’ll get an answer instantly, because we’ve decided that for questions like that, we’ll trust AI to ensure security and privacy within the company. We believe this can significantly speed up how a company works, and I don’t see anyone else doing it.

When you build a startup, you always have to think about what the future will look like. I believe that in the future, human participation will be minimal compared with what we see today. Our task is to help companies embrace this new world, because the economic benefits far outweigh the risks they see today.

Those are some of our differences. I believe data ownership and neutrality are extremely important. Look at what’s happening with Rogo or Harvey. OpenAI is creating vertical companies that compete with other companies. From a competitive perspective, you start to think, “Oh my God, these labs are truly unstoppable.” But a neutral business choosing who to work with has to think about how far up the stack those companies are going to go. Strategically, I just don’t think it makes sense for most large companies to depend on any one lab.

Neutral agents and the broken ad covenant

Amazon has obviously taken a somewhat hostile approach, which makes sense since they’re an advertising company. There’s been a certain agreement on the internet for a long time: I go to Yahoo Finance to look at stock quotes. Yahoo pays for a feed of quotes from Nasdaq or similar sources, but I see ads for E*TRADE. The deal goes like this: “I, Yahoo, give you, Alex, free quotes if you watch my ads.” And this agreement has been broken.

Those who’ve encountered this broken agreement are hostile, but there seems to be a great opportunity for synergy. It’s like, “Wow, this is the new SEO.” If I could accept traffic from agents and not block it—not think about how to stop it, but how to welcome it—that looks like a huge opportunity from the other side as well.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yeah, I mean, Amazon’s loss should be Walmart’s gain, right? Walmart doesn’t have an advertising business, so its incentives will be different. And I think, to your point, distribution has changed. The most interesting thing about agents is how distribution changes if you no longer trust your agent because it might have an interest in something. That’s an interesting question, isn’t it?

Let’s say you use a Meta agent, and Meta has attracted advertisers. You ask it, and United Airlines is advertised on Meta much more than some unknown airline. You ask it to pick a flight. What happens if you feel like it no longer offers you a neutral option? There are always human incentives to promote products and engage in marketing. What does this look like in a world where people no longer look at things themselves? That’s a very open question.

I firmly believe you need a neutral agent that belongs to you, whose sole source of funding is your wallet as a user. Whoever creates that agent should be interested in providing you, as a human being, with the best information, without distortions caused by marketing forces. You have your own taste and express it by making certain choices. You can ask your agent, “Hey, what are people talking about on Instagram?” Or, “What are they advertising there?” You might ask because, in this case, you want to experience the impact of advertising and marketing. But you want your agent to remain neutral about it.

On the question of competition or the lack of it, I find it interesting to distinguish between the friction points you enjoy and those you don’t. Walking around SoHo in New York City to shop—that’s friction I like. I like having to walk between stores. I like other people standing in line, because I can adopt their style. I like that friction. That’s the enjoyable part of shopping.

And there’s friction I don’t like. I want to order toilet paper to take home. I just want the same toilet paper I’ve been ordering for a long time, delivered as soon as possible and as cheaply as possible. Sometimes, when we think too much about agents, we focus too much on reducing friction and effort and making everything as efficient as possible. But people don’t always optimize everything for efficiency.

The Amazon example, in terms of advertising, is that sometimes I’m on Amazon buying LEGO for my kids, and I really want to see ads for other building blocks or toys for my son. I might see something that isn’t from LEGO that I didn’t know about, and it’s interesting. Then I want to ask my agent to find reviews. I can say, “This is an interesting thing. Is it popular with children? Maybe I’ll want to buy it.” In that experience, I think Amazon can make a lot of money, and there will still be value for platforms that aggregate the offer with advertising and marketing. But there are many times when you optimize friction and don’t need those things.

If I were Amazon and had $80 billion—or, what, $70 billion—in annual advertising business, the question I would ask is, “Hey, I don’t think you want to block agents.” I think there could be a company bigger than Amazon, like a headless Amazon, that could be a huge, just huge business. But I think it puts more pressure on them to create a separate experience where you actually want to see the ads, and it’s really good, and it’s worth going there for that. I think I would still go to Amazon for these things eventually.

AI is evolving so fast that it’s going to change distribution and human habits at such a rate that I don’t think anyone can predict which platforms will win in these areas. There are going to be huge losers, right? Amazon could lose a huge chunk of its advertising business trying to grapple with the future, but they can’t predict what it will look like without it.

Another example that just occurred to me is Muse. I don’t know if you’ve seen the discussions around Muse. It’s like a free, quote-unquote, personal agent. People say, “Well, one day they’ll have to advertise in Muse.” But they might never have to advertise on Muse. Maybe Muse is just giving them data that allows them to target you better on Instagram.

When you go on Instagram, you’re there because you don’t need efficiency; you want to have fun. If they can target better on Instagram thanks to the information from Muse, and Instagram can let you pay for a product you like using the wallet information they collected through Muse, or Muse can search the web for different variations of that product, it’s a really great flywheel. It means you’ve separated monetization from the agent experience for this personal use case.

And this is where Amazon, in my opinion, loses. Maybe because of agents like this, simply being an aggregator of goods may not be the best business model in the world of agents anymore. There’s really not much they can do about it. They’ll lose.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes. They must have their own agent—that’s their countermeasure. Don’t block agents; have your own. Have a better one, make it exclusive to shopping, hope that’s enough of an incentive, and add it to Prime. But I’m not sure they’re capable of that.

Alex Rampell

Interestingly, there’s a site called CamelCamelCamel associated with Amazon. It’s a price-tracking service for Amazon. You’re literally saying, “I want to know when Dr Pepper, which is currently $8, drops to $6,” and then buy it as soon as it costs $6.

Jean-Denis Greze

No, it doesn’t make the purchase for you.

It just sends an alert, and you have to buy it yourself.

Alex Rampell

Aha. This site is used by 20 million people.

Jean-Denis Greze

20 million people?

Alex Rampell

Yes, 20 million people in America. And it’s simple. This is an affiliate site that’s been around for 18 years.

Justin and I wrote an article about how the best way to predict the future is to observe the present. Again, going back to the fact that the future is unevenly distributed, this is the future. When I think about agents, I divide people into those who have more time than money.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, that’s true.

Alex Rampell

And those who have more money than time.

Jean-Denis Greze

Aha.

Alex Rampell

Those who have more money than time won’t use CamelCamelCamel, and those who have more time than money will take advantage of it. But wait a minute: What if you could give everyone who has more money than time all these tools, so an agent could do it for them? Of course they would use it.

Jean-Denis Greze

This is an IQ test.

Alex Rampell

These things are definitely going to become much more common. Sometimes you don’t even have to imagine what could happen. Just look at coupons.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

You shouldn’t use a coupon if you’re rich, because it takes too much time. You’ll spend about 2 hours searching for the right coupon. But this is another arrangement that’s falling apart, because it was a very convenient way to divide the world.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes. I mean, the Amex premium membership is the same thing. Now it just optimizes all your advantages.

Alex Rampell

Yes, all your advantages. The unused benefits model is dead.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, and so we’ll all be abusing all our Chase and Amex benefits, and they’ll have to change that. This is unprofitable for both, because then it will become a hostile confrontation. It’s a kind of confrontation between hostility and synergy.

Alex Rampell

But the bottom line is that I think supply aggregation has become much less valuable than it used to be. It used to be very important because human attention was limited, and now supply aggregation is much less valuable because human attention can be automated.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes.

Alex Rampell

It was a great conversation. Thank you again for coming today.

Jean-Denis Greze

Yes, thank you very much, Alex. It’s always nice to chat. Thank you.

来源：YouTube

item.title: Apollo’s Yahoo Playbook, 5 Years After the $5B Deal
item.description: Lanzone says Apollo has largely recovered its $4.8 billion Yahoo cost through early cash returns and disposals including AOL. The reset shut loss-making ad tech that cost hundreds of millions annually and opened inventory to competing demand, while retaining DSP. Scout restores owned search, but Lanzone makes no IPO commitment and hesitates to call Yahoo’s audience distribution a moat.
item.content:encoded:
Sourcery · Jim Lanzone、Molly O'Shea · 2026-10-19 · 56 min · 原语言 EN

Lanzone says Apollo has largely recovered its $4.8 billion Yahoo cost through early cash returns and disposals including AOL. The reset shut loss-making ad tech that cost hundreds of millions annually and opened inventory to competing demand, while retaining DSP. Scout restores owned search, but Lanzone makes no IPO commitment and hesitates to call Yahoo’s audience distribution a moat.

TL;DR

  • Lanzone says Apollo has largely recovered its Yahoo acquisition cost while retaining exposure to a growth comeback. The $4.8 billion transaction left Verizon with 10%; early cash returns and disposals including AOL helped make it “one of the fastest returning deals in the history of Apollo.” Yahoo is now “playing with house money,” in his framing.
  • The ad tech reset improved economics through both cost removal and better monetization of Yahoo’s inventory. Inherited businesses lost money and cost hundreds of millions of dollars annually to operate, while restricting access to competing advertising demand. Management let go of over 2,000 people in February 2023, shut the SSP, sold the native business to Taboola for a 25% stake and retained the DSP as a “crown jewel.”
  • Yahoo’s direct, logged-in audience is the asset supporting its advertising and AI ambitions. Sports and Finance each exceed 100 million monthly users within a 700 million-user portfolio; roughly 75% of users arrive directly, and around 75% are logged in on a given day. Lanzone says first-party data helps the DSP win nine out of 10 head-to-head tests, although he hesitates to call distribution “a moat.”
  • New products and younger users give the comeback a measurable growth case. Forty percent of College Fantasy Football users were new to Yahoo, while Yahoo Fantasy recorded its three biggest NFL days ever this year. More than half the audience is Gen Z or millennial, and Lanzone reports roughly a 31-percentage-point improvement in Gen Z “brand love” from marketing—but product repair comes before promotion.
  • Scout restores control of search by applying lightweight models to Yahoo’s proprietary data. After 17 years of outsourcing, largely to Microsoft, Yahoo grounds search history, publisher information, its knowledge graph and available user data before model processing; Scout launched using Anthropic’s Haiku. Lanzone emphasizes distinctive real-time answers and calls owning the search asset again “life-changing.”
  • Yahoo’s consumer mission gives its AI ambitions a boundary and Mail an existing foothold. Being the “trusted guide of the internet” means helping with personal goals through aggregation and useful analysis. As agents request email and calendar access, Lanzone says Yahoo already has users relying on its products for those things and an obligation to help—while conceding its favorable reception partly reflects that “we’re not building a large language model.”
  • Lanzone says private-equity investors expect an outcome, but makes no IPO commitment or market-timing call. He corrects O’Shea’s listing assumption and says some search startups commanded valuations six times Yahoo’s despite its existing audience, revenue and profitability. Asked when the cycle breaks, his answer is “if I only knew”; his conviction concerns Yahoo’s resilience.

Digest

1. Apollo bought Yahoo; Verizon had combined it with AOL

  • Lanzone puts Apollo’s purchase of Yahoo at $4.8 billion, with Verizon retaining 10%. Verizon had previously bought AOL and then Yahoo, merging them; Lanzone says the combined assets had been bought for about twice what Apollo paid. Under Verizon, their mission shifted toward supporting 5G. The September 2021 closing created a “five-year-old company managing a 30-year-old brand”: a new operating company with room to reset its priorities.
  • O’Shea distinguishes this deal from a conventional asset-stripping turnaround. Lanzone says Apollo saw “asymmetric upside” and recruited a growth team that would not have joined for a purely defensive mandate. “I only do the turnarounds to get to the fun part”—investing and building for the inherited audience. He describes private equity as seeking an outcome such as an IPO or sale.
  • His first six months focused on evaluating people and learning where internal data contradicted outside perceptions. “I don’t come in guns blazing on day one.” Prior turnarounds supplied the template: Ask Jeeves’ stock rose 50-fold before its IAC sale, while CBS Interactive’s audience grew from 70 million to 220 million. Yahoo already had the hardest asset to acquire: traffic.

2. Decentralization and a restored mission narrowed the portfolio

  • Yahoo competes in separate markets—Finance against Bloomberg/CNBC, Sports against ESPN, Mail against Gmail—but inherited one product chief, one technology chief and one content chief spanning the brands. Lanzone had made a related mistake at CBS Interactive: “I tried to have everything report to me.” His enthusiasm for the products had become an operating bottleneck.
  • The 2022 reorganization installed entrepreneurial general managers with dedicated product, technology and content leadership, plus assigned commercial support. Some leaders came from inside; others were specialists hired externally. The CEO’s job became shaping plans, holding managers accountable and helping them execute, while allowing the businesses to move independently.
  • The historical warning is search. Yahoo’s “original sin,” Lanzone argues, was ultimately giving search to Google in June 2000 after it had outsourced the service to Inktomi and others. With no business model yet, search looked like a cost center, even though he thinks 92% of internet sessions began there. Saving money on something treated as noncore ultimately surrendered a central capability.
  • Returning to the 1995 mission—being the “trusted guide of the internet”—meant helping consumers accomplish personal goals, from visiting the Taj Mahal to beating UCLA friends at fantasy. He rules out becoming an enterprise/B2B company. Aggregation and “content that provides context,” including fantasy and market analysis, fit; White House correspondents and TechCrunch did not. Private ownership gave Yahoo room to make those changes.

3. Ad tech restructuring removed losses and opened up yield

  • EdgeCast, a content-delivery network competing with Akamai, was the first disposal: Yahoo lacked a “right to operate” there. TechCrunch also went, and AOL—the largest divestiture—was sold in October of the previous year.
  • Yahoo and AOL had each acquired 30-plus ad tech companies, leaving a “three-legged stool” of SSP, DSP and native advertising. It lost money, with operating costs amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars annually. Worse, Yahoo’s own inventory only took ads from that business, limiting its ability to accept competing demand and optimize yield. Restructuring therefore addressed both direct losses and revenue constrained by internal preferential treatment.
  • In February 2023, Yahoo let go of over 2,000 people. It shut the SSP despite buyer interest because it wanted to avoid giving anyone preferential treatment on Yahoo pages. The native business went to Taboola for a 25% stake in that company. The DSP stayed: management identified a “crown jewel” worth investing in.

4. Product repairs earned the right to launch new bets

  • “You can’t skip levels of the video game,” Lanzone tells the team. Some products had not really been improved in 10 years; hiring strong product people and repairing those experiences came first. Every general manager has founded a company at least once. New launches and brand investment are the rewards for getting that operating foundation working.
  • Product judgment starts with data, but cannot end in endless experiments. His UCLA friends’ fantasy-product complaints are useful inputs, not necessarily representative problems. Yahoo can A/B test at enormous scale and use AI to experiment faster; teams still need conviction. He thinks teams can become too cautious when they want “200 tests at one time.”
  • College Fantasy Football supplied a concrete acquisition result: 40% of its users were new to Yahoo. Separately, Yahoo Fantasy logged its three biggest NFL days ever this year. Those results illustrate what he wants from the turnaround: use existing distribution to build something new that expands the audience.
  • The brand also skews younger than its reputation suggests: over 50% of the audience is Gen Z or millennial, and 75% of Gen Z uses Yahoo or one of its products. Lanzone reports roughly a 31-percentage-point lift in Gen Z “brand love” from marketing, including the Cardi B campaign. He sees substantial “latent brand love” to reactivate.

5. Direct relationships make the audience more valuable than its size

  • Yahoo Sports and Yahoo Finance each exceed 100 million monthly users; one-third of Americans have a Yahoo Mail account. Across the portfolio, Yahoo reaches 700 million users monthly and ranks in the US top five, usually also the global top five. News remains a top-three aggregator, with the strategy refocused on distributing publishers’ reporting.
  • Around 75% of users come directly to Yahoo—one of the highest percentages on the internet—and around 75% are logged in on a given day. Lanzone ties that loyalty and first-party data to advertiser performance: the DSP wins nine out of 10 head-to-head tests, he says. He nevertheless hesitates to call distribution “a moat,” because it can disappear if the products stop deserving it.
  • On trust, he concedes Yahoo’s favorable reception partly reflects that “we’re not building a large language model.” He acknowledges an earlier data issue and calls trust “yours to lose.” Mail is the “vault of your life”; agents’ requests for email and calendar access suggest an opportunity, but helping users is already Yahoo’s obligation. He describes Yahoo’s longstanding voice as irreverent, positive and tongue-in-cheek, and says its marketing should make people laugh or be different rather than try to make them cry.

6. Scout turns proprietary data into a strategically owned search product

  • Launched earlier this year, Scout combines 30 years of search history, publisher relationships, a knowledge graph and user data where available. Yahoo remains the third-ranked US search engine, Lanzone says. Yahoo grounds the inputs, sends them to a lightweight model—Anthropic’s Haiku at launch, with other models used today—and renders the returned answer itself. His claim is that Yahoo’s data creates unique results.
  • Real-time information is the clearest differentiator in his account. Yahoo was less exposed to evergreen content being absorbed into language models, though he says its own content was also taken without permission. Publisher relationships are meant to reinforce referrals: “It’s our job, it’s our legacy that we send them traffic.” He wants Yahoo partnering with publishers instead of competing with them.
  • Yahoo had outsourced search for 17 years, largely to Microsoft, leaving a major product and revenue stream dependent on an outside supplier. Microsoft remains a valued partner, but owning the asset again was “life-changing.” Lanzone spent his first 10 years in search; structured answers beyond “10 blue links” also return him to a longstanding product interest.

7. Cash recovery has arrived, while the exit remains open

  • O’Shea says Apollo has received back pretty much the acquisition price; Lanzone confirms it is “one of the fastest returning deals in the history of Apollo.” He credits early cash-return features of the deal and disposals including AOL, rather than pressure to repay quickly. “We are playing with house money now” frames the remaining upside.
  • He corrects O’Shea’s assumption that the goal is necessarily an IPO: Yahoo resembles a “later stage pre-IPO Silicon Valley company,” whose investors expect an outcome. An IPO or sale remains possible; he gives no IPO date or confirmation it will happen. Revenue and profitability are “both really good,” he says, but discloses no figures and suggests growth may surprise people.
  • Acquisition discipline reflects startup pricing. Some companies valued above Yahoo have less than one-tenth of 1% of its users; some search startups were valued at six times Yahoo, he says. He says Yahoo cannot merge with a company whose user base is in the billions when Yahoo would bring all the value. The company has bought smaller startups whose products were useful and whose people proved exceptional—more than pure acqui-hires.
  • Asked when the market pops, his answer is “if I only knew.” He argues repeated crash calls since the mid-2010s encouraged conservatism that could have been costly. Yahoo has endured multiple downturns, and he expects it to withstand another. He would welcome a golden age lasting 50 years, but says “we’ll be okay if we’re not.”

8. Experience helps when leaders keep changing the product

  • The most persistent pushback comes from established users: “they don’t want you to move their cheese.” UI changes can drive departures even when the destination offers similar features. Yet preserving the old interface indefinitely would mean losing tomorrow’s users. Lanzone treats that tension as unavoidable, particularly in fantasy sports.
  • At scale, the danger is “falling asleep at the wheel”: conservative managers lose product focus while startups move ahead. The decisive mistakes may be invisible externally—a company not bought, a feature not launched or an asset sold. His preferred operating posture is “only the paranoid survive,” with product-driven leaders continually taking chances for users.
  • IAC supplied a warning about centralization. With 60 brands lacking common infrastructure, Barry Diller tried to create a shared operating structure that Lanzone says Diller later regretted. The 2008 dispute with John Malone triggered breakups and changed the rationale for owning Ask; search was shut down and outsourced to Google. Lanzone admired Diller’s boldness and originality while experiencing the consequences of that structural shift.
  • Tinder reinforced how misleading outside perceptions can be. Lanzone kept its inherited management team, whose mission was “helping people find their person,” despite the hookup-app label. He says he would not have left except for Yahoo: a 2010 tweet had already called it “the ultimate turnaround.” The conviction that Yahoo deserved great products preceded the opportunity to run it.

Full transcript

Speaker 0 Apollo has been one of the most prolific deal makers of 2021.

Speaker 1 Private equity powerhouse.

Speaker 0 Apollo would be acquiring Yahoo from Verizon for $5 billion.

Speaker 2 Yahoo is one of the most iconic brands in internet history.

Speaker 1 This is a legacy brand.

Speaker 2 The original sin of Yahoo was giving search away to Google in June 2000. There’s this myth on the internet that they were defeated by Google because they took their eye off the ball or whatever. It was worse than that. They outsourced it. Yahoo hadn’t had its own search engine in 17 years.

Speaker 3 So where does most of the audience come from?

Jim Lanzone Yahoo Sports has over 100 million users a month. Yahoo Finance has over 100 million users a month. Yahoo Mail—one-third of all Americans have a Yahoo Mail account. All those things fit together and add up to 700 million users a month. There are companies valued more than us that have less than 0.1% of our user base.

I really believe that the best days of Yahoo can be ahead of it. I think now we’re in a comeback phase.

Molly O'Shea Jim Lanzone, welcome to Sorcery.

Jim Lanzone Awesome to be here, Molly.

Molly O'Shea Well, I know you’re traveling all around the world.

Jim Lanzone Totally.

Molly O'Shea So, thanks—

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea —for making the stopover here in L.A.

Jim Lanzone I know. We made it work.

Molly O'Shea So you’re here for the Snap board meeting?

Jim Lanzone Yep, that was why I was in town for this. I came straight from Aspen at the Forbes CMO conference, and I’m on my way to Amsterdam next week for HumanX. This is just that time of year.

Molly O'Shea Oh my gosh.

Jim Lanzone Back out of the summer, right into it.

Molly O'Shea I understand.

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea It’s like back to school.

Jim Lanzone Yep, 100%.

Molly O'Shea Well, I’m so excited to talk today about everything Yahoo and the legend behind Jim Lanzone.

Jim Lanzone Oh, jeez.

Molly O'Shea Because there’s a lot. There’s a lot going on there.

Jim Lanzone Oh, okay.

Molly O'Shea But I think it would be great to start off with Yahoo, because Yahoo’s on a tear. So, back in 2021—

Jim Lanzone Yep.

Molly O'Shea —that’s when Apollo bought Yahoo from Verizon, and Verizon sold off a couple of assets. It was AOL and Yahoo. So that was around $4.5—

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea —about $5 billion.

Jim Lanzone A little more—$4.8 billion.

Molly O'Shea Okay.

Jim Lanzone Yeah.

Molly O'Shea So, nearly $5 billion. You bought the assets. Could you walk me through that? What was that process like?

Jim Lanzone At the time, I was somebody they called during the process of deciding to buy the company. I wasn’t part of Apollo then. I left another job to come do this, which we can talk about—why I did that.

The history was that Verizon, under different leadership, had bought AOL and then, a few years later, Yahoo. They merged them into one company, first called Oath. They then changed that name to Verizon Media, but it was all those assets under one roof. The new Verizon management team decided they didn’t want to be in that business anymore. I think it took them a few years to find the right buyer at the right price, but Reed Raymond from Apollo, one of the leaders of their private equity group, got in there and figured out how to construct a deal that would work.

Molly O'Shea So what was the construction of the deal?

Jim Lanzone It was about getting the right framework for Verizon, because they wanted to maintain some ownership, which they did. They still own 10% of us. Then there was having a vision for what this thing could be going forward.

I think combined, they were bought for about twice what we bought it for. During that time, they’d had a different mission than I think either company had ever had before. It was really to help Verizon grow 5G and be a part of that. A lot of the decisions were based on that, and not really on the real mission of what Yahoo itself was about.

The company that was set up was a brand-new company. We’re a 5-year-old company managing a 30-year-old brand at this point. It was a completely new company, stood up from scratch to house these brands under one roof. They bought it in May 2021, and it closed in September 2021. I started around the end of September 2021, so it’s been almost exactly 5 years for me.

Molly O'Shea Well, congrats.

Jim Lanzone Yeah. We made it.

Molly O'Shea So this isn’t your first turnaround. When you came in, where did you come from? What were your first couple of steps for the next 6 months or so?

Jim Lanzone It was the middle of COVID. September 2021, if anybody remembers, was when I think the Delta variant was starting. We still didn’t meet people in the office for a while after that, and the decisions were, “If you come in, do you have to be vaccinated?” That’s what that time frame was like, so it was kind of a weird time to pick up a company.

I had just done it a year earlier with Tinder. I had worked for the IAC family before they bought our company in 2005. That’s how far back I go. Those same people brought me back for that job, again in the middle of COVID. That was July 2020, so it was an even more difficult time to pick up a company because we really never met anybody for that year. Here, we were back to work pretty quickly after that.

For me, this was actually the third time I was going in to lead a turnaround. The first was Ask Jeeves, which is kind of the poster child for the Web 1.0 crash. However difficult this one would be, nothing would be harder than turning that brand and those products around at that time. I think I was announced on 9/11. I think that was actually my first day on the job.

They had bought the ’90s startup I was part of, where I was one of the founders. I joined there as one of the heads of product and, over time, worked my way up to CEO. We 50x’d that stock and sold it to IAC and Barry Diller. I stayed for another 3 years as CEO, then left to do another startup. That was bought by CBS, the television company.

I joined as the CEO of their internet group, which had bought multiple public companies over time that just weren’t performing at their best. That was turnaround number 2. I think that’s still the sixth-largest internet company by unique users. I think we went from 70 to 220 million users with those properties.

I’d been through big internet turnarounds before. Yahoo was one that I knew had great bones for a great turnaround. It had the thing that was hardest to get, which is traffic. It had a lot of traffic, but the products had seen better days. Coming out of years at Verizon, the company structure and composition were not optimal. But those are things you can work with.

The first 6 months were from the playbook I’d run before: evaluate the team. I don’t come in guns blazing on day one. I get in there and get to know everybody. There are always great people wherever you go, and there are always things you don’t understand from the outside. Until you’re inside running a company, it’s never exactly what you’d think. The data will tell you differently how the products work, who the audience is, all those kinds of things. Those first 6 months are really about getting to know it, and then that leads into all the different steps of a turnaround that come after.

Molly O'Shea I think this is interesting because there are so many different angles to this. I just had a conversation with Bending Spoons, which is the opposite of a PE playbook, but this also isn’t really a traditional PE turnaround because you’re leading the way. It’s not like a private equity company is coming in and just stripping out as much as they can, but you’re really ushering this. So talk about how that’s different for you and maybe the traditional Apollo PE playbook.

Jim Lanzone It’s interesting because I still have people ask me, “What’s it like working for private equity?” The reputation isn’t always great for how they’re going to manage these things, but I’ve had the opposite experience. Reed and I still talk almost every day in some form, 5 years later. He was wearing a “Make Yahoo! Great Again” purple hat around.

PE is in it for a reason. They want an outcome, whether that’s an IPO or a sale. They’re not here to hold it forever, to be Stripe and just never have—

Molly O'Shea Yeah.

Jim Lanzone —an outcome of some kind. At the same time, there aren’t that many companies they view as having asymmetric upside relative to others, where you just run the PE playbook. They hired a team, starting with me, who wouldn’t be here if they did that. I’m a growth person. I only do the turnarounds to get to the fun part, which is when you get to start putting irons in the fire for growth, reap the benefits of the turnaround, and start investing and building new things for the huge audience you inherited.

Jim Lanzone Um, that really is how Apollo was treated the whole time. I’ve had to work for many different kinds of people, including venture capitalists. At my first startup, I’d never had a real job before; at my second, Bill Gurley and Jeff Yang were my 2 main investors. I’ve also worked for Barry Diller and Les Moonves. Everybody has to serve somebody, and I haven’t found private equity—at least with my Apollo team—to be a particularly difficult force to reckon with compared with other people I’ve had to work for.

Molly O'Shea So what are the main questions you start asking once you get into the company?

Jim Lanzone There are a couple of things. One is that Yahoo, in particular, is a conglomerate. It’s not one brand. If you look at other companies around our size in the industry—Pinterest, Snap, Reddit, Roku—they’re mostly one-product companies. Yahoo is a conglomerate of many different brands that compete independently in their spaces.

Yahoo Finance competes with Bloomberg, CNBC, and maybe The Wall Street Journal. We have a new product that competes with TradingView and others in that space. Yahoo Sports competes with ESPN and others like that. Yahoo Mail competes with Gmail. They all have very different competitors, and that creates this ecosystem of brands.

That’s not the first time I’ve seen that. IAC had 60-plus brands, and with Ask, we joined that family. CBS Interactive had 30-plus brands, many of which had nothing to do with CBS. CNET was the leading technology site. SportsLine was one of the OGs in sports and fantasy sports. Last.fm was in music. You go down the list: GameSpot in video games. We had all kinds of different brands, and we had to figure out the right structure for them.

I did it wrong at CBS Interactive the first time. I tried to have everything report to me. My background is all product, and I was a pig in slop with these brands, many of which I was a user of. It turned out I was just going to slow things down; we needed to move much faster. I had to hire general managers who could be entrepreneurial and independent. My job was to work with them on their plans, hold them accountable, help where I could, and let them run.

It was interesting when we got here. Whatever had happened through the years at Verizon, the company had evolved into one with a single head of product, one head of technology, and one head of content across all the brands. There were people and engineering teams who specialized, but they were spread across them. So the first thing we did was reorganize the company into more of a conglomerate structure, with GMs in all these groups.

That means each group gets its own head of product, technology, and content. Even for central functions, they’ll usually have their own head of sales, marketing, PR, and business development. Those people will be assigned to those divisions. We had to put that structure in place, and then I had to hire for it. Some of those people were great internal candidates who were going to be part of it. For some roles, I had to go get true experts who were badasses in their fields.

That’s what we did. We started putting that team together, and that was really the 2022 timeframe. The next step, once you have that team and understand what you’re doing, is to ask: Are we doing all the right things? Do we need to reduce our focus? Are there things we should spin off? Where are we off the mission of the company?

The mission also had to be reinstituted. If you go way back, the original sin of Yahoo was giving search away to Google in June of 2000. There’s this myth on the internet that Yahoo was defeated by Google because it took its eye off the ball or whatever. It was worse than that: Yahoo outsourced search—

Molly O'Shea

What?

Jim Lanzone

—first to a company called Inktomi, and there were actually others before that. Then the market crash happened, and to get a better deal and save money on something viewed as a cost center, Yahoo gave it away. Search was viewed as a utility that wasn’t core, even though 92% of all sessions on the internet at that point, I think, started with search. One reason was that there was no business model yet. What became Overture, and then AdWords and AdSense for Google, didn’t exist.

All the search engines—and there were 10-plus of them that were public companies, including Ask—had banner ads everywhere on their search results pages. Just imagine how bad that was. It came from the right place; it just wound up being something really hard to recover from.

Generations of Yahoo started to figure out other ways forward. In the 2000s, while they did some very interesting things in search and other places, they made forays into Hollywood. They had Yahoo Music and TV, and all kinds of other things. They hired a lot of people from Hollywood. There were then a series of different CEOs. In the 2010s, they went back at Google and tried to go that way, and then eventually sold to Verizon.

The mission of the company was to help Verizon with its mission. It turned out that underneath all that, the reason Yahoo continued to be successful all those years, with its huge audience, was the places where it was still fulfilling the original mission Jerry Yang and David Filo had in 1995: being the trusted guide to the internet, helping people through the Wild West the internet had become and helping them get things done.

In Yahoo Finance, Sports, News, Mail, and different parts of Search and Weather, and in all these places where we still had leading brands, that’s what the company was doing. So we had the benefit in 2022 and 2023 of focusing on the things Yahoo was doing well. We didn’t have the burden, first of all, of being a struggling public company. It’s very difficult to make those changes in public. And second, we could focus on the things we did really well, where we were already successful. That’s where our focus went during that timeframe, which meant we spun a lot of things out or shut—

Jim Lanzone

—or shut them down.

Jim Lanzone

That's art and science. It starts with data and understanding your user base, which you never really understand from the outside. I have a bunch of college friends from UCLA, and to help me get to know this college product, I got a bunch of them on it. They beat me up all day long for things they're finding in the product. When I then go talk to the actual product team on the sports team about what's driving things behind the scenes, whether something's really wrong or it's just one person's opinion, it's different.

Take search, where what happens on the other side of that search box is so complicated, especially now with AI, but even going back to the old days of 10 blue links. You enter that query, but what we have to do on the other side to capture that and understand what to do with it is incredibly complicated. How to do that for hundreds of millions of people and move the needle forward is different from what it might be for one user. Data is going to lead you forward.

After that, it's creativity and people who have a sensibility for users. One benefit of having a huge audience is that you can A/B test your way to things. You can have a hunch, and especially now with AI, we can experiment even more. I do think product teams can get a little too addicted to that or become too cautious and want to do 200 tests at one time. You can't do that. You have to have some passion for what you think the product should be and lead with that.

Yahoo had something I experienced at prior companies: this huge audience. That's so hard to get. If you look at the top internet companies in Comscore or Similarweb, it's incredible how many are from the '90s. It's amazing how many are from the early 2000s: YouTube and Facebook. That’s different from trying to light the wet log from scratch, which is what entrepreneurs have to do.

That’s why so many of the biggest consumer internet companies happened by accident. They really weren’t the thing they intended to be a lot of the time. We have a great platform to build great products on. We’re lucky to have that.

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

Perplexity isn’t its own large language model. They were doing metasearch on the others, which has happened before. The others are all large language models: Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude.

Ours is a product based on our own data. There was so much interesting data, which is another asset. I’ll put “moat” in quotes because I’m always paranoid about it—you can’t rest easy with this. But it’s an asset: hundreds of millions of users a month over 30 years, and we’re still the third-ranked search engine in the U.S. We have 30 years of search history. Even though we’re much smaller, that’s still a ton of search history.

Our publisher relationships are another way we’ve taken the company back. Instead of competing with our publishers, we’re trying to make sure we partner with them. It’s our job and our legacy to send them traffic.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

We firmly believe in that. It’s part of our job in the ecosystem. Having been a partner of Yahoo’s at other companies, I can attest to how much traffic they could send us.

The way Yahoo Scout, our AI answer engine, works is that we take all that data, ground it, and send it to a lightweight model. At launch, it was Haiku from Anthropic. We use others today. They process that and send it back to us, and then we do the rendering, the formatting, the UI. What that creates is an entirely unique result that can only happen because of Yahoo data.

We’re also a top-20 publisher whose content has been taken by large language models without permission. You’ll see the Yahoo brand show up all the time in citations. For the most part, our content is real-time. We excel in categories that are real-time, so we weren’t as susceptible to the evergreen content that large language models photocopied and took with them. Especially in certain categories that are more real-time, our results are awesome and totally unique.

The other reason we had to do that is that for 17 years, we were outsourcing search largely to Microsoft, with whom we’re still great partners. For us, it went back to the thing that can feel like the cheesier side of this job: the mission. It really mattered here, and I took my time with it. I rolled out a brand-new mission for the company with a 45-minute-to-an-hour-long presentation. It was actually much longer for the management team at my team offsite. What do you think are the biggest mistakes companies make at scale?

Jim Lanzone

Probably falling asleep at the wheel and becoming really conservative. People who’ve succeeded by climbing the company ladder—some of whom are probably great—tend to lead to a certain kind of management, based on what those people have been rewarded for over time. If they’re not product-driven leaders, honestly, in our space, it tends not to work.

In our space, you tend to lose sight really fast of what matters. Sometimes it’s the things an executive team misses: the chances they didn’t take, the company they didn’t buy, maybe the thing they sold, or a deal they did that they might not have done if a different set of leaders had been in place. Those wind up being the things that make a huge difference. The problem is that you’d never know from the outside, because you weren’t a part of it. You don’t know what was on the table and what wasn’t.

But you’ll start to see things catch up to them, especially on product. They’ll get beaten by a startup with something they didn’t launch, or something they didn’t get out ahead of. I just think product-driven companies, where you follow “Only the Paranoid Survive” and you’re going 100 miles an hour, seven days a week, trying to crush it for your users, are the only way to make this work.

Molly O'Shea

Are you worried at all about any startups? Are you pinching yourself or kicking yourself over any acquisitions you didn’t make?

Jim Lanzone

Here’s what I’ll say: no, because startups right now are so highly valued.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

There are companies valued more than us that have less than one-tenth of 1% of our user base. I was seeing that early on. Search companies that launched were being valued at six times what we were, even though we already had a lot of searches and search users, as well as our overall user base, revenue, and profitability.

It is funny. We’ve been at a moment in time when those things have been really expensive. I’ve benefited, and I was one of these a long time ago. My ’90s startup, which I was one of the founders of, didn’t work out. We were writing our S-1, and the market crashed, and we crashed. We went on fumes until Ask Jeeves bought us.

But a bunch of us went over in the acquisition, and we were really important to that turnaround.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

We’ve actually bought a few startups where they weren’t pure acqui-hires. We used the product, but the people we brought in were incredible and have been leading the charge on some of the most important things we’ve been building. We’ve been able to be active that way, but are we going to do a merger with somebody who has a base in the billions when we bring all the value? We can’t do it.

I don’t know that we’ve really had the opportunity to buy anything we would’ve missed, but there are a lot of things out there that I think are really interesting in search, agents, fantasy, and finance. Our Slack channels are very active every day with things we’re all looking at and playing with.

Molly O'Shea

I would imagine. It’s super exciting.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, yeah. We compete in so many areas that—

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

—it’s almost hard to keep up with it. But that’s why we have great leaders across the business.

Molly O'Shea

Because you’ve seen so many market cycles, when do you think this one pops?

Jim Lanzone

Damn, if I only knew. It’s funny, though. If you go back to the mid-teens, that’s how many times people have called it, and people have gotten really conservative, thinking the market was about to crash, but it has continued to go up. If you tried to take your chips off the table at any point, it would’ve been a huge mistake.

I’ve been through how many crashes? The first one was the global financial crisis, then COVID, then there was a mini-crash in 2022. On the other side of COVID, pretty much right after I started here, we went right into that one. Even now, with the war and certain things, and tariffs last year, there have always been curveballs thrown at you.

This is another place where Yahoo excels: we’re a very resilient company. I always say that if we were able to survive before we had a team like this building the things we’re building and growing the way we’re growing, we’re going to be okay now. We’re in a great spot to survive if something like that happens. I’m in no way rooting for it. I’d love it if we were in some golden age that lasted 50 years, but we’ll be okay if we’re not.

Molly O'Shea

Speaker 1

Founders scale faster on Deel. Set up payroll for any country in minutes. Hire anyone anywhere, get visas handled fast, and get back to building. Visit deel.com/sorcery. That's D-E-E-L.com/sorcery

Molly O'Shea

I know we started this and I said, “I want to know about the Jim Lanzone lore.” You mentioned so many people you’ve worked with and worked for. Maybe we can go back to Barry Diller and what it was like working with him. What is it like working with Barry Diller? When we talked a couple of months ago, right after the Dara interview, you also mentioned Dara. It’d be great to get into that a little bit and know what you’ve learned.

Jim Lanzone

John Foley, who founded Peloton, was one of the people at IAC. He called me a journeyman at a conference we were at together, and he meant it as a compliment. He said, “You’ve been in so many different places and seen so many things.” It’s true. I’ve been around a long time and have been part of all these different regimes and companies.

If you’re not naturally good at this stuff, experience probably doesn’t help. But if you have experience, it can help a lot, and the people you’ve worked for are a big part of that. It was a really interesting time at IAC. Dara left right when I joined.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

He left to do Expedia when it spun out, pretty much right as I joined. I had a great first couple of years with Barry. He was extremely intense. Again, this was 20 years ago.

Molly O'Shea

Yeah.

Jim Lanzone

It was very different from the IAC that Joey took over and ran later. We had 60 brands at that point, and they went through something Barry later said he regretted: trying to turn into an operating company.

Molly O'Shea

Mm.

Jim Lanzone

Jack Welch was one of his main advisers at the time. Somehow, the decision was made to take these 60 brands that had nothing to do with each other and no common infrastructure, reverse that out, and give them a common central structure. That just wasn’t easy at IAC, given the way it was put together.

Then Barry and John Malone got into it in 2008, and that led to the breakup of a lot of the IAC brands. It really changed the rationale for why they bought Ask. We shut down search, outsourced it to Google, and that was how I wound up leaving. But Barry’s such an original thinker. I still don’t think there’s anybody who’s a better interview. When you see him on stage or on CNBC, his language is so unique to him. He’s so smart and so bold in the things he does.

I loved working with him. Steve Berkowitz, who was probably the biggest mentor I’ve ever had in this space, was the CEO of Ask Jeeves when we were bought by IAC. That turnaround was so respected that Steve was poached by Microsoft to run all of its internet business. Satya reported to him.

Molly O'Shea

Wow.

Jim Lanzone

I remember, as Steve was leaving, Barry and I had tussled over something, and Steve said, “You guys are just so much alike.” I thought, “Huh.” I wouldn’t have thought that. I was the Silicon Valley internet guy, but he’s very entrepreneurial, and I’m still inspired by him. I loved his book last year and told him that. It was an amazing experience.

The CBS years were great, too. The stock had gotten down to $3 a share a couple of years before I joined, and it went back up to almost $80. I was the Silicon Valley guy going to a place where they had to wear suits. I was told that because I was the internet guy, I didn’t have to wear a tie. They were number one 13 years in a row, and the stock was a juggernaut and always delivered.

If we’re lucky enough to be a public company again, I learned so much from being part of those public companies: how they were managed, how those teams were run, what made them special, and what made them work. I can take that with me.

Molly O'Shea

So what was Tinder like?

Jim Lanzone

Short, and during COVID. Those COVID times were difficult. I loved the team. I didn’t change one person on that team. I loved the management team I inherited, and I loved the fact that Tinder was viewed one way from the outside, but on the inside, you’d never met a team of people more passionate about the mission of helping people find their person. It was always perceived by others as a hookup app or whatever, but that’s not how the team internally viewed it.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

They were also very proud of being a source of diverse relationships. I think 40% of all marriages started online, and Tinder was 25% of those. That means almost 10% of all marriages in the United States were started on Tinder. The people there are very passionate about that.

I never would’ve left. It’s the only time I’ve ever left a job. Everywhere else, I stayed for a long time.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

Someone found a tweet I posted in 2010 where I said this was the ultimate turnaround, and these were the best assets for it. There was something about it I always wanted a crack at. I was always very passionate that Yahoo deserved to be treated right, to have great products again, and to put that brand back on the map the right way.

Maybe it was just part of me being part of startups and then turnarounds. I just always wanted to take a crack at that, you know? So here we are five years later. Yeah.

Molly O'Shea

Is there anything we haven't covered yet that you'd want to go over?

Jim Lanzone

I know we'll see it in the comments.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

And I'll go, I'll call and answer.

Molly O'Shea

Okay.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, I think a lot of it is still things that we can't even talk about. We have a lot of awesome stuff we're cooking up in the labs.

Molly O'Shea

What's the biggest secret you can tell us?

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, no. I don't have an IPO date, or whether it's happening or not. I always am trying to keep the things that we're building a secret until we launch them.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

We have some really interesting things that we're working on. I really believe that this is one of those times when the best days of Yahoo can really be ahead of it.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

It took a lot to get it to this spot, but we are jamming now. I think people really have an open mind to us as a brand again, which has just been really gratifying. We don't take that for granted. We want to deliver on it, so onwards.

Molly O'Shea

Amazing. I mean, I was gonna close out and ask: what are you most looking forward to in the next 12 months?

Jim Lanzone

Yeah, I can't tell you.

Molly O'Shea

Can't tell you. It's a secret.

Jim Lanzone

Yeah. But there's some really great stuff, and it's just our team. I love our team. It's one of those jobs where I get up every day ready to go.

Molly O'Shea

Mm-hmm.

Jim Lanzone

There's just not one day where I'm dreading it. It's just, let's go.

Molly O'Shea

Awesome. Well, Jim, thank you so much—

Jim Lanzone

All right. Thanks for having me.

Molly O'Shea

—for taking the time. This was so much fun.

Jim Lanzone

Okay, good.

Molly O'Shea

Awesome. Thank you.

Jim Lanzone

Thanks, Molly.

Molly O'Shea
