Of course, I’ve been trading options since I was 18. I’ve been a very active participant in the markets for a long time. I think we’re so far from where we should be, and I think it’s incredibly destructive for young people.

Sometimes I hear Haralabob on the podcast talking about all the money he’s made betting on sports, and then he talks about how terrible it is. There’s this weird situation where you’ve made a ton of money and now you’re climbing the ladder. I understand the idea, but I think it’s just terrible.

I think this amount of apathy and lack of desire to create anything is really bad. Creation is one of the most important things for humans, and hypergambling is simply not like that.

Speaker 1 By the way, without attacking, are you creating anything? Simply put, you’re just an investor. You invest in public or private markets. Is there a desire to create? That’s what I’m trying to get at, not as an attack. The point is, where do we draw the line? Prediction gambling is definitely bad, you would say?

Michael Dempsey Yes.

Speaker 1 Prediction markets are probably bad.

Speaker 1 Robinhood’s zero-day options are probably bad.

Michael Dempsey Yes.

Speaker 1 Robinhood options are good. So where do we draw the line?

Michael Dempsey I think that part of creation is actually more about human fulfillment. I write a lot, take a lot of photos, and paint poorly. I do a lot of things that are acts of creation, more about how you get the things floating around in your head and your heart out into the world.

And of course, children are the ultimate act of creation, I could say. This is kind of a separate thing: I think it’s really important to think of life as something long, in a sense, and to think of it as a craft that you’re constantly working on, with some kind of complex effect on it. The moment you lose that, you lose so many of the fundamental pillars of society. It becomes really bad, and you get the apathy and nihilism that we see.

With hypergambling, it doesn’t even bother me that there’s no creation. It’s just so short-term-oriented, and you don’t really put any effort into it in the normal way. Again, you could say being in the Pump.fun trenches is a huge effort, and honestly, I would never want to do it. I can’t do it. I think it’s terrible, but I think it takes a lot of effort. I think it’s kind of lacking in intellect.

It’s funny how we can come to terms with this, and then these same people can think that using AI models will destroy our brains and we’ll lose the ability to think. Maybe Pump.fun actually damages your brain 100 times more than using ChatGPT every day. So I still think both are probably not great.

Speaker 1 Are you interested in investing in companies that fall into this category? Would you go long on Robinhood or buy the Pump.fun token?

Michael Dempsey No. No.

Speaker 1 You wouldn’t do that?

Michael Dempsey Yes. I don’t. I think Robinhood is—personally, I disagree with how they’ve advertised to their users throughout the history of the company.

Speaker 1 Gamified investing?

Michael Dempsey Yes. And also how they use push notifications to attract and trigger a range of behaviors. I think this is very bad.

Has Tech Lost Its Soul?

Speaker 1 Interesting. You should see the Figma notifications we receive. Tell me about this idea of romanticism.

Michael Dempsey Yes.

Speaker 1 In building a company. You mentioned Dylan from Figma. You said he had a romantic streak in building his company. I saw you tweeting about losing the sense of romance and humanity in building a company. Why are you thinking about this?

Michael Dempsey I think it’s really important to see life not as a problem to be solved, but as an experience to be felt and gone through. There are a lot of words for this, but “romance” is probably one of the better ones, simply because everyone knows the realm of feelings they’re in.

In romance, in its simplest sense, the clearest fact is that it leads to pseudo-rationality. I think this pseudo-rationality for something deeply felt is actually quite good in the world. You have to balance it, right? I’m talking about Dylan from Figma, and I don’t know him personally, but I think it says a lot about the fact that creativity and design matter, and designers matter, and so on.

That’s really great, but the problem is that on that same earnings conference call, the next person who speaks up is their CFO, who says that the number of engineering positions has doubled compared to the quarter, and starts talking about these things. You don’t want to feel like companies have a mismatched level of romanticism in their management team, because it causes a lot of problems, especially in founder-led companies. Typically, founders are basically dictators of their organizations.

On a life level, without the craziness going on around us, our lives are undoubtedly on a great trajectory, right? We have many amazing things every day. Sometimes we just can’t get out of each other’s way. I think the concept of romanticism eliminates that hyperoptimization. You don’t do something because it’s maximally a first-principles reason to do it. You do it because it creates some feeling that you know is either right or something you want to chase.

If everyone had a little more of that, we could have a little more humanity injected into the way we think about these things. I think we’ve lost that, and I think that’s one of the factors that supports your argument.

Speaker 1 What if people started building companies that were more interesting or more fun, instead of thinking about how to go from zero to $100 million in ARR in the next 18 months?

Michael Dempsey Yes. I think I would change the way I think about it. I would slightly object to that: I think you’re looking at it from a very European romantic perspective, as opposed to the Gilded Age—

Speaker 1 I feel like the Gilded Age was just the pinnacle of American business.

Michael Dempsey Okay. They actually had a lot of romanticism, but it was a kind of technocratic romanticism instead of European romanticism. They felt an extreme sense of civic duty in building their companies, and I think that’s what’s missing today.

Speaker 1

I think that’s true. I don’t think Dylan’s romanticism is right, though. You’ll probably need to change this as your business grows.

Michael Dempsey

Yes. Well, I think there’s a certain civic duty that some of the Zucks, Sams, and Darios of today’s world are lacking.

Speaker 1

How Compound Finds Its Next Bets

Yes. I think it is—I would say yes, definitely. Yes, yes, yes. Well, how do you find or choose founders? Do people come to you, or are you going to them?

Michael Dempsey

Seventy percent of our investments have historically been abroad. We spend a lot of time thinking about the world, trying to understand where we think it’s going. In that time, we talk to a lot of people, write a lot, and message a lot of people. Sometimes founders come back after 2, 3, 4, or 5 years.

For example, I read the Wave founder’s PhD thesis two and a half years before he started the company, when he was still a student at Cambridge University. His name is Alex Kendall. Then I heard from another friend, who was working on autonomous vehicles at the time, that this guy from Cambridge was starting to take some pretty strange approaches to autonomous vehicles. I checked my email because I knew the name sounded familiar, revived our thread, and said, “Hey, I think you started a company. I’d love to talk.”

A lot of what we do has the advantage of operating within a five-year time horizon for funds. The optimizations we make in the moment can be so long-term that we don’t worry too much about whether I made the best use of my time this week, or whether a meeting I went to with some random researcher was the right meeting in October 2026. Should I have postponed it to December, or maybe not gone at all because I really wanted this opportunity? This gives us a sense of freedom, and I think investing is increasingly about limiting information noise and being in a state of flow.

A lot of our process is figuring out where the world is going and talking to people. We write, and that drives a lot of inbound activity. We also organize many very specific events, for example, research events on specific topics. But I think the most important thing is that we treat research as a priority in the organization, and everything flows from there.

Compound’s existential situation is that we’re an overpaid research firm, and we’re not making a fortune for investors. We just have a lot of great ideas, but we don’t implement them. The hope is that we know enough about it that we can make sure all the resources are directed towards investment. But it’s definitely possible that one day we’ll look up and see a lot of great ideas, and we haven’t made any good investments in them.

Speaker 1

What are the most interesting portfolio companies you have today?

Michael Dempsey

You can’t choose your favorite children. They’re all interesting.

Speaker 1

Okay, let me rephrase that. There’s a tweet you had about writing a book. You said someone could write a book, but it’s actually more interesting to see someone write a collection of essays, producing an essay every few months, and to see their thinking develop and the ideas swirling around in their head. So, rather than asking you to pick your favorite child, what ideas are floating around in your head right now, and what are you focusing on?

Michael Dempsey

From an investment perspective, I’d say there are many ideas about how to shape companies. The company shape I really love is when we think about these long-term types of businesses that could exist. One of the things we’ve seen from Orbital Materials in our portfolio is building new types of foundation models for chemistry or other fields of science. That’s very valuable, but what’s really interesting is what new types of products might emerge.

Orbital did it very well with the material they put into the product. The product is a modular data center, but the secret is partly in this material, which they synthesize in the lab based on an artificial intelligence model. It’s a completely new material that absorbs heat at a very, very specific temperature. They can design it to do that, which allows them to dissipate heat most efficiently at the temperature at which graphics processors operate.

Michael Dempsey In particular, a certain class of GPUs that will soon be on the market will be able to cool very efficiently. Once you get the hang of that, you can do a lot of other things designed around the set of GPUs they’re in. This is a very interesting product.

I don’t think creating material out of nowhere is interesting. That’s great for someone doing science, but not so much for someone who has to invest in companies that make money. The question becomes, “Okay, what other types of materials are there?” Many people have a basic understanding that we have a lot of bottleneck materials in the world, like rare earth elements, uranium, and all these kinds of raw materials. They know these materials are valuable because they’re heavily used, and about 90% of their supply comes from China or somewhere else. Everyone is going crazy about this.

But there are other things, too, such as products. We were talking to a company that we didn’t actually invest in, but they were essentially taking a similar approach, less computationally driven, and creating new missiles. They said, “The projectiles are very important. There’s huge demand for them, and we can synthesize the properties and create something that’s essentially one-to-one, but with much cheaper materials and all these other things. So we can scale production.” I have no desire to invest in a missile company. It’s quite an offensive technology, not a defensive one.

But this type of business, where new materials create new products, is very interesting to us. It also allows you to have greater control over your fate. I think the biggest problem with investing in high-tech companies is that at some point you become dependent on someone, and that someone can essentially determine the company’s success or failure. Space companies today are highly dependent on launch service providers. Robotics companies have historically been highly dependent on systems integrators or customers to take them from pilots to large commercial deployments. So, as long as we can control the path to market, it’s very interesting.

Well, I would say yes. And then there are the areas we’ve spent a lot of time on in biotechnology: drug discovery platforms, new treatments, laboratory automation, and software. That’s probably where we’ve invested the most. At any given time, we have a public database of theses that contains, say, 100 items. We have a private database with a lot of research that we do, and that’s probably another 200 things.

We’re still trying to figure out what the right set of ideas is that’s worth investing money in. Based on that, it usually makes sense to invest from T0 today to 24 months into the future.

Speaker 1 I think I just realized why your tweets are so interesting to me: you’re semi-pessimistic about this moment. A lot of people are pretty fed up. It’s a big bull market, a generational bull market, and everyone’s making a lot of money. But you seem quite pessimistic—maybe that’s the wrong word. I’d say you’re skeptical about this moment.

At the same time, because of the nature of your investments, you’re incredibly optimistic, because you see that one day we can cure cancer and, I don’t know, make human eggs derived from stem cells and things like that. I don’t know if that’s the right categorization, but I think I just always want people to be more nuanced. I think that’s my problem. It’s probably a lifelong problem.

Michael Dempsey It may get worse before it gets better.

Speaker 1 Yes.

Michael Dempsey Yes. I think that’s it. I just want a little more intellectual honesty. Maybe these things work, maybe they don’t. There are different branches of the tech tree and parts of the world we don’t know about. It’s okay to have a system or set of beliefs, but we don’t have to be fanatics about everything.

Speaker 1 When a company founder presents a pitch to a venture capitalist, they often shouldn’t hedge their bets. True?

Michael Dempsey I actually like it when founders are intellectually honest about risk. For example, when they understand the complexity of their company—and even better, when they understand that complexity compared to historical attempts. It shows a certain level of understanding of building a company as a craft and as a problem to solve, or as a dark forest they’re navigating. They know what that forest looks like; they just probably don’t know all the pockets.

They can still say, “I have very high confidence in solving these problems,” but I want to know they understand what they’re getting into. I find it very difficult when people talk about very complex things and act as if they’re inevitable and easy.

Speaker 1 I know you don’t want to choose portfolio companies that are your favorites, so I won’t force you to do that. But do you see any ideas now? I keep nitpicking about the first human eggs derived from stem cells, because it’s such a crazy idea. I think people are really interested in investing in things like Ramp because the user interface is really cool or something.

I don’t think people even think about it. I think it might have been you, or maybe Sam, someone on your team, who also tweeted that we’ve lost all creativity when it comes to building companies. So maybe we can use this part to inspire some creativity in building your business. What are the most interesting things you see people working on today?

Michael Dempsey I keep coming back to the biological stuff, but I’ll try to move away from that. We’re getting to a few simple heuristics: How do we make people happy? How do we make people healthy? How do we make people sustainable?

Sustainability is energy and food supply. I think mental health is part of health. Our latest investment concerns psychiatry. It’s basically psychiatry based on artificial intelligence. It’s very clear that if we could increase the number of mental health services in America 100 times, that would be a real benefit.

We spent a lot of time in this industry, and we were one of the early investors in Talkspace back in the day because they had this crazy idea of doing therapy through video and text. I think energy issues are very interesting. It’s very crowded there now, so it’s hard for us to say. I have some personal investments there, and we invested in a company called Panthelozo, which generates energy using ocean waves.

Another area we’re trying to focus on is biosecurity. It’s more interesting now, and it’s gained traction. We’ve spent a lot of time thinking about how we can make sure the problems of the next generation can be solved. These are very interesting issues, from food supply to animal health to deadly pathogens and so on.

In software, I’ve spent a lot of time over the last few years thinking that if we assume this all evolves, there will probably be new forms of businesses using local compute that will free up a lot of creative space. But I’m not smart enough yet to know what that looks like.

Speaker 1 You’ve made great investments in biotechnology. What do you think about this? I think there’s a rapidly growing consensus that the labs are going to become biotech companies, or that the labs are going to do something big with biotech.

I think that’s probably—I said this on the podcast too—that the most important thing they can do to change public sentiment from antipathy to enthusiasm is do something like, “Anthropic saves people with cancer.” What do you think? It’s a two-part question: What do you think about the labs and their biotechnology strategy? And, from a biotechnology perspective, will this be the best decade ever? Will we cure cancer? Will we find a solution to Alzheimer’s disease and things like that, or will artificial intelligence not have as much of an impact as people like to think?

Michael Dempsey I’m optimistic about this. I think it will be—I think your pithy quote to Everett is, “I think 50% of the major diseases that are killing us won’t kill us in about 20 years.” I think you and I will live to be over 120 years old. There are many things we will solve.

I don’t know if the AI labs will be directly responsible for this. I think there’s a very clear reason why, narratively, it makes sense to bring biotechnology into the labs today, especially in the context of an IPO. This is probably a much larger market than the software market. Despite SpaceX’s beautiful S-1, where they talk about the whole SaaS thing being the biggest market ever, I think it’s very likely that every single person working in biotech at Anthropic—and maybe even more so in AI—won’t be working there in five years.

The reality of what people are learning, the tacit knowledge of biotechnology, is still very real. It’s not something that can be recursively self-improved in the way people think. I think we’re going to have significant regulatory reform around all of these things, which is going to make the next wave of biotech companies very valuable and make many more resources available to solve these problems.

There are still some things I find difficult. It’s funny, if you believe it—and I’m not someone who knows enough math—but let’s be honest: how did OpenAI solve math last week? They’ve solved all the evals, they have all this stuff, and everyone looks around and thinks, “Okay, so we’ve solved it.” What does that mean? If we have these things, our understanding of mathematics is probably still orders of magnitude better than our understanding of the brain. There’s a lot of complexity in all of this.

If we can arrive at an answer rationally, we still need to know the full trace before allowing someone to inject something into their body that will affect their brain. But I think further regulatory changes are happening. The last downside to this nihilism might be that a lot of people will just say, “Screw it, I’ll do it myself,” and a large number of people will experience negative effects from their biological experiments in the next 10 years.

Speaker 1

This is already visible with peptides. People want to take them and do it themselves. They’re pretty safe, right? I have a friend who had a pretty bad reaction to peptides.

Michael Dempsey

I think they’re pretty safe, but people will keep pushing. It doesn’t end there.

Speaker 1

I saw that Eli Lilly has around 1,000 Blackwell GPUs, and they’re building their big LillyPod or something like that with Nvidia. I think it was the CEO of Eli Lilly on Cheeky Pint—

Michael Dempsey

Yes.

Speaker 1

—with John Collison?

Michael Dempsey

Well, yeah—Collison, John Collison.

Speaker 1

Will Eli Lilly win, or will the small biotech company win? Maybe Eli Lilly will be a multi-trillion-dollar company in the future. I mean, it’s a one-trillion-dollar company. Do you have long positions in Eli Lilly?

Michael Dempsey

Yes. Generally, this isn’t investment advice, but I think there will be a lot more companies that ultimately generate very valuable assets. Then the question is consolidation: Do people simply surrender to the massive infrastructure, economies of scale, expertise in conducting clinical trials, and regulatory apparatus that larger pharmaceutical companies have? Or will they try to act on their own and actually make a revolution?

Lilly is very interesting because they’ve also started taking a more direct-to-consumer approach and taking on more of the distribution. It’s a little more difficult in the United States, but if you look at technology companies, you can vaguely see a path where some of these biocompanies can continue to grow and go through multiple inflection points over time.

Speaker 1

Definitely. Are they multi-tasking companies or not?

Michael Dempsey

On the other hand, we have Novo Nordisk, which is trading lower today than the price it was at when they started investing in GLP-1. There’s a lot of volatility, but I think these companies, with a lot of cash and really smart people, are going to grow in a way we didn’t think GCP could—at 50% year over year, to hundreds of billions in revenue.

Speaker 1

The cost structure in biotech is interesting because—

Michael Dempsey

That actually causes a lot of companies to go public quite early.

Speaker 1

Yes. At a SaaS company, you might have a billion dollars in revenue before you go public. Biotechnology is—

Michael Dempsey

Yes, you have 8 people in Jersey, and it’s as if you were a public company. If Phase 2b goes well, it’s like you have a winner, and if not, there’s no company. But this is a public company, so you end up with all these shells. It’s quite an interesting capital structure. Will this change as AI makes drug development cheaper?

I think what’s going to change is that AI will make access to medications safer. We’ll know they’re safe to give to people in a shorter time, and this way it’ll be cheaper and there’ll be less regulation.

Speaker 1

Yes.

Michael Dempsey

This will also result in cheaper and faster market dynamics. Secondly, Montana has something called the Right to Try Act, which could be another interesting early regulatory change. If a drug is deeper into clinical trials and you’re in Montana, you can choose to take it. It’s a very interesting libertarian view of the world. Again, you can start getting evidence from human studies quite quickly.

We’re very interested in human challenge trials as a concept. We believe they’re one of the most underrated endeavors in biology. In human challenge experiments, we have a drug, we give it to infect you, and I’ll give you that drug and see if it works. We’ll do a blind trial with another group of people and keep them in the center for 2 weeks. We think it can be done in a lot of different areas. Today, it mainly concerns respiratory viruses, but I think the apparatus will change.

Most people in biology take the opposite position. It reminds me of very early AI, where we had people like Yann LeCun today, or even worse, Gary Marcus, saying, “These are just predictors of the next token. They don’t really know anything,” and so on. In biotechnology, a group of people think the problem isn’t discovery; it’s all these other things. It’ll never work anyway. It won’t change anything. All you AI experts are wrong.

Why Still Invest In Crypto?

One thing people often get confused about in biotech is that our biggest advantage is that we can sit between hyper-naive, very optimistic people and hyper-blasé, very intelligent and talented people. Our specialty is knowing when to ignore these people. If we hadn’t ignored them, I think we would never have made any of our investments.

Speaker 1

Michael, this is actually a podcast about cryptocurrencies, so we should talk about them for 70 minutes. I just realized 70 minutes have passed. With all the things you’re doing in biotech, high tech, new materials, and so on, why are you still investing in cryptocurrencies?

Michael Dempsey

I think this is one of the most asymmetrically tilted-upward areas. If you think about it long term, and take the societal perspective we talked about, even if society is in some form of pendulum swing, a lot of the principles that underpin cryptocurrencies will survive. Then we just figure out what the use cases and areas are, starting with capital organization and then creating more efficient systems through programming, with smart contracts in a simple form.

Speaker 1

What areas should we invest in?

Michael Dempsey

I think that’s it. We started investing in cryptocurrencies because weird people were really interested in them, and we should figure them out.

Speaker 1

I would say so. It was really cool, but also a bit disappointing for Ramp.

Michael Dempsey

Looking forward, I still think there are a lot of things, like rare diseases, that are among the best uses for cryptocurrencies.

Speaker 1

Funding for rare disease research: How do you allow companies that don’t really have any funding to raise capital and introduce amazing solutions? Do you have any thoughts? Shelby has—

Michael Dempsey

Yes, I looked at all the DCI tokens.

Speaker 1

Yes, more investors in HairDAO.

Michael Dempsey

But yeah, I think those deep questions are super interesting, and obviously I’m a huge fan of Bitcoin.

Speaker 1

When you say it’s interesting, you have a private fund and a public fund. Are you buying cryptocurrencies or tokens? What tokens do you have now?

Michael Dempsey

We don’t disclose all of them, but some of our larger positions are things like Hyperliquid. Historically, we had Helium. We have HairDAO and Kinetic, and probably 13 other crypto assets.

Speaker 1

What stage do you think we’re at in cryptocurrency investing? You could call it a four-year cycle, a cycle, or just the phase of crypto we’re currently in.

Michael Dempsey

I think crypto ventures have been pretty much dead for 2 years now.

Speaker 1

Yes.

Michael Dempsey

I don’t think we know yet why, each time crypto cycles repeat, the bar for reinvesting is higher. What’s cool is that people are starting to believe that one day they won’t be called before Congress if they create something in crypto, which is great. I think that’s the main limiting factor.

The bigger problem is actually a technology problem. If you put crypto at the top of the tech industry rankings, it’s somewhere near the very bottom. All the technology has just been absorbed by artificial intelligence. Nobody wants to create anything but AI. Bio is this weird thing where people have a very specific set of skills they’ve spent 8 years honing, but everything else is dead, too. It’s not like we’re prospering everywhere.

In 2021, the most interesting thing was that everyone was creating all sorts of things, and then they switched to cryptocurrencies anyway. Now, of course, no one will switch to cryptocurrencies because everyone is dealing with artificial intelligence. So the main issue is, first, how do we attract more talent? Secondly, how do we solve the many problems associated with tokens? Tokenization is great, but it obviously really hurts the long-term incentives that I care about. I think the regulations will sort themselves out.

From a liquid-assets perspective, it’s very, very interesting for us right now, especially as we have a lot of fully distributed tokens that are starting to accrue value. You can understand these things fundamentally and narratively, and some of them are starting to work. From a venture capital perspective, unless you’re creating new perp DEXs, there aren’t many people making innovative attempts to hit the target right now.

Which Crypto Companies Could Go Public?

The interesting thing that will happen next year is that there will be a lot of IPOs. We should see a lot of them. If the market develops well, it’s going to be a really interesting market for cryptocurrencies because we now have good companies that own them.

So we have real companies generating real cash flow that decided they didn’t want equity; they wanted a token. That’s okay. The market will also have companies listed on the stock exchange. So now, if you’re a public investor and you want exposure to crypto, it’s really something like Coinbase, BitGo, Circle, and Securitize. I’m sure I missed one or two.

You could have a few IPOs next year and then over 20 in the next 24 months, let’s call it that.

Speaker 1

That’s probably too optimistic. Let me say 10.

Michael Dempsey

Yes, 10 in the next 24 months. There are many of them, for example, Fireblocks and Chainalysis. They’re not ready for an IPO yet, but they could be. Ledger, too. Again, many of these companies aren’t at this stage yet, but they could be.

Speaker 1

Are there any private companies you’d like to see on the public markets?

Michael Dempsey

I’ve been trying to buy Chainalysis stock for the past year and a half. I’m constantly under pressure by some investor.

Speaker 1

Interesting. Why are you trying to buy Chainalysis?

Michael Dempsey

First of all, they traded at a very, very large discount in the last round.

Speaker 1

I’m blowing up my Chainalysis transaction in real time. I wanted to ask why you’re sharing this. At this point, I capitulate.

Michael Dempsey

Yes. Secondly, I think they’re one of the three reasonable companies that have a right to win if we assume that cryptocurrencies will continue to become more important in the world and cybercrime continues to grow at a very rapid rate. I’ve been in cybersecurity for a very long time.

They have some proof points, both in terms of cryptocurrency security and, from my outside understanding, they’ve put a lot of hard work into finding the toughest clients to try to win over.

Speaker 1

I think there are two other companies that are directly competing. Did you do a round in TRM Labs, or maybe a round in TRM?

Michael Dempsey

No, no.

Speaker 1

Michael, thanks for this.

Michael Dempsey

Thank you. It’s great fun. I appreciate it.

来源：YouTube

item.title: 20VC: You Need $1BN To Do Seed Today: The Untold Truths of Venture | Who Wins and Who Loses in the Next Decade of VC | Why Margin and Price Matter Less in a World of AI with Sameer Dholakia, Bessemer
item.description: Dholakia sees AI surpassing the internet and cloud combined, with capital intensity concentrating frontier intelligence. He expects open and closed models both to become enormous businesses, while testing premium entry prices against forward growth, revenue quality and credible margin improvement. Bessemer’s $1.75 billion early-stage and $4 billion growth funds reflect the capital bar that favors scaled platforms or differentiated specialists.
item.content:encoded:
20VC · Harry Stebbings、Sameer Dholakia · 2026-10-19 · 75 min · 原语言 EN

Dholakia sees AI surpassing the internet and cloud combined, with capital intensity concentrating frontier intelligence. He expects open and closed models both to become enormous businesses, while testing premium entry prices against forward growth, revenue quality and credible margin improvement. Bessemer’s $1.75 billion early-stage and $4 billion growth funds reflect the capital bar that favors scaled platforms or differentiated specialists.

TL;DR

  • Dholakia underwrites AI as a larger opportunity than the internet and cloud combined. “Oil powers all the machines. Intelligence powers all the humans.” Bessemer’s Anthropic investment at $15 billion pre-money followed a cloud-style thesis: capital intensity would concentrate frontier intelligence among a few providers, with hundreds of applications above them.
  • Open models and frontier labs can both become enormous businesses without investors correctly forecasting their market-share split. Dholakia rejects the claim that open models will capture 99% of tokens while closed models capture 99% of dollars. He admits he underestimated the open-token economy 12 months ago; Fireworks and fal now express that revised conviction.
  • Entry price matters, but Dholakia tests high current ARR multiples against what a business could become over the next 12 months. He considers 10–15x on an NTM basis reasonable for extraordinary businesses; Legora’s move from $20 million to $200 million illustrates his argument. Revenue quality still affects the multiple, while weak margins require a defensible improvement mechanism over his five-to-seven-year holding period.
  • Capital can reinforce market leadership, but it cannot substitute for an exceptional product. Dholakia sees funding driving faster expansion, stronger branding, better recruiting and more customer wins. Legal AI illustrates the opportunity: he frames worldwide legal services as roughly $1 trillion, with lower prices potentially unlocking previously unserved demand.
  • Venture’s strongest positions are giant global platforms and specialists with a clear edge. Bessemer raised $1.75 billion for seed and early stage plus $4 billion for growth; Dholakia struggles to see how small seed funds obtain enough “shots on goal” in capital-intensive AI. He calls the undifferentiated middle a difficult place to make money, while allowing that cheaper, slower-growing businesses can still deliver venture returns.
  • Dholakia believes large growth funds can still produce 5x-plus returns because outcome sizes have expanded. Bessemer may invest $200–400 million per company across rounds, and its previous growth fund put approximately 20% into Anthropic. Both speakers favor late-stage opportunities offering potential 10–20x outcomes with more developed businesses; those remain underwriting ambitions.
  • Longer private-company lives do not eliminate the need for liquidity or the possibility of an IPO reopening. Dholakia supports partial secondary sales and predicts an IPO unlock “later next year, and in 2028,” driven by demand for pure-play AI exposure. Stebbings challenges the structural appeal of listing when private companies can already finance acquisitions, support employee liquidity and make substantial long-term investments.
  • Autonomy and therapeutics are Dholakia’s next major expressions of the intelligence thesis. Bessemer invested nearly $200 million in Waymo; he thinks personal-car subscriptions, trucking and logistics could extend it into “a trillion-dollar business. Easy.” In therapeutics, he believes AI and automated wet labs could compress half a century of discovery into the next decade.

Digest

1. Anthropic required a reset in the imagination of scale

  • After 31 years in software, Dholakia associates rare moments of technological “magic” with trillion-dollar cycles. Jasper’s marketing application on GPT-3 in winter 2021 supplied the latest recognition. He thinks this cycle exceeds the internet and cloud combined because intelligence serves consumers, businesses and governments: “Oil powers all the machines. Intelligence powers all the humans.”
  • His Anthropic underwriting was “a cloud redux”: compute intensity implies capital intensity, concentrating frontier providers while allowing hundreds of applications above them. Microsoft had OpenAI, Google was building Gemini, and AWS had made a substantial Anthropic investment. AWS mattered twice—training compute and early distribution—making its relationship pivotal to the investment case.
  • Bessemer joined Anthropic’s Series D at what Dholakia recalls as $15 billion pre-money and $18 billion post-money, alongside Menlo and Lightspeed. According to Byron Deeter, it was the lowest-voted investment during his tenure at the firm. Partner empowerment allowed conviction to prevail: “If you guys really believe, go do it.” Dholakia’s regret: “I just wish we had written a bigger check.”
  • Stebbings says he passed on an OpenAI opportunity at $30 billion, reasoning that even a $100 billion outcome would be only about a 3x before dilution. Dholakia says he also passed on an OpenAI opportunity after the ChatGPT moment, but gives no valuation for it. He recalls that OpenAI had grown from about $40 million to well north of $1 billion—perhaps $1.5–2 billion—by the time Bessemer looked at Anthropic’s first round. “Our imaginations were capped.” Anthropic offered a chance to correct an important mistake rather than treating the missed investment as final.

2. Open intelligence does not require a closed-model collapse

  • Dholakia rejects forecasting a precise open-versus-closed split in a market this large: “This is ‘and,’ not ‘or.’” He also rejects the suggested 99% open-token/99% closed-dollar allocation. Asked whether he sees a frontier-lab bear case, he answers, “I really don’t,” arguing that intelligence can address vast numbers of unsolved problems and solve others at previously unimaginable speed.
  • On Chinese open models, Dholakia argues that once hosted by Fireworks, a model is “no longer a Chinese model.” Stebbings pushes back: some CIOs reject Chinese provenance regardless of where downloaded code runs. Dholakia acknowledges encountering exactly that objection and sees a gap for a strong US open-weight model. The exchange leaves buyer perception as a commercial constraint.
  • A leading open-model provider can generate venture returns through enterprise delivery and support, Dholakia argues, citing Red Hat. Whether it can reach $500 billion: “I don’t know.” His own changed view concerns the open-token economy’s size: “I just didn’t see it 12 months ago.” That reassessment supports larger commitments to Fireworks and fal, the latter spanning generative media and infrastructure.

3. Forward growth can justify the multiple, but revenue quality still matters

  • Dholakia’s examples look extreme on current ARR: Abridge at $5 million ARR and roughly $700–800 million valuation; Anthropic at approximately $100 million ARR and $15 billion; Legora at $20 million ARR and $1.8 billion. These required difficult investment-committee conversations. His question was whether the companies could grow into a reasonable multiple over the next 12 months.
  • The horizon is specifically next-twelve-months, rather than the end of the following calendar year, which could mean underwriting 18–24 months ahead. His operating experience makes that distance uncomfortable. Depending on the business, 10–15x NTM is reasonable when growth is unprecedented. Legora subsequently going “20 to 200” makes him comfortable with the $1.8 billion entry.
  • Stebbings asks whether customer mix and creative run-rate calculations change that comfort. “Quality of revenue matters deeply,” Dholakia replies. He favors sticky, strategic enterprise products with strong gross and net dollar retention; consumer or prosumer businesses deserve substantially lower multiples because “churn, it can kill you.”
  • Margins receive a different time horizon: a growth investment may last five to seven years. Dholakia is not principally worried about the next 12 months, but demands an explanation for any forecast reaching 60–70% gross margins. Scale economies and market position can support improvement; spreadsheets cannot establish it. He reports “factors improvement inside of 12 to 24 months” in AI investments.

4. Legal AI exposes both the market opportunity and the limits of vertical upside

  • Stebbings tests Legora’s outcome math: a $300 billion US legal market, a hypothetical 20% software share yielding $60 billion, and competition including Harvey might support $5–10 billion in company revenue. Can an investor entering near $2 billion still make 10–20x? Dholakia says that framework is “not terribly off,” but the geography is too narrow.
  • Dholakia uses roughly $1 trillion in worldwide legal-services spending and says the US represents only 40% of the market. Lower prices could also unlock needs currently left unserved. A business reaching $5–10 billion in revenue need not capture much of that spending to become enormous; its eventual valuation would determine the investment return.
  • Competitive breadth has not fundamentally changed, he argues; the capital behind competitors has. Funding accelerates expansion, builds brand, attracts talent and reinforces customer wins. “Markets pick winners,” creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Dholakia explicitly endorses king-making, but calls capital “necessary but not sufficient”: scarce compute requires a war chest, while leadership and a product customers recommend still determine whether it works.
  • Fieldguide reveals a boundary. Dholakia thinks it was below $10 million ARR when he invested, probably below a $200 million valuation; model improvements around January–February accelerated adoption of its auditing product. He wishes he had invested more. Stebbings questions whether even a $10–20 billion outcome is “generational.” If that requires $100 billion, Dholakia concedes Fieldguide is “probably not that.”

5. Venture’s middle faces pressure from both scale and specialization

  • Bessemer’s $5.75 billion raise comprises $1.75 billion for seed and early stage and $4 billion for growth. Dholakia struggles to see how small seed funds obtain enough “shots on goal,” particularly in compute-intensive AI. Historical seed checks were $3–5 million at $20–40 million valuations; he supplies no specific current figures, only that they are “factors higher,” while allowing less capital-intensive niches.
  • Venture has expanded across geography, sectors and stages, from pre-seed through enormous pre-IPO checks. Dholakia sees professionalization favoring either a giant global platform or an extreme specialist with differentiated picking and support. “If you’re in between, good luck.” His automotive analogy: mass-market giants at one end, Porsche or Ferrari at the other, with a difficult middle.
  • Traditional triple-triple-double-double growth struggles to attract capital when alternatives are growing 10x at scale. Nevertheless, Dholakia says these businesses can still generate excellent returns at dramatically different entry multiples. Capital-efficient application companies resembling the older 1Password or Qualtrics growth-investment pattern may emerge over time; he simply does not expect them to attract the near-term concentration of venture dollars.
  • Stebbings challenges retail access through adverse selection: oversubscribed firms already serve institutions such as hospitals and pension funds, potentially leaving retail investors weaker managers. Dholakia favors access but says investors should choose strong platforms or genuine specialists and understand the risk. For those uncomfortable with that, he explicitly raises public-market compounding without venture’s liquidity sacrifice as an alternative.

6. Early options become large positions only after businesses earn them

  • Defending Menlo’s Venky’s description of early investments as options, Dholakia distinguishes the portfolio logic from entrepreneurs feeling diminished. Follow-on capital depends on progress: “You have to earn the right to keep scaling.” Bessemer’s $1.75 billion early fund includes reserves, while the growth fund can invest far beyond pro rata. He dismisses signaling anxiety when a business has not yet demonstrated the necessary acceleration.
  • In the $4 billion growth vehicle, Bessemer may deploy $200–400 million into one company over several rounds. Dholakia describes 5–10% as a comfortable late-growth allocation, with flexibility for extraordinary conviction. Its previous growth fund, Century II, placed approximately 20% into Anthropic. The larger fund preserves concentrated underwriting.
  • Stebbings mocks dividing growth into early and late categories. Dholakia concedes the cutoff is arbitrary but distinguishes $20–40 million-revenue companies, perhaps worth $500 million–$1 billion, from entering Fireworks at $15 billion: information, risk and checks differ. Stebbings insists the decisive metric is invested-capital multiple, observing that infrastructure can have a larger addressable market than a vertical application.
  • Dholakia wants 5x-plus funds. Early portfolios need some 50x outcomes to offset lower hit rates; growth investments can require less upside because more business risk has been resolved. He still seeks 10–20x opportunities and says, “We want nothing less than a five,” while acknowledging some investments may return less. Forced to choose one vehicle personally, he favors late-stage growth.

7. Culture becomes concrete through hiring and behavior under stress

  • “Teammates and friends beat colleagues and coworkers every day and twice on Sunday,” Dholakia argues. Coordinating large groups is difficult; people who care about one another work harder for the team. SendGrid’s four Hs—happy, hungry, humble and honest—were operating standards. A high performer could not receive an exemption, and everyone needed permission to call out violations.
  • Stebbings objects that values should permit disagreement: nobody advocates unhappy, unambitious liars. Dholakia makes the definitions concrete. Humility meant “we not I,” tested by counting pronouns in interview answers about accomplishments. Happiness meant optimism under pressure rather than cheerfulness. Someone consistently bringing the team down, or preferring individual credit, could be a poor fit despite otherwise strong performance.
  • SendGrid flew the whole company to Mexico each January: one day aligning on direction, another spending time with people from other offices. The mechanism mattered when things broke. Colleagues might blame sales, blame marketing or leave; friends who had kayaked or mountain-biked together were more likely to work through the problem. Stebbings separately endorses blunt IC debate—“feelings are expensive”—while Dholakia emphasizes “intellectual honesty.”

8. Longer private lives still require DPI and leave room for IPOs

  • “Our LPs are not in the business of handing us the money for perpetuity,” Dholakia says. Although he thinks the AI wave remains early, prudent investors should take some chips off the table and return capital. Late-stage partial sales are increasingly treated as ordinary portfolio management. He likewise encourages founders to establish family financial security, potentially making them more willing to swing for larger outcomes.
  • Longer private-company lives are a “permanent structural shift” in his view, supported by a larger venture asset class. Crossovers and LPs must respond because substantial appreciation happens before listing. Public investors waiting for an IPO may miss much of the earlier value creation.
  • Nevertheless, Dholakia predicts an IPO unlock “later next year, and in 2028.” His mechanism is supply and demand: successful listings demonstrate appetite for pure-play AI exposure, public investors want dozens or hundreds of companies rather than a handful, willingness to pay improves, and more issuers follow. This is his forecast for reopening the window, not an established timetable.
  • Having taken SendGrid public, Dholakia believes being “IPO worthy” forces predictable execution and operational discipline. Stebbings counters that large private companies already face high expectations, while Stripe’s private status permits strategic investment, acquisitions and liquidity. On diminishing IPO attractiveness, Dholakia concedes, “Maybe. I don’t know.” His portfolio companies still want to list, sometimes because customers view public status as evidence of credibility.

9. Fireworks combines enterprise ownership with a stronger commercial engine

  • Asked for Fireworks’ $250 billion bull case, Dholakia begins with people rather than a detailed valuation model: its technical leadership and team from Meta, now joined by president George Hu. Having worked alongside Hu at Twilio, he considers him exceptionally strong at strategy, analysis and building go-to-market engines. Hu joined a month or two before Bessemer’s investment: “That is the pitch right there.”
  • The enterprise proposition is owning intelligence rather than exclusively renting it. Dholakia expects “a healthy, healthy amount of both,” but finds it difficult to imagine businesses wanting to own none of their intelligence. Stebbings sees a possible 20x return from their approximately $15 billion entry; Dholakia agrees.
  • Sovereign models need only win particular buyers and use cases. Bessemer backs Sarvam in India and is “invested in or investing in Mistral right now.” Indic languages and local multimodal content underpin the Indian case; government, military and regulated use cases support sovereign preferences elsewhere. Dholakia’s argument rests on segments of a huge market choosing local models, rather than every buyer doing so.

10. Judgment includes contrarian selection and the ability to close

  • Dholakia initially names Byron Deeter Bessemer’s best picker, then revises his answer when asked separately about closing founders. David Cowan gets the selection distinction for apparently strange investments such as Rocket Lab; Deeter gets closing for his experience, intelligence and ability to build relationships.
  • Stripe is the miss that particularly hurts because Bessemer backed developer-API companies including Twilio, SendGrid and Auth0. His dream partnership addition is Lightspeed’s Ravi, whom he praises for deep technical and market thinking—and willingness to take risks that look “borderline insane,” exemplified by a $1 billion Anthropic check in the $60 billion round.

11. Autonomy and therapeutics extend the thesis beyond software

  • Bessemer invested nearly $200 million in Waymo. Stebbings challenges its roughly $115 billion valuation against Uber’s $120–125 billion market capitalization. Dholakia’s objection: “You’re looking at the ride-hailing market as the only market.” His case requires thinking beyond today’s principal business.
  • Having bought his 16-year-old son a car, Dholakia would readily pay a monthly subscription for a Waymo driver. He sees potential across other automakers, followed by trucking and logistics. Personal-car licensing is not Waymo’s near-term focus, he acknowledges. Combining those possibilities with expanded ride-hailing use cases, he thinks it becomes “a trillion-dollar business. Easy.”
  • Embodied robotics is “probably” around 2021 relative to generative AI, with a couple or few years still to go, Dholakia thinks; progress could arrive faster than most expect. He is interested in autonomy across construction, mining and agriculture, but cannot recall offhand whether Bessemer owns a robotics-data company.
  • Therapeutics offers what he considers AI’s greatest potential impact: “drug the undruggable.” Automatable wet labs paired with systems reasoning across datasets beyond a single human’s capacity could accelerate biological discovery. Echoing Dario’s forecast, Dholakia believes the next decade could deliver what otherwise would have taken half a century: “I really believe that.”

It was because of what happened in the intervening time. You remember that OpenAI opportunity that I also passed on? Harry Stebbings

In a world of $2 trillion assets, do you care about price anymore? Is LP focus on price misplaced?

Paying for AI Growth

Sameer Dholakia

Entry price always matters. Every venture capitalist has taught me that. By the way, you know me: I’m four and a half years into this second career of mine, so I’m still learning. I appreciate that it’s a craft like every other, and I don’t pretend to have all the answers by any stretch. But I know how important entry price is.

What matters most is whether you believe it can grow at scale and compound for a very long time and still make you a venture return. I’m focused on looking out the windshield, as they always say, as opposed to the rearview mirror. Some of the investments I’m most proud of were at current ARR multiples that would make most venture capitalists throw up. They were difficult conversations in our firm’s IC—in the investment committee.

When we invested in Abridge, they were at $5 million of ARR, and we were paying a $700 million or $800 million valuation, whatever it was. When we invested in Anthropic in that $15 billion round, I think they were at $100 million—like 150 times current ARR. Lagora had $20 million of ARR when we invested and led that $1.8 billion round. That’s insane.

If you’re only looking at the present and the past, you’ll say, “Sameer, do you not understand math? A hundred times? That’s what you’re paying to get in?” But if your view, as mine was in each of those instances, is, “Yeah, but on an NTM basis”—that’s what I care about—“what do I think this thing can be in the next 12 months, and do I feel like this is a reasonable multiple in the next 12 months?”

Harry Stebbings

So you look at the end of next year?

Again, this is me trying to learn. You look at the end of next year, and then you look at gross profit on that.

Sameer Dholakia

Not even the end of next year. I look at NTM, the next 12 months. Depending on the business and where you are in the year, that could be more like 18 or 24 months, and I won’t pay that far forward because it’s really hard to see that far ahead in any business. I’ve been an operator and a CEO, and I know how hard it is to predict that far into the future when you’re scaling at these rates. But you should be able to get your arms around the next 12 months, or at least get closer.

Harry Stebbings

What is exciting enough in that respect, then? When you look at NTM, what’s green versus red?

Sameer Dholakia

Depending on the business, it’ll vary. Something in the 10 to 15 times NTM range isn’t crazy, especially if these businesses are growing at rates that have never been seen in the history of business, and that I’ve certainly never seen in my 31-year career. I don’t think paying 10 to 15 times NTM is all that crazy, because they’re going to blow through it.

Look at Lagora. We invested at a $1.8 billion valuation, leading that round, and that seemed insane at the time. But the company went from $20 million to $200 million. I think we’re in that together, and I know you know Max.

Harry Stebbings

Yeah.

Sameer Dholakia

They’re on fire, and I feel pretty good about that $1.8 billion.

We’re going to get to Lagora, and I completely get that. Does feeling good about that $1.8 billion change depending on customer makeup, quality of revenue, or run rate versus enterprise revenue? We see some quirky ways to calculate revenue today. Does that change things?

Sameer Dholakia

For sure. Quality of revenue matters deeply. I’m old-school. I’ve been in enterprise B2B software since 1995, so that’s my bias. I prefer the gross dollar retention and net dollar retention rates of highly sticky customers, for whom your product is super strategic and who are going to keep expanding.

I would pay a much lower multiple for a prosumer or consumer business. Churn can kill you.

What about margins? You look at someone like Lagora, who we both love. Their margins are good, but they’re not enterprise-level—

Sameer Dholakia

Look, I think—

You have to be really thoughtful if the gross profit picture doesn’t look pretty and you’re envisioning some spreadsheet magic where it’s suddenly going to hit 60% or 70% in five years. I can remember that, for most of the businesses I invested in, gross margins at the time we invested were meaningfully lower than they are at scale today in this AI world. Meaningfully lower—improvements by factors of multiple inside of 12 to 24 months.

Sameer Dholakia

That math isn’t terribly far off. I’d just say we included the whole world, because you and I both know Max has global ambitions. When you add in the rest of the world, you don’t grow the TAM a little bit; you add another 60%. The U.S. market is only 40% of it.

Capital Becomes a Moat

Sameer Dholakia

I actually don’t believe the competitive breadth has changed. What’s changed is the capital intensity behind the competition, which leads to this competitive intensity. If you look at the war chests—the amounts of money that companies like Lagora and Harvey have raised—that creates a competitive intensity that’s absolutely different from what I dealt with in my era.

Harry Stebbings

Is capital a moat today? Is that the differentiator?

Sameer Dholakia

I absolutely believe capital is a moat. I’ve always said that markets pick winners, and then it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. In our day, SendGrid and Twilio were the API building blocks developers plugged into their applications to send communications. Once developers had decided, it was game over. We had won. You were the default; you became the market winner.

That happens, and we see it in these markets, too. There are lots of legal tech companies and AI legal providers, but if you asked anybody at a big law firm who the major legal AI companies are, they’d name those two. I believe capital creates both the ability to scale at an extraordinary pace and a brand for those businesses. Talent then flocks to them, and you get this reinforced flywheel. They win more customers, and the virtuous cycle continues.

Harry Stebbings

Do you believe in kingmaking? I do. To your point that capital is a moat, excessive amounts in a short amount of time give you inherent advantages. Do you agree with kingmaking, like I do, or not?

Sameer Dholakia

Yes, because I believe everything you said: capital is a moat, and it’s a signal to the market. Having built software companies for a very long time, I know your product has to be exceptional, and your company leadership has to be exceptional. In math-speak, I’d say it’s necessary but not sufficient. Having the biggest war chest and the most capital is a necessary condition for winning the market. I really do believe you’re in that kind of a game.

It’s because compute is so scarce, and therefore so expensive, that if you don’t have it, you just can’t play. So I agree with the first part of your statement, but it’s not sufficient. You then have to deliver an amazing product that your customers rave about, love, and tell their friends about if you want to be king. Otherwise, you have no chance.

Harry Stebbings

I agree with you completely there. I also agree with what you said earlier: the 10 to 12x and the growth rates now are very different from what they were. When you look at growth rates today, is triple, triple, double, double—the model SaaStr, Jason, and I always talked about—wrong? Is that not enough anymore?

Sameer Dholakia

It’s not enough to attract capital from venture capitalists who have opportunities to put their money into these hyper-growth companies that are growing much, much, much faster. All of us as venture capital funds have scarce capital. As big as these funds are—we just raised $5.75 billion—it’s still scarce.

That said, I do still believe in finding companies doing T2D3, because the entry prices for those companies in this environment can be dramatically different, at a very different multiple, and you can still make a great venture return on them.

Harry Stebbings

Do you buy that? Sameer Dholakia Cake.

Harry Stebbings You mentioned the $5.75 billion. It’s quite a lot, to be honest. Let’s start with the $1.75 billion for seed and early stage.

Sameer Dholakia Yeah.

Harry Stebbings Do you need a billion dollars to do seed today? We just saw USV announce its $900 million funds earlier today. Do you need a billion to do seed?

Sameer Dholakia Seeing the prices and valuations we’re seeing for the early-stage deals coming in from my teammates on the early-stage side, and thinking about the number of shots on goal you need to find the winner, I don’t know how you’d have a small seed fund and be successful. I don’t.

Harry Stebbings What are you seeing in terms of pricing and ownership levels?

Sameer Dholakia It depends on the business. If it’s a capital- and compute-intensive business—and a lot of these AI businesses are—then it also depends a little on where you want to play. But in this era of intelligence and AI, I think a lot of them do. If you assume that’s the case, the math just won’t math for the entrepreneur or for you if you’re not paying enough. In my day—I’ve been doing this for 31 years—a seed check was $3 million to $5 million on a $20 million to $40 million valuation. It was a dramatically different time.

Harry Stebbings And what is it today?

Sameer Dholakia I don’t have the specific numbers, but I know it’s factors higher. It’s way more. When you’re factors higher than that, you really have to hope that you’re a great picker.

This gets into one of my other worldviews, if you will. I’m just a humble business guy, Harry, and I think about the venture industry like any other industry. When I was evaluating coming in and starting it as a second career, I looked at the venture capital asset class and said, “This looks nothing like what I grew up with in the mid-to-late ’90s,” when everything was hardware and software in Silicon Valley, principally at the early stage.

Now it’s global, in every sector you could imagine, and covers everything from a pre-seed check all the way up to IPO, where you’re investing hundreds of millions of dollars. Every one of those vectors I mentioned—location, stage, and sector—is dramatically different and broader. It’s just the professionalization of this asset class.

If you think of it in that context, in most industries, when they professionalize and scale, you either have to be at one end of the spectrum—a giant global platform that consolidates a whole bunch—or an extreme specialist. You might say, “I’m doing AI deals in San Francisco, at the early stage.” You have to optimize for specialty on all three dimensions. You can be one of those two things, and if you’re in between, good luck. I think that’s a rough place to be.

Bessemer is a big global platform. But not being a giant global platform or an incredible specialist who can add differentiated value and be better at picking because you’re a specialist makes it hard to make money.

Harry Stebbings So what happens to the billion-dollar funds?

Sameer Dholakia I don’t know, but I’m glad I’m not at one of them. I think you have to be on either end. I really do. I’m sure there’s a path to success for everybody. Good luck. I’m just giving you my outside-in, unvarnished view as a business guy looking at an industry. I’m analyzing it clinically, and what I’ve seen in the history of business is that when markets get big, they consolidate and have specialists.

Take the automotive industry. It doesn’t matter what industry you pick. You’ll have your Big Three in the US, or Toyota and Honda in Japan. You get a handful of giant players on one end, and then you can be a Porsche or a Ferrari, a specialist on the other side of the spectrum. Being in the middle is a tough place to be, I think.

Harry Stebbings It is. I think it’s a very tough place to be. Can I ask you, when you look at the two different vehicles today? I had Venky from Menlo on the show, a mutual friend of ours.

Harry Stebbings I spoke to many people on your team beforehand, and they said you really focus on culture. I thought, “Oh, gosh, how boring.”
