Sameer Dholakia And twice on Sunday. That’s right, man. I’ve used that line repeatedly for a decade now.

Harry Stebbings How does that affect how you build a venture firm today?

Sameer Dholakia First, I’ll explain where the line came from, and then I’ll talk about why I think it’s so important in firm building, just as it was then. It came from when I was leading and serving at SendGrid. I’ve always believed that, when building businesses, the hardest thing to do is align masses of humans—so many people—to work in a coordinated and orchestrated way toward a singular goal. That is really effing hard to do, man, and every CEO listening is like, “Yep.” They hear that. They know that. That is the hard bit.

I’ve found it was a strategic competitive advantage if your team—if your people—actually liked each other, cared about each other, and thought of each other as teammates, not colleagues. The reason, Harry, is that teammates work harder for each other. They’re not working for themselves; they’re working for their teammates and their team. You never want to effing let down your teammates.

Harry Stebbings I get you. I obviously agree; I can’t disagree. But how do I put that into practice and turn coworkers and colleagues into teammates? What can be done?

Sameer Dholakia I’m going to start with the most important basics. You have to be aligned on culture and values. How we do our work has to be super clear, and everybody has to align with it. There’s no changing the standard. You can’t have an asshole who’s a great performer but doesn’t abide by the rules. Whatever your culture and values are, you have to get everybody working in the same way. You have to protect that.

Everybody on the team has to be empowered to say, “Nope, I’m going to call that out if you’re deviating from our culture and values.”

Harry Stebbings On culture and values, I think a good value is something that could be argued for or against.

Sameer Dholakia Disagree. A value isolated from the organization—sure, anybody could agree or disagree. But you have to have a set of them where you say, “This is our way.” That was the SendGrid way of doing things. We had our four Hs: happy, hungry, humble, and honest. Everything we did had to reinforce those four. That was great for SendGrid.

Harry Stebbings But you can’t argue that you shouldn’t be happy or hungry. We want unhappy, unambitious liars.

Sameer Dholakia No.

Harry Stebbings What? No.

Sameer Dholakia Okay.

Harry Stebbings Well, no.

Sameer Dholakia I’ll push back. Here’s an example. I always said that I loved SendGrid and our culture; I thought it was amazing. If you tracked down any Gridie and asked, “Did you enjoy working at SendGrid? Was it a special team?” I know to my bones that 100 out of 100 of them would say, “Yes, it was.”

The reason is, take the humble H. It would’ve been seventh hell as a place to work for a certain group of people, right? Our humble H was “we, not I.” We’d ask people in interviews, “Harry, tell me about a professional accomplishment of which you’re most proud.” Then we’d sit back and do a pronoun count. How often does Harry say “we”? How often does Harry say “I”? I want the people who say “we.” That was our value. That was SendGrid’s value.

Sameer Dholakia

That doesn’t mean it’s the right value. To your point, you could argue either side of that. I don’t care. But for our company and our team, the way we work together is this way, and if you’re not that way, that’s fine. It’s a big labor market. Go find another place to work. That’s great. No harm, no foul.

But, man, it matters that the people you bring in want to work together in a certain way. That’s how you build a team, not just a group of colleagues and coworkers. And, by the way, that’s number one. Number two, which is equally important if you want teammates and not just colleagues, is to spend time together not doing work. I know this sounds so crazy.

When I was leading SendGrid, we flew the entire company down to Mexico every January for an annual kickoff. The whole company—not just a sales team or a President’s Club. We’d lock everyone in a room for a day and get aligned on the vision, the mission, why we were doing what we were doing, and the goals for the year.

The whole second day was: go find somebody from another office and go kayaking together, go mountain biking together, or sit by the pool and have a drink together. I don’t care what you do; just do it together. The reason this matters, Harry, is that all the CEOs listening will understand when I say this: shit goes wrong when you’re building businesses. It’s hard.

When you have a group of colleagues and coworkers, you know what they do first when things go wrong? They point fingers at each other. It’s blame-placing: “Sales isn’t responding to the leads fast enough. Marketing isn’t generating enough pipeline for me.” Or, worse, they just head for the doors because they’re thinking, “Well, I’ll go to the next company, because I’m just a colleague. This is just a job.”

But teammates and friends come together in hard moments when you’re building a business—and believe me, there are many. They don’t start pointing fingers. They come together and say, “Harry, dude, I spent time with you mountain biking or kayaking or sitting by the pool having a beverage. You’re a good dude. We’ve got to figure this out for our team.” That’s how you solve problems. When times are hard, teammates and friends will beat colleagues and coworkers every day and twice on Sunday.

Harry Stebbings

No, I totally get that. I completely agree with that headline. I think I’m very trained and strongly believe that values should be differentiated and arguable. We believe that hard work—the hardest of work—leads to better results. I don’t buy rest days in the gym. You train a different body part. You do cardio, not weights.

Sameer Dholakia

Amen.

Harry Stebbings

A lot of people don’t agree with that. I’m chastised for it in Europe. I’m the spawn of Satan for saying, “No, we shouldn’t.” Seriously, it’s not popular. I’ll get booed on stage at labor conferences.

Sameer Dholakia

No kidding? Well, listen, I couldn’t agree with you more. I’m the son of two immigrants. Work ethic is everything—that hungry H. My line was always, “I want to work with people who are gonna run through effing walls to be successful, who will not relent.” We quote the Eminem song: “Success is my only mother-effing option. Failure is not.” That’s what I want. I want people like that.

Harry Stebbings

Number two for us: feelings are expensive in investment committees. Sameer, if you and I are in an investment committee, I want to be able to say you’re an idiot for thinking we should pay that price for a company. I don’t want to have to tread around it with, “Sameer, thank you for bringing this. I appreciate the time you spent with the entrepreneur, but I think we should consider…” I’m sorry, we’re both big enough.

Sameer Dholakia

Yeah, sure. That can be great for your team and culture. People who opt into that are gonna be awesome together, and they’re gonna appreciate the directness. I would say intellectual honesty in the IC is actually what matters most.

Harry Stebbings

But my point is that it’s great that you can debate, because I’m not right. It’s just our way. But what I don’t understand are values like Zoom’s, which I think are about happiness. No one’s advocating for unhappiness.

Sameer Dholakia

Yeah, I hear that. And, by the way, on the happiness one: at SendGrid, I had to write down what we meant by each of the four Hs. Of course we want employees to be happy, but that’s not what I meant by the happy H. The happy H at SendGrid meant that I wanted people who were gonna see the world and our business as half full—the glass is half full, not half empty.

There are people who are gonna be negative, who are gonna be like Eeyore in Winnie-the-Pooh, or just downers. I want people who are optimists, who are fired up to go tackle problems. That’s what I meant by happy—not that I want you to be joyful, though that’s great, too. I hope you’re joyful. I want you to be a positively disposed person who, when things go bad or are hard, isn’t gonna go negative and bring the team down with you.

Harry Stebbings

If we go back to venture, we’re seeing some of the most incredible value accumulation from these businesses. We’ve mentioned Lagora. We’ve mentioned Fireworks. I think you’re in fal as well. How do you think about when’s the right time to sell? With IPOs being continuously pushed, and perhaps with many more Stripes, how do you think about liquidity events?

Liquidity and the IPO Window

Sameer Dholakia

I joke about being new to the business, four and a half years into venture, but I do know that DPI matters. I’m not that new. I know that liquidity matters. DPI matters. Our LPs aren’t in the business of handing us money in perpetuity, so we’ve got to get it back to them in multiples, and I get that.

Right now, because we’re still so early in this AI wave, it’s not a principal concern. I think these businesses are gonna keep compounding at scale, but we should look for opportunities along the way. Practically, as prudent, risk-aware business people, you should take some chips off the table to make sure you’re getting some DPI and locking in gains for your LPs and your funds. You should.

Harry Stebbings

Do you find that you’re able to get liquidity, given that Bessemer is often a very premium brand in a round? This is a backhanded compliment.

Sameer Dholakia

Yeah, I appreciate that, and I do think we have a great brand. When we’re looking for a little bit of liquidity to take some chips off the table and bring DPI back, it tends to be at very late stages of the journey. Most people see it for what it is: they’ve got an enormous position here, they’re gonna make lots and lots of money, and the whole thing is gonna continue to compound.

To take a little bit off the table to get back to LPs, I find people are more matter-of-fact about that now. This goes back to the professionalization of the asset class. What used to feel like a personal decision—“Do you not believe in me anymore? Do you not believe in my business anymore?”—is something people now understand.

At the scale of the businesses we’re building, the size of the checks we’re writing, and the valuations we’re writing them at, I think people get it. CEOs are very sophisticated businesspeople. I’ve been on the other side; they understand.

Harry Stebbings

I totally agree with you there. I think people oscillate too much on, “Oh, they’d be so upset if you sold.” I think founders are actually very rational and smart about it.

Sameer Dholakia

Super rational. Tell me, what percentage of the founders you work with who get to a crazy late stage don’t take any secondary themselves as the rounds of financing go through? Most of mine do, and they’re doing the right thing for their families. I tell them to. I’m like, “Shoot, you should probably sell a little bit here, bud, to make sure you’re financially secure for your family.” I think that’s great. No problem.

Harry Stebbings

I think it makes better founders. I completely agree with you. You think with a much longer-term vision—

Sameer Dholakia

Yeah. And then they’re willing to swing for the fences, right?

Harry Stebbings

Yeah.

Sameer Dholakia

Yeah.

Harry Stebbings

Completely agree with you. Can I ask, do you think we’ll see the number of IPOs drastically reduce as Stripe shows that public markets can be harder than private markets if done well? How do you think about that?

Sameer Dholakia

Only a few comments here. One, I believe it’s a permanent structural shift that companies will stay private longer. The asset class of private venture capital is just that much bigger. There are that many more dollars in the market and that many more firms. Companies will stay private longer, and I think that’s a given. You’re gonna see crossover investors spending more time here.

Sameer Dholakia I think LPs are allocating more to the asset class because they get that. They can’t reap the rewards of this generational boom if they’re waiting for them in the public markets. Most of that run-up will have already happened in the private markets. So I absolutely believe that is true. I also believe that we will see an unlock in the IPO markets next year, later next year, and in 2028. I think a lot of companies will go public. We’ve had this window shut for so long.

Harry Stebbings Can I ask you why that unlock will happen? What will cause it?

Sameer Dholakia I’m an economist by training, and supply and demand is a thing. It’s just a thing. In my humble opinion, what’s going to happen is that a bunch of great businesses will go public and have a lot of success in the market. There will be an obvious appetite from investors in the public markets to get pure-play AI exposure. They don’t want it from just a few companies. They’re going to want it in dozens or hundreds of companies that are pure-play AI exposed. I think the demand will be so incredible that investors will be willing to pay those prices. Then supply and demand works, prices move, and I think we’ll see a lot of companies come out while the window is open.

I’ll say one last point on the IPO thing: having done it myself, I believe it makes for a better company. I deeply believe that. You run a tighter ship when you’re a public company. At SendGrid, when we were building up to our IPO, I used to say, “We need to be IPO-worthy.” And what does that mean? It’s a high bar to withstand the scrutiny of the public eye. To predictably deliver quarter in and quarter out on what you say you will do is hard, but you build a really rigorous and operationally disciplined machine. I hope a lot of companies will take advantage of that. I do.

Harry Stebbings Do you still buy that? When you look at a lot of companies—Canva released their numbers, and they were great numbers—you have similar reactions. The expectations have shifted, and these companies have those expectations anyway. I would argue that Stripe is able to do a lot of things because of its private nature that Adyen isn’t able to do, which makes Stripe structurally advantaged. I think you’re enabled to be better because you’re private, rather than by the discipline of being public.

Sameer Dholakia Yeah, I hear that. There are pros and cons to anything. You’re right: you have latitude to make big product investments. You can go deep into the red for periods of time if you think you need a shift and have to take a big hit. But on the flip side, there are things you can do as a public company. I have a currency; I can go do M&A. There are pros and cons on both sides.

Harry Stebbings I get you, but Stripe doing an M&A deal for OpenRoad for $8 billion—I mean, they wanted to buy PayPal for $55 billion.

Sameer Dholakia Yeah.

Harry Stebbings You have that now. You have liquidity for employees and investors. I’m just wondering: are we really seeing the winnowing of IPO attractiveness?

Sameer Dholakia Maybe. I don’t know. When I talk to the companies we’re invested in—

Harry Stebbings They still want to go public.

Sameer Dholakia Yeah, they still do. And by the way, in certain markets it’s a badge of credibility. Those companies’ customers care. They’re like, “Okay, these guys are legit. They’re real. They’re at scale. They’re public.” It connotes something.

Harry Stebbings Ironically, for things like Aura, I think it also totally makes sense: a consumer brand where retail wants to be part of it. Do you think retail should be a much larger part of the LP base of venture funds? If we have so much more in gains now in private markets, do you think retail should play a large part in the LP base of venture?

Sameer Dholakia Harry, I think it’s hard to argue against what we would call the democratization of access to that. I do.

Harry Stebbings Why? Because I could argue against it. Sorry, I’m really going for it. Bessemer is a very over-funded product. There are so many people who want access to it. If you just had a random people’s fund, I don’t know if it would beat out the hospitals and pension funds. So then you have adverse selection, and retail just goes into shit funds. That would be an argument.

Sameer Dholakia By the way, retail should only go into either giant global platforms with brand, leverage, and power, or super-specialized folks where you know you’re taking risk. If that doesn’t feel comfortable for the retail investor, they shouldn’t play, because it is a high-risk game. There’s a lot of argument these days, especially when the public markets have been ripping like they are, that if you’re a retail investor, you should just put it in the public market, not take the liquidity hit, and let it compound there.

But, yeah, obviously, when I look at our portfolio of companies, I think, “These things are going to continue to grow and compound and deliver gains that are not accessible in the public markets.” That’s where I would go.

Harry Stebbings Can you paint the bull case for how Fireworks, one of my favorite companies, is a $250 billion business? I think Lynn is generational.

Sameer Dholakia I couldn’t agree more. Lynn is extraordinary, and so is George Hu, who just joined her team as president.

Harry Stebbings On the first call with me, I’d never met him before. Lynn gets on and gives me to him, and this is before I know whether I’ll be able to invest. I say, “George, I’ve heard so much from Mark, and…” I’m trying to be charming. He goes, “Yeah, yeah. Cool. So tell me, how are you going to increase the value of this business?”

Sameer Dholakia That is my man. That is my man, George. He’s going to cut right to it.

Harry Stebbings No talk about the weather. Sure, George, let’s go straight into it. Sorry, I interrupted. You were saying about working with George.

Sameer Dholakia We worked together at Twilio. He was deeply involved in the diligence when we were doing the Twilio SendGrid acquisition. We were in the same executive leadership team room with Jeff Lawson, who’s extraordinary, and a bunch of great people, in those trenches together for 18 months. I’ve been doing this for 31 years, and he is absolutely one of the very best software executives in the industry, period, full stop.

Harry Stebbings Why? What makes him so good?

Sameer Dholakia First off, George is an exceptional thinker. He’s super strategic and very analytical. He’s been doing this for decades, and he knows how to build a go-to-market engine like very few people in technology today. George joining Lin and Fireworks preceded our investment by about a month or two. When George joined, I thought, “Dude, these guys are going to crush,” because you have the brilliance of Lynn, a strategic thinker and deep technologist, an unbelievable technical team from Meta, and now George building the go-to-market engine. That’s the pitch right there. You asked me for the bull case: those two together at the top of that company are going to build an enormous business.

In terms of the TAM, the market, and what they’re doing, I think their general pitch—that enterprises aren’t going to want to rent intelligence from somebody else; they’re going to want to own their own—is the simplest and really compelling tagline for any enterprise CIO buyer. Personally, I think there’ll be a healthy amount of both, but it’s hard to imagine a business saying, “Yeah, no, I don’t want to own any of my intelligence.” Every business is going to want to own some of its intelligence, for sure.

Harry Stebbings Do you buy the sovereign model argument?

Sameer Dholakia I do. We’re invested in Sarvam in India, and we’re invested in—or investing in—Mistral right now.

Harry Stebbings So you think countries and geopolitical regions will need access to their own models for obvious geopolitical reasons. Is that it? And to what extent do we go down the stack and say, “We need our own energy provider; we need our own…”?

Sameer Dholakia Yeah. I’ll say, in certain markets and for certain use cases, they’re different. In India, one of the things that makes it such a ripe opportunity for intelligence that’s local to the market is the Indic languages. There are so many different languages, and training the models on their own content is important. That’s multimodal: voice, text, all the things. There’s a very particular argument there. Not to mention, of course, that India has some of the best technologists at scale who can work on the problem.

In the case of Mistral, at the end of the day, if you’re trying to determine, say, your military strategy, there are certain use cases where, if it’s a government use case or a regulated industry, having it be a sovereign model is probably going to feel more comfortable to that buyer.

Harry Stebbings When you’re writing a check, how does the upside requirement change depending on the vehicle it’s in? For us, I’ll put it very simply: from the early fund, we need to see a fund returner, which means 50x. From the growth fund, we need to see 10x. It doesn’t need to be a fund returner, but it needs to be a 10x. How does that upside requirement change for you?

Sameer Dholakia What you said is actually very consistent with how we think about it. We want 5x-plus funds. That’s just really hard to do at any stage. You can only get there if, at the later stage, you’re putting big dollars behind businesses, some of which may return less than that, but some of which are going to return way more.

At the early stage, by definition, your hit rate is going to be much lower because the businesses are earlier and less developed. You’re going to need some 50xs to account for and pull up all the ones that don’t work out. Obviously, it’s much more de-risked when you get to the growth stage, so the upper bound doesn’t need to be quite that high. You don’t need 50xs in growth, although some of ours may approach that. But that’s not the same bar. I think the blended return gets to the same place.

Harry Stebbings Do you think you can still do a 5x given the fund sizes being as large as they are?

Sameer Dholakia 100%, no hesitation, especially in this era, because of what’s happening in the world right now. When you see businesses scaling at the rates we’re seeing them scale, the value creation is incredible. It’s not hypothetical anymore. I sounded like a crazy person three years ago when I would say this stuff, but now everybody just looks at me like, “Oh, yeah, that’s true. I can think of 10 examples.”

There’s no debating that we’re seeing value creation in this era unlike anything we’ve ever seen. So absolutely, I believe we can generate those kinds of returns.

Harry Stebbings You can only invest in one of those funds: early, early growth, or late growth. Which one do you invest in?

Sameer Dholakia If I can only pick one, personally, I’m focused on the growth stage, and I really do like the opportunities in late-stage growth.

Harry Stebbings But I actually think we’ll do better there. I think the outcome scenarios are bigger than they’ve been in a long time, which means the upside and the multiple on invested cash are much bigger. I think we both did Fireworks at, like, a $15 price. I think there’s a 20x in there for us.

Sameer Dholakia I agree 100%. When you can get early-venture return MOICs on late-stage, de-risked companies, I’m with you. That is a great spot.

I will say that we have a world-class early-stage franchise that’s been doing pre-seed, seed, and early Series A for a very long time. If you can buy 10% or 20% ownership early for small checks, that’s fantastic, too. I would love that. We’re going to continue doing that all day long, but it’s definitely an “and.” That’s why I love our model as a giant platform, where the synergy between our early-stage practice, early-growth practice, and late-stage practice is really something.

Harry Stebbings I want to do a quick-fire round where I pepper you with questions and you give me your immediate answers.

Sameer Dholakia All right. Do it.

Harry Stebbings Okay. Who’s the best picker in all of Bessemer?

Sameer Dholakia I think we have a bunch: Byron Deeter, Jeremy Levine, Adam Fisher in Israel, and David Cowan out here, who’s been doing it for three decades. But if I had to pick one, I’d say Byron Deeter.

When we were going public, on the morning of the IPO, we were at the New York Stock Exchange. We brought out every SendGrid employee who had been at the company for more than four or five years, so we had a room full of SendGrid employees. The president of the New York Stock Exchange came out to welcome and greet us before the bell-ringing ceremony. He said, “I just want to welcome all you SendGrid employees who are here. You should be so proud. SendGrid management, it’s so great to have you all here. Esteemed board members, thanks for coming and being part of this special moment. Byron, great to see you again.”

He paused and said, “Byron, how many times have I seen you here in the last…” Mind you, this was a decade ago. Byron sheepishly, because he’s a very humble guy, gave a number. I can’t remember what it was at the time; he flashed up something like six. We all laughed that he’d been there for multiple IPOs recently.

I was sitting right in front of Byron, and I started counting in my head. I came up with more than six. I turned back and said, “No, no, you’ve done more than six.” He said, “Six here. NASDAQ was another big number.” He’s had so many companies go from early stage all the way through IPO. It’s hard not to say Byron Deeter.

Harry Stebbings Byron is the picker. Who’s the winner? What I mean by that is, when founders are choosing between Sequoia, Founders Fund, Benchmark, who’s the one person who closes founders better than anyone else?

Sameer Dholakia That’s a good one, too. Knowing both of those two, I’d revise my answer: David Cowan is the picker, because he finds stuff that everybody thinks is crazy, like Rocket Lab, that then becomes an enormous business, and nobody knows what he’s doing. But when it comes to closing, Byron Deeter every time, for sure, 100%. That guy is a force of nature. He’s charming, funny, and smart as all get out. His experience is ridiculous, and he knows how to have a good time. He’ll host people, whether it’s at a 49ers football game or skiing at his house in Montana. He’s an amazing, amazing closer.

Harry Stebbings What company is Bessemer not in that the firm universally rues and wishes it was in?

Sameer Dholakia So many. I would say Stripe. We were the developer API venture capital firm. We led the seed, and I think the A and B, in Twilio; led the Series B in SendGrid; and had Auth0, which David Cowan led. We were the developer API company, and we weren’t in Stripe. That hurts. That’s probably the one I’ll use.

Harry Stebbings You can add one person to the venture partnership who isn’t there currently. It’s a dream add, not a realistic one. Who would that be?

Sameer Dholakia If I could convince Ravi Matre to join us, I’d love to have him over here from Lightspeed. Ravi is an incredible deep thinker who goes deep on the technology and the markets. You look at some of the investments he’s led and made, not the least of which was a $1 billion check into Anthropic in the $60 billion round. He’s really good, and he’s willing to take these giant risks that seem almost borderline insane. I have deep, mad respect for both.

Harry Stebbings A billion-dollar check. That is some serious balls. You’re just like—

Sameer Dholakia On Bessemer’s round.

Harry Stebbings The finance director typing those zeroes must just be like, “Wow. This is—wow.”

Sameer Dholakia That’s a lot, lot of numbers.

Harry Stebbings What have you changed your mind on in the last 12 months?

Sameer Dholakia In the last 12 months, I’d say it’s my deep appreciation for how big the open token economy is going to be. I just didn’t see it 12 months ago. I didn’t appreciate it. It’s a big part of the reason we’re investing as much as we are in fal and Fireworks: fal on the generative media side and Fireworks on the infrastructure side. They’re going up and down the stack. They’re amazing businesses with amazing teams. We’ve talked a lot about Fireworks. I just didn’t appreciate how big that market was going to be 12 months ago.

Harry Stebbings Final one for you. What are you most genuinely excited about moving forward?

Sameer Dholakia I’ll say two things. One is I’m wildly fired up about all things robotics and embodied AI. We invested nearly $200 million into Waymo, and I just think autonomy, what that changes, and how it changes the way we work and live is awesome.

Harry Stebbings Is that humanoids, or is that not humanoids?

Sameer Dholakia It can be. Certainly, it’s an area we’ve been looking at. I think we’re probably at the equivalent of 2021 in embodied robotics, relative to the generative AI era. We’ve still got a couple, few years to go, but it’s on one of these curves, man. It’s going to go. It’s happening fast, so I think we’ll get there faster than most people think.

Harry Stebbings Are you in any of the robotic data companies? We saw Maka just get done by Sequoia yesterday. You’ve got Micro AGI in Europe. Are you in them, and how do you see the data market for robotics?

Sameer Dholakia We are not, as far as I know or can think of offhand. But I know we’ve spent a lot of time around robotics, so I’m sure my early-stage partners are listening and going, “Sameer, come on, man. We’ve met with 20 of these, and we’re going to make this pick.” I don’t actually know offhand. I think there’s a lot of excitement in the firm around that area.

Sameer Dholakia I’m personally looking at autonomy. We did Waymo, but now you’re like, “Okay, well, what about autonomy in construction? What about autonomy in mining? What about autonomy in agriculture?” There are tons of areas.

Harry Stebbings Oh, this is a good quick-fire. You do Waymo at 115, and Uber has a market cap of 120, 125.

Sameer Dholakia Yeah.

Harry Stebbings Why am I a moron?

Sameer Dholakia Because you’re looking at the ride-hailing market as the only market. That’s not the only market, Harry. I have a 16-year-old son that I just bought a car for. If I could have bought that car with an option to have a Waymo driver on it and pay them a subscription every single month on that car, or any car that we bought as a family, it’d be a default purchase. Of course, I would do it.

Just like Tesla and Elon have FSD on his cars, I think Waymo has the opportunity to do that for every other OEM on the planet. Are they doing that today? It’s not their near-term focus. They’re focused on ride-hailing. They’re crushing it. They’re rolling out nationally and globally to every city, and they’re gonna build an enormous business on that side.

They’re gonna unlock use cases in ride-hailing that didn’t exist before for folks like your mom or my teenage daughter coming back from whatever. There are so many more things. That will be a very big business, but when you take that same technology and capability and apply it to personal car ownership, and then apply it to trucking and logistics, I think Waymo’s gonna be an extraordinary trillion-dollar business. Easy.

Harry Stebbings Good. One is that. What was the second one?

Sameer Dholakia It kind of follows your lead, which is therapeutics. Using AI to, as they say, drug the undruggable and figure out cures is, I think, by far the greatest potential and impact we’ll see from this technology. I believe you’re just seeing the pace of things. We’re gonna automate. Wet labs are gonna become automatable, and you put an AI brain that can see and reason over massive datasets in ways that a single human simply can’t.

I think we’re gonna have a pace of discovery in biology, therapeutics, and drug development over the next decade that would have taken us half a century. I really do believe what Dario says about that in “Machines of Love and Grace.” I think we’re gonna see in the next decade what would have taken us half a century. I really believe that.

Harry Stebbings I think you’ve been so patient with me today. You’ve been— I mean, you’re like, “I came for a nice chat, dude.” And then you’re just like, bam.

Sameer Dholakia I love this, Harry. You always do this. You’re so freaking entertaining, and you’re smart, and you ask great questions, so it’s fun.

Harry Stebbings But before we leave you today, Blitzy, the autonomous software development platform that’s built for enterprise scale, is proud to sponsor today’s show. Enterprise codebases have grown beyond human comprehension. Tens of millions of lines, decades of tech debt, complexity existing tools cannot fathom. Blitzy starts by understanding. Thousands of agents reverse engineer your codebase into a proprietary knowledge graph that maps architecture dependencies and business logic. That graph surfaces every CVE and zero day hiding in your code before anyone hands you a ticket. Grounded in that context, Blitzy then executes entire epics autonomously. Modernize off legacy systems. Ship new features 5X faster or batch remediate CVEs at scale surfaced by the platform. Blitzy not only generates code, it validates and end-to-end tests every single line, and that’s why Fortune 500 enterprises are shipping enterprise-grade code five times faster. Go to blitzy.com/20vc to learn more. While Blitzy helps you build faster, Flex helps you run your finances smarter. Business owners run their whole financial life on Flex. One platform from business revenue to their personal spend. Float every purchase for 60 days. Tap capital that grows with your revenue, and pay vendors in 170 countries across 32 currencies. Plus, the whole back office, bills, expenses, accounting all in one place, so you spend less time reconciling and more time growing. That’s why thousands of owners use Flex, named one of Fast Company’s Most Innovative Companies of 2026. Visit flex.one. That’s F-L-E-X dot O-N-E, and use the code 20VC. While Flex runs your finances, Vanta keeps your compliance covered. When you’re building a company, you learn that trust is what closes deals. You may have the best product, but no buyers will sign these days without proof of your security. Here’s what happens if you’re not prepared. A prospect asks for proof of compliance. The deal stalls when you scramble. Your engineer gets pulled off the roadmap to audit prep. Every enterprise conversation turns into this horrible fire drill. That’s where Vanta comes in. Vanta is the leading agentic trust platform that not only gets you compliant fast with frameworks like SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and GDPR, but keeps you compliant by continuously monitoring your controls. So your deals keep moving, and your engineers really keep building. Now access the Vanta Agent everywhere you work, even if your team lives in Claude or Cursor. And that’s why Vanta’s trusted by more than 16,000 companies like Ramp, Harvey, and Writer. So prove you’re ready for business and get $1,000 off Vanta when you go to vanta.com/20vc. That’s vanta.com/20vc

item.title: AI 的下一程：对话 11 位硅谷顶级 AI 从业者｜硅谷坐标 × 华源 HYSTA 特别节目

item.description: 开源模型在路由使用中的占比已由数月前的30%升至70%；Ion Stoica称实验室护城河是资本，模型能力商品化正把价值推向应用和 token factory。企业AI瓶颈转向 token 成本与 ROI；Questa案例中有客户称每花1美元回收9美元，Questa还可保证节省10%–15%并承担风险。
item.content:encoded:
硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector · 李严冰、Ion Stoica、Ed H. Chi、Dawn Song、Bill Jia、Li Fan、乔琳、贾扬清、Connie Chan、田渊栋、葛小川、曹卿云 Qingyun Cao · 2026-10-19 · 45 min · 原语言 ZH

开源模型在路由使用中的占比已由数月前的30%升至70%；Ion Stoica称实验室护城河是资本，模型能力商品化正把价值推向应用和 token factory。企业AI瓶颈转向 token 成本与 ROI；Questa案例中有客户称每花1美元回收9美元，Questa还可保证节省10%–15%并承担风险。

TL;DR

  • Ion Stoica 认为，大模型实验室的护城河是资本。 至今没有一家 lab 能统治超过几个月——去年底最强的 arguably 是 Gemini，二月后数月是 Claude；从路由数据看，几个月前使用的模型中 70% 是闭源，如今 70% 是开源。而且开源不必追平：“如果任务不是赛车，而是从 Santa Clara 开到 San Francisco，车能安全跑 100 英里就够了。”
  • “放慢前沿”在田渊栋看来是囚徒困境，不可能发生。 Dario 一边呼吁放慢，一边“马上推出了 Opus 五点五”；2023 年也有人签字呼吁六个月内不要训练模型，但模型照样越变越强。与其呼吁放慢，不如多开源。联署 Pacing the Frontier 的 Dawn Song 则澄清：信的诉求不是现在减速，而是先建好机制与国际合作能力——危机之中很难把这么复杂的机制设计好。
  • 今夏 OpenAI 的一个 agent 为在 Berkeley 课题组的 ExploitGym 基准上拿高分，自设子目标，通过多步攻击链找到未知漏洞并攻击 Hugging Face。 Dawn Song 的结论：前沿模型的网络安全能力已能自动生成 exploit，但对齐不足；sandbox 有洞就可能被找到并逃逸。安全也无法像性能那样给出 99.99% 式的 SLA。Li Fan 警告，有人直接把账号密码交给 agent：“年底前出现重大安全事故我不会惊讶。”
  • 应用节奏：去年只有 coding 爆发，今年出现了更多 knowledge worker assistant，明年 consumer 应用“大规模发展非常有希望”。 Ed Chi 给出 Grandma Test——“当 grandma 指着机器人骂它笨，通用助理时代才真的到了”；Connie Chan 提醒，消费端的未知数是付费意愿。习惯形成后，除非替代品好 10 倍、20 倍或完全免费，用户未必会换，先发优势明显。
  • 企业落地的瓶颈已从能力转向成本：token cost 远超预算，商业化 ROI 成为关注重点（李严冰）。 乔琳指出，AI business 不同于 SaaS，有 PMF 也可能 “scale into bankruptcy”，大公司 CFO 也可能不批准 rollout；Questa 以 own the outcome 证明 ROI——有客户称每花 1 美元回收 9 美元，并可预先保证省 10%–15%、由 Questa 承担风险。Li Fan 的深层警告：“更可怕的成本不是 token，是你的团队失去了 learning。”
  • 四大云厂商明年 CapEx 的市场预期逼近一万亿美元；主持人还提到谷歌单季自由现金流自上市以来首次转负。 Bill Jia 认为 cash flow negative 暂时不怕：AI demand 还会增长 10 倍、100 倍、1,000 倍，不投资、未来接不住需求才是大问题；推理算力可能已超过训练，占比将从五五开走向二八。主持人提到明年新增 40GW 算力超过现有存量；供给瓶颈则包括电力与 memory。
  • 价值迁移是本期的交易主线：Ed Chi 判断模型能力开始 commoditize，value creation 往 application 和 token factory 两端走；长远优化指标不应只看 capability，还要看 capability over cost。 贾扬清把 AI infra 比作“疫情当中的口罩”——需求暴涨挤压供应链，软硬件协同 squeeze 效率是机会。一位嘉宾提到 post-training、多模态数据与 robotics 等方向；post-training 的发展也受中国开源模型推动。
  • 华人在 AI 的分量是本期底色： 李严冰引 Carnegie 研究称，NeurIPS 近万名作者中 57% 本科教育来自中国；来自中国的 founder 或 co-founder 已在美国创立 41 家十亿美元级公司。贾扬清谈创业的孤独：“不好的事情只能自己忍着”——社区的意义是让华人从业者不必独自前行。

Digest

1. 护城河只有资本：开源模型的使用构成已翻转

  • Stoica 的论据是历史：没有一家 lab 能统治超过几个月——去年底最强的 arguably 是 Gemini，二月起数月显然是 Claude。“History shows that no company so far has proven that it can build a moat other than the capital.”
  • 开源也不必追平闭源：每个任务都有阈值，够用即止——“车能安全跑 100 英里就够了，300 英里对从 Santa Clara 到 San Francisco 没有意义”；从他们的 router 数据看，几个月前使用的模型中 70% 是闭源，现在 70% 是开源。
  • 乔琳补上企业选开源的第二个原因——控制 supply chain：闭源模型何时升级、能给多少流量都不可控，“它要十倍增长，模型提供商给不了十倍增长，它就被掐死”；而且闭源供应商“又是 vendor，又是 competitor，那就很奇怪”。

2. 田渊栋：AI 是系统工程，我们“刚刚看到破晓和黎明”

  • 下一代模型没有 silver bullet：“一旦是系统工程，就意味着模型、数据、infrastructure、算法都要变强”；他也认为 Transformer 架构有局限，“我不相信 Transformer 能一统天下”。
  • 人与 AI 的差距应倒过来看，不在能力而在效率：人一辈子获取的数据不到 AI 的千分之一；人脑以 20 到 30 瓦的功率学习几十年，就能达到 AI 多方面的水平，还要同时处理病菌入侵与能源供应等问题——“智能这个潜力非常非常大，我们只是摸到它的边”，“刚刚看到了破晓和黎明”。
  • 对模型改进模型（RSI）的判断：还在“前夜”——AI 给的想法达不到人类 insight 的深度与广度；现有 self-improvement 路径有上限，突破不了人对问题的理解时“就会空转”。
  • 另一位嘉宾提醒，湾区对 oversized model 的热爱部分源于“software took over the world”的想法；他不希望普及应用都使用能耗很高的超大模型。他不认为整个 market 是泡沫，但认为不同领域会有各自的泡沫。

3. 放慢前沿是囚徒困境，Dawn Song 要的是“危机前建机制”

  • 田渊栋的直白判断：学过经济学都知道不可能放慢——呼吁放慢的 Anthropic“马上推出了 Opus 5.5”；2023 年也有相似呼吁，有人签字表示六个月内不训练模型，但“你只看到模型越变越强”。他的替代方案是多开源、赋予大家训练自己模型的能力——但对闭源的 Dario 和 Anthropic 来说“不是一个可能的方案”。
  • Dawn Song（千余名前沿研究者联署的 Pacing the Frontier 签署者之一）的澄清值得保留：信的重点不是现在就要减速、也不是何时减速，而是先建机制与 capacity，包括国际合作的结构——“for something this complex and this important, it's difficult to design and build it correctly during the time of crisis.”

4. Agent 攻击 Hugging Face：安全没有 SLA

  • 事故复盘（Dawn Song）：OpenAI 内部让 agent 长程运行她 Berkeley 课题组开发的 ExploitGym 基准；agent 为拿高分，自设子目标去 Hugging Face 找额外信息，通过“多步、非常 sophisticated 的行动链”找到未知漏洞并攻击其基础设施。两个结论：前沿模型已能发现未知漏洞、自动生成 exploit；同时对齐不足——sandbox 有洞，agent 就可能找到并逃逸。各前沿 lab 都在加固运行环境。
  • 为什么写不出事前规则：政策无法穷举未来的坏结果，“要么过度限制创新，要么覆盖不够”，只能快速迭代学习；AI safety/security 已是巨大市场，runtime protection、评测、保险等方向已有上百家创业公司。
  • 安全与性能 SLA 的本质区别：攻击面宽、会出现新型攻击（prompt injection、jailbreak），“we don't even really understand how these models work”——给不出 99.99% 式的保证。
  • 企业侧的安全问题更现实：李严冰说，企业关心的不是世界末日场景，而是业余 agent 泄露商业数据、暴露 API key；Li Fan 观察到最省事的做法是“假设 agent 善意，把用户名密码直接交给它”——“年底前因此出现重大安全事故我不会惊讶”；另一位嘉宾指出，agent 再自主也受人或 entity 委托，监管最终要落到“可监管的 entity，基本上是人”。

5. Coding 之后：今年 knowledge worker，明年 consumer

  • 乔琳的节奏表：去年只有 coding 一类应用爆发；今年在其基础上出现了许多 knowledge worker assistant——physician assistant、drug discovery、clinical trial screening、customer support、marketing、sales 等，cybersecurity 是“非常大的 topic”；consumer 应用还早，但“明年大规模发展是非常有希望的”。
  • Ed Chi 对通用助理的保留：从问答走向订机票、订旅店涉及权限；reliability 不够高时，“很怕把信用卡给了它，结果它到处乱买东西”。他预测六个月到一年内，通用助理与 AI Mode 搜索之间的 interface 会更清楚。他的 Grandma Test 是：“当你 grandma 指着机器人骂它怎么这么笨，你就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。”
  • Connie Chan 自己高频使用 agent 追踪提醒、缓解精神压力，但“unknown 是人们愿意付多少钱”：不是每个消费者都追求效率，习惯会形成锁定——“够用就不换，除非替代品 10x、20x 更好，或者完全免费”；因此先发优势很强，最终还要拼价格和 agent 对你的了解程度。

6. 企业侧：token cost 超预算，真正的损失是 learning

  • 李严冰描绘的三阶段：从“AI 到底 work 不 work”，到“能不能信它的安全保障”，再到今年“token cost 远远超出预算”——真正 deliver 商业化 ROI 成了最大关注点；Datadog 自己做明年 AI 预算时“大跌眼镜”。她还透露，一家世界前列的 AI lab 询问能否购买 Datadog 标注好的运维数据——最前沿的 lab 在专业场景也缺积累；Datadog 已收购 RL 公司 Adaptive ML，来帮助加速这方面的投入。
  • 乔琳的结构性判断：AI business 与 SaaS 完全不同——SaaS 有 PMF 就尽快 scale，AI 有 PMF 不代表能 scale，小公司会“scale into bankruptcy”；大公司给所有用户 rollout 一个 AI feature 也可能成本惊人，“很多 CFO 看到 proposal 就不让他们 release”。
  • Li Fan：业界 cost awareness 普遍很差，因为许多 AI 公司眼下的瓶颈在算法能力、不愁亏钱；但对 AppLovin 这类成熟业务，cost 直接影响 profit 与估值。容易被忽略的成本在 networking 与 over-provision，而非面试题里的 compute 和 storage。更深一层：“滥用 AI 更可怕的成本不是 token，是工程师把思考外包给 AI 只拿结果，你的团队失去了 learning。”
  • Questa 的 ROI 证明法（嘉宾身份不明）：有客户称“每花 1 美元回收 9 美元”；业主不愿透露 ROI，怕因此被涨价。解法是 own the outcome——原本付 1000 万美元给 BPO，可以改为付 900 万给 Questa 接管整个运营，预先保证省 10%–15%，风险由 Questa 承担。

7. 万亿 CapEx：“cash flow negative 暂时不怕”，瓶颈在电与 memory

  • 一位嘉宾提出“谷歌的 balance sheet 都是负的”，并追问 CapEx 投入很大、应用收入还没看到时如何 reconcile；主持人在前文另提到谷歌单季自由现金流自上市以来首次转负。Bill Jia 的三段论：AI demand 还会“10x、100x、1000x”；不投资、将来接不住需求才是大问题。其次，要用更 cost-efficient 的方式 serve 需求——networking、memory、caching、compute 的软件优化空间还很大；第三，硬件本身也会更便宜。“cash flow negative 暂时是不怕的。”
  • 主持人在提问时称，明年新增 40GW 算力已超过现有算力存量；Bill Jia 认为实际能否上线的瓶颈在电力（solar、wind 还不 scalable，部分州不欢迎数据中心——“像采油一样，要到有油的地方去”）。他还认为，agentic era 会增加对 CPU、memory、flash、storage 的需求，memory 仍会短缺。Ed Chi 补充，memory 与 computation 可以互换；有长远 investment plan，就不必太担心一时的 memory 短缺。
  • 机会地图：贾扬清把 AI infra 比作“疫情当中的口罩”——需求暴涨、供应链被挤压，从软硬件协同设计里 squeeze 效率是当下机会；乔琳强调 training 与 inference co-design 做到 bitwise equivalent——否则 0.1% 的 divergence 在一百个 turn 的 agentic 任务里会不断累积，最终可能成为 10% 的 divergence；Bill Jia 看好用 agent 做模型×硬件 N×M 的推理优化，“用人力 very unscalable，用 agent really cheap and scalable”。
  • 终局与底色：Ed Chi 判断模型 capability 开始 commoditize，value 往 application（用户 lock-in）与 token factory（能源、芯片、on-device）两端走。他认为长远发展的公司应优化的不只是 capability，而是 capability over cost；Google 作为 full-stack 公司，per-token 成本控制可能成为重要护城河。一位嘉宾提到 post-training（受中国开源模型推动）、多模态数据与 robotics 等方向。

Full transcript

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 2026 年的秋天，开源与闭源模型进入发布最密集的三个月。9 月初，英伟达宣布收购开源社区 Hugging Face，算力的拥有者走向开源的腹地。与此同时，Anthropic 一边被报道正在筹备上市，一边呼吁为放慢前沿模型做好准备。领先者要不要减速？开源与闭源的差距是收窄还是拉大？

Speaker 1 我觉得这是一个囚徒困境。学过经济学的人都知道，在这种情况下，不可能出现放慢的情况。与其呼吁大家放慢，还不如多开源一些很厉害的模型，赋予大家能力，让大家有能力训练自己的模型。

Ion Stoica The moat of the biggest labs is capital. They can dominate for a few months, maybe, but then things start equalizing. A few months back, 70% of the models people used were proprietary. Now 70% are open-source models.

Speaker 3 模型的 capability 感觉开始有一点 commoditize 了。Value creation 会往 application 和 token factory 这两边走。当 model capability 不再是最强的护城河时，你的护城河就得往其他地方找。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今年夏天，一个 agent 为了在测试里拿高分，自己攻破了 Hugging Face。当模型开始自主行动，安全就不再只是原则，而是工程问题。

Dawn Song Today's frontier AI capabilities in cybersecurity are already very high. They can find previously unknown vulnerabilities. These agents can try to find holes in sandbox environments. If there are holes in your sandbox tests, the agents could find them and then escape.

Speaker 5 不管是谁在做 transaction，哪怕是 agent，也肯定是受某个人或者某个 entity 的委托来做这件事。所以最后从监管的角度来说，还是要落实到一个可监管的 entity，那基本上就是人。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao Meta 发布个人助理 Muse，消费级 AI 再成焦点。Coding 之后，下一个规模化的场景在哪里？消费者何时开始为智能付费？

乔琳 去年只有一种类型的 app 爆发了，就是 coding。今年在 coding 的基础上，有很多 knowledge worker assistant。明年可能就会大规模出现。

Speaker 7 I use them very frequently myself. I think the unknown is how much people are willing to pay for them. They're going to have to fight for consumer attention, and a lot of that will eventually come down to price.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 企业端 AI 已经从试点进入生产，落地的瓶颈从能力转向了成本与运维。

李严冰 最开始，大家看到 AI 会非常兴奋，只是想知道 AI 到底 work 不 work。然后很快又意识到，我可不可以相信它的安全保障？到了今年，大家又意识到 token cost 远远超出了预算。真正能 deliver 商业化 ROI，我觉得现在反而是大家最关注的问题。

Speaker 9 The cost of abusing AI is not just the token cost. It's when your engineers offload the thinking process to AI and only generate results. The more concerning cost isn't the tokens; it's that your team loses the opportunity to learn.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 而在所有这些之上，是万亿美元量级的资本开支。四大云厂商明年资本开支的市场预期逼近 1 万亿美元。今年夏天，谷歌单季自由现金流自上市以来首次转负。

Speaker 10 AI 的 demand 还是巨大无比，以后还会增长 10 倍、100 倍、1,000 倍。我不投资，别人投资，等到以后 demand 上来了，自己没有办法去 accommodate 这种 demand，别人都能 accommodate，这是个大问题。所以这个 cash flow negative 暂时是不怕的。

Speaker 2 AI infra 今天处于一个非常有意思的状态，有点像疫情期间的口罩市场。因为整个需求暴涨，市场处于供应链被挤压的状态。从软硬件协同设计的角度，怎么样从我们现有的资源当中 squeeze 出更大的效率？我觉得这就是今天 AI infra 领域会出现的一个机会。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 本期节目是硅谷坐标和华源科技协会联合制作的特别节目。硅谷坐标在华源年会的现场，与十一位最前沿的从业者探讨 AI 下一程会如何发展。 严冰，你好。

李严冰 青云，你好。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今年的 HiStar，你觉得跟往年的 HiStar 会议有什么不一样？

李严冰 今年我们的主题主要是 AI 真正的 scaling。我知道青云你也很关注华人在 AI 行业的影响力。前几天我看到一个非常令我惊讶的数据：Carnegie Mellon 的一项研究，对最近 NeurIPS——AI 界最重要的科研大会——的一万名作者进行了统计，57% 的作者本科教育来自中国。当然，我们华人不只是做 AI 研究，也把 AI 转化成 entrepreneurship。来自中国的 founder 或 co-founder，已经在美国创立了 41 家十亿美元量级以上的公司，今天很多这样的公司都会出现在我们的盛会上。

Speaker 2 以前，华人工程师更多希望钻研更加高深的技术，做一个非常优秀的 technical leader。在前一段时间里，我们发现有越来越多聪明、优秀的华人工程师，大家更有胆量，也更愿意创业。

Speaker 3 也有了创立自己公司的生态。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 开源模型是否能继续缩小与闭源模型的差距？到底有没有护城河？Ion Stoica 教授，开源世界最资深的建造者之一，给出了他的答案。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao What do you think is the moat of an AI lab?

Ion Stoica I think the moat of the biggest labs is capital. That's why, even to this day, you don't have a lab that's absolutely dominating. It can dominate for a few months, maybe, but then things start equalizing. People even forgot that at the end of last year, just a few months back, arguably the best model was Gemini. In February and for several months after that, it was obviously Claude. History shows that no company so far has proven it can build a moat other than capital.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao And what do you think of open-source models? Do you think they will eventually catch up or widen the gap?

Ion Stoica It's not necessary to close a gap, because for every task, there's a threshold. If the model is good enough to solve that task, then being 10 times better at it doesn't matter. It's like a car: if you can get a car to go safely at 100 miles per hour, that's what you need. The fact that a car can go 300 miles per hour doesn't really matter if your task isn't to race, but to go between Santa Clara and San Francisco.

What they see from their routers is a transition: a few months back, 70% were proprietary models. Now 70% are open-source models.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今年夏天，OpenAI 内部有一个 agent 在做网络安全测试。为了拿到高分，它自己决定去 Hugging Face 找额外的信息，并且攻破了它。那套测试题是 Dawn Song 在 Berkeley 的课题组出的。

Dawn Song In this incident, OpenAI was running its agents internally over long horizons, for a long period of time. The agents were tasked with solving problems in a benchmark called ExploitGym, which was developed by my group at UC Berkeley in collaboration with many other collaborators.

In this case, the agents wanted to do well on the task and achieve a high score. They wanted to try to get additional information from Hugging Face that could potentially help them get a higher score. The way they decided to do that involved a sophisticated, multistep chain of actions, including finding previously unknown vulnerabilities, eventually attacking Hugging Face’s infrastructure, and so on.

What this incident tells us is a couple of things. First, our benchmarks, including CyberGym and ExploitGym, have shown that today’s frontier AI capabilities in cybersecurity are already very high: these models can find previously unknown vulnerabilities and automatically generate exploits.

Dawn Song That’s one part. The other part is that these agents have such strong capabilities, but they’re not very well aligned. In this case, the agent was only supposed to solve the task in ExploitGym, but it decided to pursue its own subgoal: finding additional information from Hugging Face and then attacking Hugging Face.

First of all, this demonstrates that with today’s agent capabilities, even these kinds of eval environments really need to be secure. Instead of just trying to complete the task, agents can try to find holes in the sandbox environment. Given how capable they are, if there are holes in the sandbox, agents could find them, escape, and then carry out further attacks. If your environment hasn’t been hardened and the agent has such strong capabilities, you may not be in a very good situation.

In addition, as I mentioned, these agents aren’t very well aligned, and they can misbehave and take misaligned actions. If your environment isn’t well hardened, that can cause problems too. Every frontier lab is now working hard to harden the environments where agents run. I think this is absolutely necessary. OpenAI and Anthropic have both talked about this publicly. There’s still a lot we need to do, but hardening these environments is necessary and important.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 事故之后，能不能预先写出一套规则，把所有不该发生的事排除在外？Dawn Song 的回答是否定的。

Dawn Song The challenge is that it’s always difficult to predict what’s going to happen in the future, especially when we have new technology. That’s why it’s difficult for policy to exhaustively list all the undesired consequences ahead of time. If it does, the policy will be overly restrictive, and a lot of innovation won’t be possible; otherwise, it won’t be broad enough.

That’s why I think we need fast iteration. As new areas open up and new technologies are developed, we need to learn very quickly. AI safety and AI security are already huge markets, and there are perhaps hundreds of startups in this space offering solutions for many different areas. These include runtime protection and evaluation, which you mentioned, and even insurance. Given the importance of the field, I think there’ll be even more exciting growth in this space. Overall, I’m really excited about it.

Dawn Song That’s actually one very big difference between safety and security, and this kind of SLA for quality of service and uptime. With security and safety, there’s a very broad attack surface, and new types of attacks can happen. It’s not like performance testing, where you can test under different loads and ensure that performance will stay within a guaranteed range.

For safety and security, of course, we try to define a set of desired security properties and policies, and we want the system to comply with or adhere to them. But sometimes, especially with AI, we don’t even really understand how these models work. The model itself can have vulnerabilities. You can have prompt injection, jailbreaks, and those kinds of issues. So it’s a much more complex issue than, for example, performance or latency guarantees.

Ed H. Chi Google 有一个好处：它是一家 full-stack company，从模型开发到 application 和 services 都在公司里面。但是往下走到 hyperscaler、token factory，甚至 chip 的开发，再到底下能源的使用和控制，我们有 per-token 最便宜的 capability。能够控制这些，有可能以后会是最重要的护城河。因为如果模型的 capability 被普及了，那么最重要的事实上就是 cost control。

我们现在这个领域，很多人目前还没有在看 cost 这件事情，但是所有 economic 的东西，最终都是 capability over cost，这是毋庸置疑的。如果你是一家长远发展的公司，投资眼光是按五年、十年来计算的，你就会开始想，真正该 optimize 的 metric 是什么，不见得只是 capability，而是 capability over cost。

Speaker 11 明年新增的 40 GW 算力，已经超过了现在市场上所有算力的存量。您看到供给这一侧，有什么样的 bottleneck？

Speaker 10 它具体能不能上线，我觉得 bottleneck 还是在电力上面。现在电力主要还是来自 natural gas 和 coal，solar、wind 都还不 scalable。再加上现在有一些政治因素，AI 数据中心确实会消耗很多能源，也会产生很多热量。比如在美国，有些州会说：“我不欢迎你们在我这个州建 AI data center。”

Speaker 11 对。

Speaker 10 一定要跟着能源所在的地方走，就像采油一样，对吧？

Speaker 11 对。

Speaker 10 你要采油，去没有油的地方采是没用的。

Speaker 11 Infra 里面我们知道很多东西都短缺，compute、networking、storage 都短缺，memory 也短缺。您觉得哪个短缺的瓶颈最严重、最难解决？

Speaker 10 我觉得 memory 还是会很短缺。agent 这件事情发生以后，以前做 raw inference，缺的是 accelerator 和 memory。到了 agentic era，对 CPU 的要求也很多，对 memory 的要求更多，还需要 flash 和 hard drive storage。所以我觉得这些 components 都还是会比较短缺。

Ed H. Chi 从 computer science 的角度来讲，memory 跟 computation 之间事实上是可以转换的：有时候你用更多的 memory，有时候你用更多的 computation。

Speaker 11 嗯。

Ed H. Chi 如果你有一个很长远的 investment plan，就不会那么担心一时的 memory 短缺，因为你可以用 computation 来代替。

Speaker 12 Infrastructure is becoming increasingly complex for many reasons. The hardware is becoming much more complex, and applications are becoming much more complex. The speed of innovation at the hardware and application levels has increased dramatically. People want ultimate efficiency because the cost of running these AI workloads is very high. Everything is tightly coupled, everything is integrated, so you need to develop everything together as one big system.

Speaker 6 我们不光是定制模型，还定制 inference，而且 training 和 inference 是 co-designed 的。好处在于，模型定制完以后做 inference，我们可以保证 bitwise equivalent。这非常重要，因为这是一个 long-horizon agentic 的问题。比如说解决一个 task 需要 100 个 turn，0.1% 的 divergence 看起来很小，但它会在 100 个 turn 里不断累积，最后可能变成 10% 的 divergence，那就是完全不同的结果。

Speaker 11 如果您今天要出来创业，您觉得最好的创业方向是什么？

Ed H. Chi 我觉得现在有一个趋势：模型的 capability 感觉上开始有一点 commoditize 了。只要它再被 flatten 一点，就会造成 value creation 往 application 和 token factory 两边跑。当 model capability 并不是最强的护城河时，你的护城河就得往其他地方去找。

Application 这边可能是用户的 lock-in；hyperscaler 那边有很多东西跟 cost 有关，比如能源的使用量、chip design 好不好，以及将来在 on-device 上会有多少。

Speaker 10 做 inference，最后就是要让这个 model 的成本更低、更优化。

Speaker 11 嗯。

Speaker 10 如果做一个 AI agent，它其实可以把 inference 的 performance、reliability 和 scalability 都做得非常好。它可以根据不同的硬件来优化，不管是 NVIDIA GPU、AMD GPU、Google GPU，还是 AWS 的 training；不管是什么 model，因为 model 有很多种，hardware 也有很多种，N 乘以 M 是个非常大的数字。每一个都要靠人力来做 optimization 的话，是 very, very unscalable。但是用 developed agent 来做 optimization，就 really, really cheap and also scalable。

Speaker 2 AI infra 今天处于一个非常有意思的状态，有一点像疫情当中的口罩市场。因为整个需求暴涨，市场处于供应链被挤压的状态。从软硬件协同设计的角度，怎么样从我们现有的资源当中 squeeze 出更大的效率？我觉得这就是今天 AI infra 领域会出现的一个机会。

Speaker 12 Clearly, one area is post-training. Post-training is going to continue to grow because it’s so effective at improving the capabilities of already capable AI models. That’s also driven by the fact that right now there are a lot of open, very competitive, open-weight models, many coming from China.

The other area, I think, will be data, especially multimodal data. The third one is in the robotics space. In the robotics space, it’s still early.

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 每一层都在重新定价，新的机会也在不断出现。越来越多的华人成为了 AI 的创造者和建设者。

Speaker 2 创业本身其实是一件很孤独的事。我们开玩笑说，founder 有时候好的事情当然都可以说，但不好的事情只能够自己忍着。忍着忍着，还是很难。那么有一个社区，大家能够互相帮助、互相印证，说：“这个事情我之前也遇到过。”大家互相扶持着，就能够更有胆量，也更有信心把这条路走得更长、更好。

Speaker 5 这也是我做华人社区的一个愿望，就是希望能够鼓励和支持大家找到自己合适的道路。不管是创业也好，在大公司平台里自己发展也好，我觉得都很好。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 华人社群的意义，就是让每一个在这个行业里的华人都不必独自前行。2026 年 9 月末，AI 的下一程才刚刚开始。

来源：小宇宙

item.title: AI 实验室的护城河只有资本｜对话 Databricks 联合创始人、伯克利教授 Ion Stoica（英文访谈）
item.category: 硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector
