Instead of thinking about clients in terms of which regional silos they access, we think about how we can serve them anywhere in the world.

David Senra

Okay. The way I think of you—tell me if you disagree—is that you’re kind of obsessed with incentives.

Kurt MacAlpine

I’m obsessed with alignment. It’s very simple what we want to do: we want to be the best in the world at serving ultra-high-net-worth clients. In a human-capital business, it’s imperative that I have strategic, cultural, and financial alignment to achieve that. Incentives are a huge component of that. They drive a tremendous amount of behavior.

David Senra

Charlie Munger has this great line: “Incentives rule everything around us.”

Kurt MacAlpine

Yeah. Once you start to create fractures in the incentives, you run into problems. I feel very strongly that every client of Corient, regardless of where they live or how they entered the business, should have the same opportunity for an equally elevated experience. Similar to clients, I want to make sure all of our employees have the same opportunity, regardless of how they entered the firm.

If you joined through a direct hire in Seattle or an acquisition in San Diego, I want to make sure every person here is treated fairly. To treat somebody fairly, they should be paid for what they deliver for the business, not for whatever historical entry point or position they ultimately had. It’s equally imperative that you pay people for things that drive collaboration and better outcomes, as opposed to things that drive personal, independent, or siloed behavior.

We’ve been very adamant about ensuring that clients can always get the elevated experience and that every employee of Corient is treated fairly. With one compensation plan, I can walk into any one of our offices in the world, and every person knows that for an equal level of performance, they’ll be treated exactly the same as all of their colleagues.

Acquiring great partners and building one company

David Senra

Okay, I love how you summarize that: you’re obsessed with alignment. I want to talk about acquisitions. Since you started, how many acquisitions have you done? There are about 20 or more?

Kurt MacAlpine

Probably closer to 50.

David Senra

Closer to 50. As you have more AUM, do the acquisitions have to keep getting bigger, or not? How do you think about this?

Kurt MacAlpine

It’s a great question. I’m not looking for scale in acquisitions. I’m looking for exceptional people who align. I keep saying the same thing, but it’s important: strategic, cultural, and financial alignment. Whether it’s a $50 billion acquisition, a $500 million acquisition, or anything in between or on either side of those parameters, that’s less relevant to me.

In a partnership model like ours, I need those strategic, cultural, and financial alignment criteria to be true. We never look at it from an AUM or scale perspective. We look at how it’s additive to the business we’re aspiring to build. Given the scale of what we’ve built, I think our model is currently resonating really well, and we’re excited to take advantage of that.

It’s ultimately a screening criterion. If someone sees our model and is looking for something totally different, they’re not going to come here. That’s great for us because we can filter through the structure, and it’s great for them because they have total clarity about what they’re looking for.

David Senra

Let’s go back to this obsession with alignment. Explain what happens when you acquire my company.

Kurt MacAlpine

The business is about 6 years old, a little more than 6 years old. There are really 3 phases of building the business to get to where we are. The first phase was acquiring enough scale. This was a proof of concept. I thought there was a tremendous opportunity, but the question was whether it would resonate and take off. So, for the first 18 months or so, we focused on accumulating scale.

That’s important because scale drives how you think about integration, the services you integrate, and the providers you use. If you’re going to build a $5 trillion company versus a $500 billion company versus a $50 billion company, how you think about integration is very different. There was a period when we were accumulating the scale to start the integration journey.

The second piece was starting down that integration journey. We had scale, and it became a matter of making the various decisions that drive integration and transform the organization. Some things come faster than others. The third piece is where we are now: a fully integrated state. I think that’s really important.

If you had asked me when I started which of those 3 phases people would be most comfortable with, I would have said the first phase, because it involves the least amount of change at the start. That’s actually not true. People are most comfortable with the current state because they know exactly what they’re getting into, which is interesting.

If you’re selling a firm to us, you’ll know exactly what life is going to look like on the other side. You’ll know from our conversations, but also because there are now 3,000 people you can reach out to and talk with about what life is like here. The people who’ve been through the journey with us tend to be our greatest ambassadors.

I think a lot of our success, and the reinforcement of that success, comes from people who’ve come over. The clients and the people themselves have had a great experience, and they become great ambassadors for the business as we continue to grow.

David Senra

But what does total integration look like?

Kurt MacAlpine

Everything. On day 1, you’re on our brand, you’re using our technology, you’re working in our offices, you’re collaborating across the firm, the collateral has been changed, and you’re on our compensation and benefits. So it’s effectively a full integration, with one caveat: this business is all about continuous improvement.

I’m a huge proponent of constantly changing, constantly evolving, and constantly pushing ourselves. So while that state of being integrated is true, every acquisition we make, every hire we make, and every conversation we have creates an opportunity for us to think about how we continuously improve the business. We benefit from these acquisitions in the same way the acquisitions benefit from us.

David Senra

Explain a little bit more about that.

David Senra Yeah, because if I think about it, if you have a business in the space—

Kurt MacAlpine

The only reason we should work together is if 2 things are true: I make you better, and you make me better. If those aren’t true, in my opinion, then it becomes a financial transaction. That’s fine, but that’s not ultimately the objective we have in place.

We’re looking at what you’re doing for clients and how we benefit from that. What expertise do you bring, and how does that expertise translate to better outcomes for the clients we have? The same goes the other way. Hopefully there are things we’re doing that benefit you, so it immediately becomes a mutually beneficial experience.

I’ll give you an example. When you grow up in management consulting, a lot of the work tends to be high-level strategic work that often skews more confidential in nature. You tend to do a lot of work in a vacuum, to some extent, and then there’s an implementation phase. There are a lot of pros to that, and a lot of challenges around driving adoption.

Giving employees a voice in building the brand

I’ll tell you a story that I think is relevant to how I think about integration. We’re building the company, and I need to pick a brand. Picking a brand for the business can be an emotional thing for people, right? Entrepreneurs often name the business after themselves, so it extends beyond just the name. It actually becomes personal.

There are a lot of different ways you can handle it, but let’s say there are 2 extremes. One is that you pick a name and tell people what it is: the fastest pathway to an outcome, but the least collaborative way to do it. The other end of the spectrum is to make the process as broad as possible. I’ll tell you exactly how we picked the name Corient, which I think is a pretty neat story.

I held a town hall across the firm and said, “Look, we’re at a point in our integration journey where we need to name the firm, and I have no idea what the name is going to be. I don’t actually care what the name is going to be, but it’s really important to me that everybody here who wants to be involved in naming the firm has a voice in doing so.”

I said, “We’re going to hire a third-party firm to help us with this. Our chief marketing officer and I are going to facilitate a series of focus groups. Anybody who wants to participate can put their hand up. The goal is to take an infinite list of names and narrow it down to finalists.” The firm was a lot smaller at that point. We had about 75 people participate in the focus groups.

We got all the way down to a list of finalists, then had a firm mock up the names. I ran a town hall with the partner group, and my chief marketing officer presented the names. Branding is fascinating, right? If you like golf and there’s a logo with a golf course behind it, you’re more likely to vote for it than if you don’t like sailing and there’s a logo with sailing behind it. So we mocked everything up under the same brand. I held a partner town hall, presented the names, and ran a live vote. We named the firm together.

That was important because on day 1, every person who wanted a voice in the process had one. It was totally transparent, and everybody knew where we were going. So when people were calling and telling their clients about the firm on day 1, everyone who was here had an opportunity to name the firm and be a part of it.

Those little decisions change how people think about and embrace change. I try to take that concept and apply it wherever we can. I think it leads to way better outcomes because you get more people providing input, and people embrace the change better because they can see their input reflected in whatever you ultimately decide.

David Senra

Okay, I love that you just told a story about branding and marketing because that’s one of the things I wanted to talk to you about. I want to give some background on how I actually found you, which is kind of hilarious and a twist of fate. It involves our mutual friend Rick Gerson.

I get all these inquiries into my website all the time. Obviously, there’s huge demand for corporate speaking. People are always reaching out: “Will you come speak at this company?” I don’t do any of that. I have a very tight partnership with my partners. There’s one way to work with me: through the podcast. It’s comprehensive. It’s not just ads on the podcast; it’s events, too. That’s the way to do it.

I got a few inquiries from this company called Corient. They were like, “Hey, we listen to your podcast. We’re in Miami, too. Would you do this?” I never responded. I’m essentially embedded in Michael Dell’s merchant bank, and I’m close friends with Greg Lemkau, who’s one of the co-CEOs.

I love Greg. I absolutely love him. We hit it off from day 1. He sent me this interview and said, “Hey, check out this interview Byron and I did. Tell me what you think, because we don’t do much media.” I think it was on CNBC’s “Wealth,” or something like that.

I watched the whole thing, and there were 4 ad breaks with 1 sponsor the entire time: Corient.

I was like, “I know that name.” I searched my email and thought, “Oh, this is the same company. That’s interesting.”

Then I was having breakfast in Miami with our mutual friend. I’d already met you by then, but I didn’t know that. Rick’s in finance, obviously, so I said, “Have you heard of Corient? It’s a very interesting choice to have 4 ad breaks with 1 sponsor. I actually like that a lot. I think it’s really smart, for other reasons we don’t have to get into.”

I said, “Have you heard of this company called Corient?” He said, “Yeah, you met the CEO at my house when we were doing jiu-jitsu.” I was like, “You’re a brown belt or something, right? You’re the guy choking Gee, our mutual instructor—mine and Rick’s, that is.”

Then he was telling me that you’re in Miami, and that’s how we got connected. Ever since I saw that, I see Corient on Bloomberg and everywhere else. I’m very curious: Why sponsor that program? How do you think about branding, advertising, and marketing, and how does it tie into your mission of trying to build this company?

Kurt MacAlpine

It’s a great question. By brand standards, the brand is new. The company is 6 years old, and the brand isn’t even 6 years old. Part of it is just creating awareness: awareness for clients, potential colleagues, and potential partners. There are a lot of different ways we think about that.

We do lean into marketing. We think it’s an incredibly impactful and powerful tool. The way we choose to lean into it is through 3 or 4 different approaches. One is advertising, a lot of the things you’ve mentioned. Every industry is changing: how people consume television, watch things, and engage with things is totally different. We’re trying to respond and reflect that.

We’re trying to advertise in places where people are watching something live, which is why you see us on business television and in sports—places people choose to engage, where they’re sitting in a structured and focused setting. We do a lot of digital marketing, too, really trying to micro-segment and target individuals we want to build and establish relationships with.

And we do a lot around experiences: client experiences, convening people across the business, and collaboration. I don’t think of them as individual silos, because there are lots of different ways people come across Corient. Maybe an ad introduces them to Corient, maybe it’s a friend or a mutual connection, maybe it’s a referral, or maybe it’s a business partner.

And the goal is to help bridge the gap between who Corient is, what we do, and how we can be helpful to people and their families as quickly as possible. By wealth management standards, or at least independent wealth management standards, I think we’ve taken a relatively unique but ambitious approach to advertising.

Today, we’re advertising in every market we’re in globally. You’ll see our ads in the US, Canada, the UK, Paris or France, and across the world. We intend to continue doing that. It’s really helped to short-circuit the discovery process: people say, “Hey, you’re a new company. Yes, you have all this scale.” They can learn about us as quickly as possible, and then hopefully we can start to engage and provide value to them and their families.

David Senra

It’s shocking because these aren’t new ideas. They’ve been documented for at least 120 years. I’ve read every single biography about the great copywriters and advertising agency founders. They all say the same thing: repetition, repetition, repetition. The idea is that I didn’t just see Corient in one segment of the Greg Lemkau interview. I saw it again and again and again. By the time you get to it, I may not use your services. I might not sell my wealth management firm, but at least I know you exist.

Kurt MacAlpine

Exactly.

David Senra

And so this is what we’re doing with our partners. In addition to all my partners on both my podcasts, I also run the podcast strategies for these companies.

Kurt MacAlpine

Yeah.

David Senra

It’s just because I’m obsessed with it and I like to do it. You should know where your customers are paying attention. It’s very simple. We just pulled the numbers: there are 446,000 podcasts in the business category, I think, and 300,000-something that are still updating. There are 5 in the world that matter.

Kurt MacAlpine

Yep.

Building a business that lasts for generations

David Senra

There’s your strategy. It’s very simple: this is how you do it. And once you partner with them, you stay with them forever.

Kurt MacAlpine

Yeah. But it comes back to the theme around conviction. A lot of times, advertising is one of these areas where, on a relative basis, you’re investing a tremendous amount of capital in advance of any underlying tangible benefit. You’re right: it is a proven strategy over time, but it depends on how people are thinking about their business.

The reason we have the ambitions we do, and the reason we built the business the way we have, is that I think this should be the forever business in ultra-high-net-worth wealth management. If you think about it with a forever time horizon, you’re going to think about brand building very differently than if there’s a temporary lens or a temporary owner. In a lot of areas and industries, particularly financial services and wealth management, there are a lot of temporary owners. They’re thinking about the business in 18- to 36-month increments. They’re not thinking about it across generations.

If you’re thinking about it over that period of time, you’re optimizing for a return and an exit. You’re not optimizing for a client experience, an employee experience, or building a forever brand. I think that’s probably how—

David Senra

That’s the only thing I’m interested in.

Kurt MacAlpine

Yeah. So, if you were to segment who you ultimately engage with in your business, it’s probably people, agnostic of industry, who meet those characteristics.

David Senra

My friend Sam Hinkie has this great line. He’s like, “The person with the longest-term view in the room wins.”

Kurt MacAlpine Yeah.

David Senra Because it also goes against human nature. I have another question for you. You were in Chicago for the majority of your career, like the last—

Kurt MacAlpine Mostly New York. I was born and raised in Canada. Most of my professional career was in New York, and then I moved to Miami.

David Senra I want to get to Miami. Why are you so bullish on it? Why did you pick it for the headquarters? You have crazy office space that I went to.

Kurt MacAlpine Yeah.

David Senra Why Miami?

Kurt MacAlpine It’s a great question. I launched the business at the start of COVID.

David Senra You said April 2020. I was like, “Oh.”

Kurt MacAlpine Yeah. That creates a tremendous amount of challenges, but also a tremendous amount of opportunities. Effectively, the world stopped. Everything about everybody’s normal schedule and agenda halted in March 2020. You can either let that impact you or take advantage of it. That allowed us to accelerate the building of the business, start having those conversations, and lay a great foundation for the company.

As we were building the business, Corient was a separate, distinct, independent entity from CI. I needed a headquarters for the business. Because of how I built it, I had free rein in terms of where to put it. There was no particular transaction or corporate historical tie to any one area. If you think about it with a totally clean slate, where do you ultimately want the headquarters for the business to be? I picked Miami.

I picked Miami for a lot of different reasons. One thing that really stood out, and that I think makes Miami unique not only in America but in the rest of the world, is how engaged people are locally in creating positive reinforcement for building a community. One of my good friends—one of our good friends—is the mayor, or former mayor, of Miami, Francis Suarez. Francis was the ultimate ambassador. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a better ambassador for a city than him: take personal involvement, create connections, build relationships.

You think about it: there’s a decision about where you want the business to be, and then there’s a secondary decision about how you actually establish the business once you’ve made that decision. I find that a lot of times, people will sell the ambition and leave the second part up to the individual. What Francis in particular—and the Miami ecosystem he really created under his tenure as mayor—did was create an incredibly welcoming environment.

So I chose Miami as the headquarters, moved there myself, and effectively built the business. It’s been absolutely amazing because we were by no means pioneers of moving to Miami. I picked the headquarters at the end of 2020, but we were a little bit early relative to the flood of movement that’s happened since. My worry at that point was whether there would be enough local talent to hire as the business continued to grow. The answer was yes, even when we moved, and it’s even more true now given all the great migrations we’ve seen since.

You know this from your time in Miami: once you get there and spend time there, the quality of life is unbelievable. You build momentum around something and continue to reinforce it. I think we’re still in the early days of what we’ll see in South Florida. It’s worked out significantly beyond my expectations across the board: in how we’ve established a presence and operated the business, employee and colleague satisfaction, and what we’ve been able to do.

David Senra I love how, when I asked you where you picked your headquarters and how you designed your business, it was the same exact idea: you started from a blank sheet of paper.

Kurt MacAlpine You have to. I mean, look, sometimes you end up too far down the path, and it’s very, very hard. So you have to push yourself, right? If you’re going to build something from scratch, how do you avoid pitfalls? You have to learn and study mistakes you’ve made and mistakes other people have made, just as you study successes you’ve had and successes other people have had. How do you really draw on the best of it?

We didn’t really cover it today, but we talk a lot about the partnership. When I launched the partnership, the goal I set for ourselves was that the structure and features of the Corient partnership would be better than those of any partnership that had come before us. The reason I wanted that to be true was that we’re building this thing from scratch.

You want to be able to say, “Look, I’ve drawn on all of these lessons from all these other great partnerships that existed in other industries. How do I take the best of them, improve on the areas I think are ripe for improvement, and use that as a catalyst?” Not only was it a partnership, but when people actually got in and audited it, they were like, “Wow, this is really built in a way that’s friendly.” It’s done that way because you become a student of all the things that have come before you and try to use them to influence your decision-making.

David Senra And it should be if you’re going to do this forever.

Kurt MacAlpine Exactly. Exactly.

David Senra Perfect place. Thanks for taking the time to do this.

Kurt MacAlpine Thanks, man.

David Senra Awesome.

Kurt MacAlpine Appreciate it.

David Senra I hope you enjoyed this episode. Please remember to subscribe wherever you're listening and leave a review. And make sure you listen to my other podcast, Founders. For almost a decade, I've obsessively read over 400 biographies of history's greatest entrepreneurs, searching for ideas that you can use in your work. Most of the guests you hear on this show first found me through Founders.

来源：YouTube

item.title: 硅谷坐标 x 谷歌DeepMind研究副总裁 Ed H. Chi（纪怀新）：个性化通用助理的未来
item.category: 硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector
item.description: 通用助理仍处早期，权限与可靠性尚无实际订票数据；Ed Chi预计6–12个月后，其与AI Mode Search的界面关系会更清晰。模型能力若普及，Google全栈及低成本token供给或成成本护城河；能力差距收窄则可能让价值更多流向重视黏性与体验的应用。
item.content:encoded:
硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector · Ed H. Chi（纪怀新）、曹卿云 Qingyun Cao · 2026-10-18 · 32 min · 原语言 ZH

通用助理仍处早期，权限与可靠性尚无实际订票数据；Ed Chi预计6–12个月后，其与AI Mode Search的界面关系会更清晰。模型能力若普及，Google全栈及低成本token供给或成成本护城河；能力差距收窄则可能让价值更多流向重视黏性与体验的应用。

TL;DR

  • Ed Chi 判断通用助理仍处“很初期的阶段”，并给出 6–12 个月的时间表：届时通用助理与 AI Mode Search 之间的关系和 interface 会更清楚。权限与 reliability 是卡点——大家会担心把信用卡交给通用助理后，它到处乱买东西；至于它帮人买机票究竟买对还是买错，这类实际结果的数据至今还没有真正出现。他用 Grandma Test 描述通用助理的成熟标尺：“当你的 grandma 指着你的机器人骂它‘你怎么这么笨’，你就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。”
  • 他强调，经济活动最终要看 capability over cost；若模型能力普及，成本控制可能成为最重要的护城河。Google 的优势在于 full stack——从模型、application、hyperscaler、token factory 到芯片与能源控制，并有能力以最低成本提供 token。Ed 也指出，现阶段很多人还没有关注 cost。
  • 关于模型竞争力，他认为 Google 不可能放弃模型开发，理由是用户期待 Google 拥有自己的模型技术。近几个月发布偏小模型是刻意为之——通用助理和个人化应用需要小模型；更大的模型也在开发中。他还提到湾区一些 AGI-pilled tech bros 信奉 software took over the world，因此热衷 ultra-size model；他个人不希望手机应用都跑超大模型，因为计算能耗太高。
  • 他认为，把能力商品化或开源与闭源模型差距的走向说成定论还不成熟。开源模型能追上，其中一个原因是借助他合著的 Chain-of-Thought 论文所述方法研究并复制推理方式；大厂正在设法隐藏推理链，以降低被复制的可能性。Multimodality 等能力目前也还看不出会被商品化。市场并非整体都是泡沫，但不同领域可能各有泡沫；Physical Intelligence 可能有不切实际的预期，很多模型的 visual reasoning 也很糟糕。
  • 若今天创业，他认为模型能力的差距若缩小，value creation 会更多流向 application 和 token factory。Application 端看用户 lock-in、stickiness 与体验；hyperscaler 端则涉及能源用量、芯片设计、memory 与 computation 的关系，以及 on-device 计算的占比——这些仍是 open questions。
  • Memory 是他眼中尚未被充分理解的瓶颈：它不只是存取，也涉及 ranking。Transformer 的 context buffer 目前约一两百万 tokens，在他看来完全不够；从认知角度，memory 也是一种 program。至于 DRAM、NAND、HDD 的供应短缺，他认为 memory 与 computation 可以互相转换，长期投资规划也能降低对一时短缺的担忧。
  • 商业化的下一波，他看好 consumer 崛起——Anthropic、OpenAI 的收入有很多由 enterprise subscription 带动，而 consumer services 是他留在 Google 的原因之一。推理能力从三四年前解决小学生数学题、当时 accuracy 只有 33%，发展到如今能解 Navier–Stokes 这样的数学问题，但能力仍集中在特定领域。AlphaGo 之后下棋的人反而更多；大语言模型时代，Google 也看到 search 应用增加而非减少。他认为，即使解决了 software 问题，也不代表所有问题都解决了。

Digest

1. 推理三四年登顶：从小学数学 33% 到 Navier–Stokes，但仍集中在特定领域

  • Ed Chi 的开场坐标：过去 30 年、尤其前 20 年，关注的很多是 recommendation 和 search；近 10 年，借助神经网络的 next-token prediction 与 Chain-of-Thought，才开始发掘机器的基本认知与推理能力。下一步的学术问题包括更复杂的 reasoning、memory，以及 RSI（recursive self-improvement）。
  • 他给的跨度最具冲击力：写 CoT paper 时，模型解决的是小学生数学问题，accuracy 只有 33%；如今最大的模型已能解决 Millennium Prize Problems 中的数学问题，例如 Navier–Stokes equations。他认为推理能力在三四年间已达到一个巅峰。
  • 但他随即补充，这些推理能力仍集中在特定领域。他以自己的高尔夫爱好举例：模型对高尔夫原理、球杆、球和装备的理解及推理能力究竟如何？“这些都和数学不一样”，做应用前必须弄清模型在不同领域的推理水平。

2. 通用助理极早期：Grandma Test 与六到十二个月的 interface 走向

  • 主持人曹卿云提到 Instinct 和刚发布的 Muse Spark 带来的个人助理讨论。Ed 的框架是：Google 的 AI Mode Search 属于 consumer service；大型语言模型应用中最大的一类事实上从搜索开始，后来发展成 AI Mode 这样的搜索或问答方式。Muse、Instinct 则想从问答走向能订机票、订旅店、买东西的通用助理。
  • 卡点在权限与 reliability：大家会担心把信用卡交给通用助理后，它到处乱买东西。2026 年初，OpenClaw 这样的探索让大小厂开始试水；但让助理买机票究竟买对还是买错，这类实际结果的数据还没有真正出现。他预测，未来 6 个月到 1 年，通用助理与 AI Mode Search 的关系和 interface 会更清楚。
  • 谈到产品护城河，他强调用户体验与容错：consumer 产品只要犯过一次严重错误，用户就可能改变看法。他在台湾参加另一个 podcast 时提出过 Grandma Test：有一天，grandma 指着机器人骂它“你怎么这么笨”，就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。由于 grandma 对通用助理的期待很高，严重错误会让人觉得产品有问题；目前大家仍在探索这个边界。
  • 对“现象级产品会从哪家公司出来”的问题，他认为来源有时没那么重要，关键是如何普及、什么才是正确的人机 interface。初创公司做出产品后也可能被大厂收购；他希望行业能有一个 healthy ecosystem，让大家都能探索。

3. Google 不会放弃模型开发；长远看要衡量 capability over cost

  • 面对主持人关于 DeepMind 人事变动与模型发布节奏的提问，Ed 说 Google 没有停下模型开发。近几个月发布的模型偏小，是因为通用助理和个人化应用需要小模型；更大的模型也在开发中。他形容团队人才济济，但想做大模型的人多、资源永远不够。
  • 他表示，Google 用户会期待 Google 不用别人的模型或 open-weight 模型，而是拥有这项技术；从这个角度，Google 不可能放弃模型开发。
  • 大小模型之间的资源分配没有唯一答案。他把 ultra-size model 的热潮与湾区一些 AGI-pilled tech bros 的信念联系起来：他们相信 software took over the world，做好 coding 和 software 就能 take over the world。但他个人不希望手机应用都用超大模型，因为计算能耗太高。
  • 主持人提出 CapEx 投入和现金流压力后，Ed 从长短期投资角度回应：短期公司会盯着 quality、accuracy；以 5 年、10 年为尺度投资，则要想清楚应优化什么 metric，不只看 capability，也看 capability over cost。他说 Google 会多重布局：模型、application、chip 和整个 full stack 都在创新；公司有能力以最低成本提供 token。若模型能力变得普及，cost control 可能成为最重要的护城河。

4. Memory 不只是存取，也涉及 ranking；context buffer 一两百万 tokens 远远不够

  • 对 DRAM、NAND、HDD 可能短缺的问题，Ed 提到过去的研究指出 memory 与 computation 可以互相转换：有长远投资计划，就不必太担心一时的 memory 短缺，因为可以用 computation 代替。Memory 研究还要考虑计算方法需要多少 memory 和 bandwidth，以及神经网络设计是否应该降低 memory requirement。他举例说，Timi 做出的 Delta Attention Model，其计算和内存用法不同于 full attention、O(n²) attention 或 sparse attention。
  • 这还只是 sequential Transformer model 的 memory 问题；个人化应用、KV cache，以及日常所说的 memory 也有各自的问题。从人类认知角度看，memory 也是一种 program：它不是没有生命的东西，而是不断变化、指导事情如何发生，并用来编程 AGI machinery 的 program。研究因此也关注底层 memory 运用与 context buffer 里的信息整理。
  • 他指出两个 bottleneck：Transformer 的 context buffer 目前大约能做到 1 million 或 2 million tokens，在他看来完全不够；更根本的是，大家常把 memory 看成存储与提取的 retrieval 机制，而没有把它当作人类认知或思考能力的一部分。
  • 他的修正是：“memory 事实上是一个 ranking 的问题。”比如提到 Paris，人会想起去巴黎时相关的记忆中较重要的内容，而不是所有与 Paris 有关的东西一下子涌出来。
  • 对 memory layer 初创公司能否立足的问题，他说硬件领域已有一些大厂之外的新想法，也有大厂在做；memory 与 computation 的关系未来几年可能会有新发展。

5. 能力差距缩小会把价值推向 application 和 token factory；开源追赶部分得益于 CoT 方法

  • 他的创业方向判断是：模型 capability 开始有一点 commoditize 的迹象，但并非完全商品化。如果最好与最差模型之间的 gap 缩小，value creation 就会更多流向 application 和 token factory。Application 端要看用户 lock-in、stickiness 与体验；hyperscaler 端涉及能源用量、芯片设计、memory 与 computation 的关系，以及多少计算会在 on-device 完成——这些仍是 open questions。
  • 谈到开源模型追上闭源模型，他说原因之一是自己合著的 Chain-of-Thought 论文：研究者用 CoT 方法发掘模型里的思维链，再研究模型的思考模式、复制其推理方式。大厂如今也在设法把推理链藏起来，降低被复制的可能性；multimodality 等能力也可能很难复制。他认为，把能力的商品化趋势说成定论还不成熟：有些 capability 会因蒸馏变得更 commoditize，有些目前还看不出会 commoditize，相关问题仍有很多 debate。
  • 对 AI 市场是否有泡沫，他不认为整体都是泡沫，但认为不同地方可能有不同泡沫；例如 Physical Intelligence 可能存在一些不切实际的预期。他还指出，很多模型的 visual reasoning capability 很糟糕。
  • 他认为现实与信念并不总是一致。如果相信 software 问题一解决，所有问题就都解决了，那么他前面谈到的很多事就不适用；但如果认为解决 software 仍不等于解决所有问题，“我们还有很多戏可以唱”。

6. 下一波看 consumer：硬件与人机 interface 仍有探索空间

  • 谈到 coding 之后的机会，Ed 说 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的收入有很多由 enterprise subscription 带动；他看好 consumer 接下来的崛起。他继续留在 Google 的原因之一，是 consumer services 一直是 Google 的强项，但他也不排除未来出现新领域。
  • 他从整个行业角度谈未来产品形态：可能是 super app，也可能是整个手机发生变化；眼镜、耳环、耳机乃至衣着都可能变化。他认为 consumer hardware 仍有很多探索空间，包括 on-device 与 off-device 模型的交互；Apple 曾提出 hybrid intelligence 的概念。
  • 他还回顾，家里的智能音箱做了四年后，突然好像没人做了；以前有人喊着做智能冰箱，而从私人通用助理角度看，冰箱上放个屏幕、连上 Internet，就能把智能做起来，比七八年前简单多了。进入通用助理时代后，人们也不应该还得整天给机器人下载 app——那是 15 年前担心的问题。
  • 收尾谈到 AI 与教育，他用 AlphaGo 作类比：近 10 年前 Google 开发 AlphaGo，很多人在它和棋王对决后说人类以后不下棋了；结果下棋的人和想研究围棋的人反而更多。他认为数学也可能如此：AI 能解 Navier–Stokes，不一定会让人不想学数学，反而可能吸引更多人。研究动力或许会从探索知识边界，转向理解、娱乐和乐趣，让更多人出于好奇心做研究。
  • 他还提到围棋应用降低了学习门槛、激励更多小朋友学棋；大语言模型出现后，Google 看到 search 的应用增加而不是减少。AI 会改变现有结构，也可能带来新机会；他认为 enterprise 和 consumer 领域都“creativity seems to be everywhere”。

Full transcript

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 开源模型之所以能够追上闭源模型，其中一个原因是我合著了 Chain-of-Thought 这篇论文。他们用 Chain-of-Thought 的方法来复制推理方式。等到有一天，你的 grandma 指着你的机器人骂它“你怎么这么笨”，你就知道，通用助理的时代真的到了。所有 AI 产品最终都要看 capability over cost，这是毋庸置疑的。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 你怎么看 DeepMind 在大模型竞争中的实力？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这是一个很好的问题。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao Ed，很高兴今天能来采访你。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 嗯。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今天你在 panel 上讲了哪些内容？能跟我们 recap 一下吗？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 当然可以。我今天最主要想让大家知道的是，过去 30 年，特别是前 20 年，我们关注的很多都是推荐和搜索。但过去 10 年，因为神经网络的发展，我们已经知道怎么用 next-token prediction 和 Chain-of-Thought 的方法，发掘机器的一些基本认知和推理能力。

从思维链这个部分，我们可以做出一些思考动作。它的由来和背后的理念是什么？今天我跟大家分享的就是这些基本认知，以及怎么思考下一步更复杂的 reasoning、memory 问题，或者 RSI，也就是 recursive self-improvement 的问题。这些都是未来学术研究需要思考的方向。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 嗯哼。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 今天我们想跟您探讨一下 consumer AI 这个方向。最近硅谷很火的 Instinct，还有刚刚发布的 Muse Spark，都让我们觉得，个人助理似乎又掀起了新一轮讨论。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 对。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 您怎么看个人助理这样的产品？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 从 personalization，也就是个人化的角度来看，Google 的 AI Mode Search 这类能力，原本就属于 consumer services。大型语言模型应用中最大的一类，事实上是从搜索开始的，后来才发展成 AI Mode 这样的搜索或问答方式。

Muse 或 Instinct 想从问答往通用助理发展，也就是说，它甚至可以帮我们做一些事情，比如订机票、订旅店或者买东西。这方面会涉及很多权限问题。之前的 reliability 还不够高，大家会担心把信用卡交给通用助理之后，它到处乱买东西。

所以，2026 年刚开始时，OpenClaw 这样的探索让大家慢慢了解这项技术。现在一些小厂和大厂都在探索通用助理服务。我个人认为，我们仍处于非常初期的阶段。比如说，你让它帮你买机票，买对了还是买错了，这类问题我们还没有真正看到新的数据。

我预测，未来 6 个月到 1 年，我们会更清楚通用助理和刚才提到的 AI Mode 搜索之间的关系，以及它们的 interface 会是什么样子。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 对，你们 envision 的未来消费级 AI 应用是什么样子的？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这是我个人的观点，不代表 Google 公司的观点。我一直觉得，AI 的推理能力在不断增强。你们想想看，三四年前我们写 Chain-of-Thought 这篇论文时，解决的是小学生的数学问题；到了今年，我们已经在解决 Navier–Stokes equations 这样的物理或数学领域中最困难的问题。这代表它的推理能力在三四年里已经达到了一个巅峰。

不过，到目前为止，这些推理能力还是比较集中在一些特定领域。通用助理的 universal 部分，比如它对产品的推理能力如何？我个人是个高尔夫球爱好者，那么它对高尔夫球的原理、设备的理解，以及对球杆、球这些东西的推理能力到底有多少？这些都和数学不一样。所以我们做这方面的应用时，一定要了解模型对不同领域的推理能力达到了什么水平。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 其实我们感觉，个人助理现在很简单，有时候就是在 text message 里。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 对。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 或者是一个 app。您觉得好的个人助理，它的护城河是什么？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 我觉得很多人会认为，特别是在 consumer 领域，真正的护城河往往是用户对产品的体验。用户怎么感受这个产品？有些人比较保守，是因为产品只要犯过一次很严重的错误，你可能就会改变对它的看法。

不管它是 AI 通用助理，还是你花钱请来的私人助理，无论是在家里还是公司，你对它做出错误决定或错误行为的容忍度有多高，都是同一个问题。之前我在台湾参加另一个 podcast 时，提出过一个叫 Grandma Test 的概念：有一天，你的 grandma 指着机器人骂它“你怎么这么笨”，你就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。

因为 grandma 对通用助理的期待非常高。如果它犯的错误很严重，你就会觉得有问题。所以现在无论是从产品角度，还是从科学角度，我们都在探索这个边界。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 你觉得跟现在市场上已有的竞争对手相比，谷歌做消费者 AI 产品的优势是什么？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 从 consumer 的整个 ecosystem 来看，可以分成 software 和 hardware 两部分。有很多公司现在关注的是 hardware，比如记忆体和产业链上的问题。hardware 这边看起来还有很多探索机会，其中一个原因是 on-device 和 off-device 模型之间的交互问题。比如 Apple 之前提出过 hybrid intelligence 这样的概念。未来 consumer hardware 会怎么发展，我认为还是一个很大的空白。

另一边是 software。我们现在讲的当然是 services，而不是 downloadable software 或 downloadable apps。我觉得比较有意思的是，未来人们会通过搜索这样的渠道进入通用助理的环境，还是通过手机、智能眼镜或其他设备？

过去一两年，我们已经看到 software services 这边有一些很新颖、比较大胆的探索，但我觉得还没有得出任何结论。比如，为什么我现在还是得整天想着我的 app 有没有更新？这是我们 15 年前担心的问题。进入通用助理时代后，你不应该还得整天往机器人身上下载 app，对吧？所以 consumer services 这边基本上也还处于起步阶段。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 如果未来有一个现象级的消费级产品，你觉得它会是谷歌、Meta 这样的公司做出来的，还是像 Apple 这样做硬件的公司，或者是某家初创公司？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 从整个生态系统来看，它是从哪里来的，可能有时候反而没那么重要。重要的是它怎么普及，以及什么才是和人互动的正确 interface。从科学家的角度来看，研究这方面的人会觉得这是最有意思的地方。

如果是一些初创公司开始做这些事情，也有可能被大厂收购。所以从投资人或开发者的角度来看，大家希望未来能有一个 healthy ecosystem，让整个行业都可以探索这个领域。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 关于 DeepMind，我们看到有很多人事变动。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 嗯。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 模型发布的节奏也有一些变化。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 嗯。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 您怎么看 DeepMind、谷歌的模型在整个 Frontier Lab 里的竞争力？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这是一个很好的问题。我们当然没有停下脚步，一直在继续发展模型。最近几个月我们发布的一些模型可能比较小型，因为我们想把小模型用在应用上。像刚才聊到的很多通用助理和个人化应用，事实上都需要小模型，而不是大模型。

大模型的好处是推理能力更强。最近这段时间，我们发布的模型大部分稍微小一点，希望能在应用上有更多提升。当然，我们也在开发更大的模型，大家可以拭目以待。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 明白。所以，前沿的 AGI 目标还会继续追求，谷歌的算力也还是会给这些 AGI 模型，对吗？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 对。从整个生态系统发展的角度来看，如果你有很多资源，该把多少放在 application development 上，多少放在大模型、更强推理能力的模型或 coding capability 模型上？从长远来看，这件事见仁见智，并没有唯一的答案。

现在所谓 AGI-pilled 的那帮人，特别是在湾区、旧金山的这些 tech bros，会觉得 software took over the world。只要把 coding 和 software 做好，就能 take over the world。所以大家才会这么热衷于超级大模型，也就是 ultra-size model。

但从我们刚才聊的话题来看，比如应用的普及、手机上的应用，这些东西以后不见得都需要 ultra-size model。至少我个人不希望它们都用超大模型，因为这类计算需要的能量实在太高。所以大模型和小模型之间的平衡，事实上连大厂内部的投资分配都是一个难题。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 那你觉得 DeepMind 跟其他 Frontier Lab 相比，团队的优势是什么？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 我觉得我们这边可能是人才济济。人才实在太多了，大家都想做大模型，但资源永远不够。

我觉得可以从另一个角度来看。Google 的用户对 Google 一定会有一种期待，希望我们的模型不是用别人的，也不是用 open-weight 模型。他们一定希望 Google 拥有这项技术，这或许可以说是一种技术主权。所以从这个角度来说，Google 不可能放弃模型开发，这完全不可能发生。

Google 的一个优势是它是一家 full-stack company。我们在公司内部开发模型，也做 application 和 services；再往下有 hyperscaler、token factory，甚至芯片开发，还有底层能源的使用和控制。我们有能力以最低的成本提供 token，这种控制能力将来可能是最重要的护城河。

如果模型能力变得普及，最重要的可能就是 cost control，也就是以最低的成本提供最好的 capability。现在这个领域的很多人还没有关注 cost，但所有经济活动最终都要看 capability over cost，这是毋庸置疑的。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 大家会担心 Frontier Lab 已经投了很多 CapEx，今年、明年可能更夸张。特别是像谷歌这样的大厂，现金流也被拖成了负的。我们看到 cloud 这块的 revenue 有起色，margin 也在增强，但 AI 应用的收入可能还没体现出来。刚刚听您说，之后谷歌也会继续把重点放在应用上，提高应用的 IOI。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 没错。你可以这样讲，从长远角度来看，如果你是一家 short-term 的公司，就会只想着 quality、accuracy 这些问题。如果你是一家着眼长远的公司，按照 5 年、10 年来投资，就会开始想未来是什么，真正应该 optimize 的 metric 是什么。不见得只有 capability，也要看 capability over cost。

谷歌最厉害的地方事实上就在这里。它在技术和很多其他领域都会做多重布局。只要有可能，这边投一点，那边也投一点。它不是不肯 innovate，而是在各个地方都 innovate。我们不只在模型上创新，也在 application 和 chip 上创新，整个 full stack 都在做 innovation。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 因为您现在也在做 memory 方面的研究。我们知道谷歌的哲学是能存的东西就尽量存，而现在整个 memory supply chain 又出现短缺，DRAM、NAND，还有 HDD 可能都短缺。你们怎么 balance 这个问题？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 从 computer science 的角度来看，以前的研究已经告诉我们，memory 和 computation 之间可以转换：有时候你需要更多 memory，有时候你可以用更多 computation。如果你有一个长远的 investment plan，就不太会担心一时的 memory 短缺，因为可以用 computation 来代替。

所以现在的 memory research，不只是供应链和 hardware 的问题，也要看计算方法需要多少 memory、多少 memory bandwidth，以及神经网络的设计是否应该降低 memory requirement。计算方法也有影响。比如 Timi 做出来的模型叫 Delta Attention Model，它的计算和内存用法，跟 full attention、O(n²) attention 或 sparse attention 模型都不一样。

这只是 sequential Transformer model 里面的 memory 问题，我们还没聊到个人化应用里的 memory 问题、KV cache 的 memory 问题，以及我们平常所说的 memory。我们常常讲的是硬件或软件里的记忆，但从人类认知的角度来看，memory 也是一种 program。它不只是一个没有生命的东西，而是一个不断变化、指导事情该如何发生的东西，是一个用来编程 AGI machinery 的 program。

所以我们做研究时，也会关注的不只是底层 memory 的运用，还包括 context buffer 里的信息整理，以及 context buffer 相关的研究。我们在这方面也花了很多精力。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 现在最大的 bottleneck 在哪里？memory 研究最大的挑战是什么？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 我个人认为，从 Transformer 模型的角度来看，我们现在最大的 context buffer 大概可以做到 1 million 或 2 million tokens。在我看来，这完全不够，这是一个 bottleneck。

另外，我们对 memory 的看法往往还是把它当成存储和提取，也就是 memory retrieval 机制。但我们没有把它看成人类认知或思考能力的一部分。memory 事实上非常重要，不只是 retrieval。我认为这也是研究上的一个 bottleneck，大家还没有把 memory 这个东西想清楚。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 对，感觉人脑可以主动遗忘、学习新东西，还能把原来的东西压缩起来。这基本上就是模型现在的 continual learning 问题。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 没错。很多学过 computer science 的人会觉得，机器的 memory 不需要这么想，它不需要忘记东西。但事实并非如此。很多人觉得 memory 是你还记不记得的问题，事实上 memory 是一个 ranking 问题：什么东西最重要，这才是 memory 真正重要的地方。

memory 最重要的问题之一就是 ranking。比如我随便说一个地点，Paris，你会想起去巴黎时有什么记忆。这事实上是一个 ranking 问题，而不是把所有跟 Paris 有关的东西一下子全部涌出来。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 所以现在有很多创业公司专门在做 memory layer。您觉得 memory 这么重要，应该由初创公司来做，还是基本上都由大厂来做？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 现在硬件领域也有一些人在想怎么把 memory 和 computation 结合起来，有一些新想法并不是在大厂里做。当然，大厂也有人在做这方面的事情。我觉得 memory 和 computation 之间的关系，未来几年可能会有一些新的发展。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 如果您今天要出来创业，您觉得最好的创业方向是什么？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这是个好问题。我觉得现在有一个趋势：模型的 capability 好像开始有一点 commoditize 了。我不是说它完全 commoditize，而是说，如果最好的模型和最差的模型之间的 gap 变小一些，value creation 就会往 application 和 token factory 这两边走，因为大家都在找护城河。

当 model capability 不再是最强的护城河时，就得去别的地方找。application 这边可能要看用户 lock-in、stickiness，以及使用体验有多好。hyperscaler 那边则有很多和 cost 有关的问题，比如能源使用量、芯片设计得好不好、memory 和 computation 之间的关系有没有处理好，以及未来有多少会在 on-device 上完成、多少不会在 on-device 上完成。

所以在我看来，这些都还是 open questions，非常 exciting。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 您怎么看开源模型和闭源模型？现在我们知道开源模型追得很紧，您觉得未来这个 gap 会变大还是变小？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这个问题非常有意思。开源模型之所以能够追上闭源模型，其中一个原因是我的论文。我合著的 Chain-of-Thought 这篇论文，他们用 Chain-of-Thought 的方法发掘模型里的思维链。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 嗯。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 他们研究模型的思考模式，然后用这种思考模式来复制它的推理方式。现在大厂里有很多工作在想办法把推理链、思维链藏起来。藏起来之后，被复制的可能性就会更低。

事实上不只是这个问题。我认为模型继续发展之后，比如 multimodality 的 capability，也会很难复制。所以我觉得很多人好像把这件事说得像是定论，但我个人认为这种想法还不成熟。看起来有些 capability 会因为蒸馏而变得更 commoditize，但有些 capability 到目前为止还看不出会 commoditize。现在有很多 debate。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 大家好像觉得开源模型能做的事情越来越多，留给 SOTA 模型 monetization 的空间就更小了。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 嗯。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 您会担心它能不能撑起这样的估值和这么大的 CapEx 吗？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 这就是为什么有人会想，AI 市场是不是有一部分存在泡沫。我不觉得整个市场都是泡沫，但不同地方肯定有不同的泡沫。比如 Physical Intelligence 可能有一些不切实际的预期。刚才讲的 multimodality 这一块，很多模型的 visual reasoning capability 也非常糟糕。

这就能看出，现实和大家的信念并不一样。如果你觉得 software took over the world，认为我们用 agent 解决了 software 的问题，所有问题就都解决了，那我刚才讲的很多事情就不适用了。但如果你觉得即使解决了 software，也没有解决所有问题，那我们还有很多戏可以唱。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 现在很多 Frontier Lab 已经在 coding 上实现了商业化。您觉得下一个更 exciting 的机会可能在哪些领域？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 刚才讲到，Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的收入有很多是由 enterprise 这边的 subscription 带动的。我挺看好 consumer 这块接下来的崛起。

当然，从龙头公司的角度来说，我为什么还留在 Google、继续在 Google 工作，原因就是 consumer services 一直是 Google 最强的地方之一。这不代表未来不会出现新的领域，大家拭目以待。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 接下来我们该期待什么样的产品？比如谷歌未来一两年有没有什么 AI 产品值得期待？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 我从整个 industry 的角度来回答这个问题。我觉得现在已经有人在想，未来会是 super app 的时代，还是整个手机都会改变？甚至我们佩戴在身上的眼镜、耳环、耳机，都会有很大的变化，甚至衣着也会改变。

家里的智能音箱，我们之前做了四年，突然好像就没人做了。以前还喊着要做智能冰箱。从私人通用助理的角度来看，冰箱上放个屏幕、连上 Internet，就可以把智能做起来。这比七八年前要简单多了。所以我觉得 consumer hardware 这边还是相当 exciting 的。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 我的问题问完了。您有什么想补充的吗？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 没有，我觉得你问的问题都很好。作为一个科学家，我觉得特别 exciting 的地方是，大家都能看出来，不管是在 enterprise 还是 consumer 这边，creativity seems to be everywhere。

我刚才在台上也分享过，当年我们做 Chain-of-Thought 思维链研究的时候，解决的只是小学生的问题，比如 1 加 1 等于 2，或者买了 5 个苹果，又买了 6 个苹果，一共有多少个苹果，5 加 6 等于 11。当时我们的模型 accuracy 也只有 33%。

现在我们刚刚经历了最大的模型，它已经可以解决 Millennium Prize Problems 中的数学问题，比如 Navier–Stokes equations。从这个角度来看，我们现在能想象到的 capability 肯定还不够，它还会继续扩展。对科学家来说，这是非常 exciting 的事情。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 很多人觉得现在 AI 已经能把数学做得这么好。如果要从小培养孩子，他们的时间应该花在数学上吗？还是应该把更多精力放在 AI 解决不了的问题上？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 我觉得这个问题很有意思。快 10 年前，我们在 Google 开发 AlphaGo 时，很多人在它和棋王对决之后就说：“完了，人类以后不下棋了。”结果后来下棋的人反而更多了，想研究围棋的人也更多了。

我觉得数学也一样。很多人会觉得，既然现在连 Navier–Stokes equations 都能用这种方法解决，以后就没人想学数学了。我觉得有可能恰恰相反，会有更多人觉得数学这么有意思，想要去研究它。以前的动力可能是探索知识的边界，但现在很多动力会来自理解，也会来自娱乐或乐趣。

所以以后从事数学研究的人，可能会更多地出于内心的好奇心去研究。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 有没有可能以前数学的门槛很高，如果把数学变成 AI 可以使用的工具，很多文科生也可以利用这样的工具去解决更多、更有创造性的问题？

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 以前学围棋，你得请教练、找老师，还要找棋力相当的朋友一起下棋，花很多时间。现在拿个手机，就可以下载一些相当不错的围棋应用，反而带动了围棋界很多小朋友学习，也有很多人在用这些软件。

这事实上激励了很多人。这也和刚才讲的 search engine 有关系。当时很多人会觉得，大语言模型来了，search engine 就没那么 relevant 了。但 Google 反而看到很多 search 的应用在增加，而不是减少。

所以我觉得还是有一些乐观的地方。当然我不否认，它会改变我们现有的很多结构，但也会带来新的可能性。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 对。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 嗯，非常感谢。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 哪里。

曹卿云 Qingyun Cao 非常非常感谢。

Ed H. Chi（纪怀新） 谢谢，谢谢。

来源：YouTube

item.title: Flying Tesla Car, Robot Brains Halving in Cost Every 3 Weeks, and Why Incentives Decide AI Alignment
item.description: RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark showed robot-subtask costs down 84%, from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September. As intelligence gets cheaper, hardware and supply chains may constrain deployment; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Tesla’s flying Roadster is planned for 2028, but regulation and insurance remain unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Moonshots · Peter Diamandis、Salim Ismail、Emad Mostaque、Anousheh Ansari · 2026-10-17 · 106 min · 原语言 EN

RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark showed robot-subtask costs down 84%, from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September. As intelligence gets cheaper, hardware and supply chains may constrain deployment; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Tesla’s flying Roadster is planned for 2028, but regulation and insurance remain unresolved.

TL;DR

  • The cost for a frontier AI model to complete a physical robot subtask fell 84% in two months — from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September on YC startup RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark. The panel discusses task costs halving every three weeks; Peter Diamandis says that trend could make robotic intelligence effectively cost nothing within a year. Emad Mostaque cites Unitree’s CEO questioning whether specialist robot models are still needed, while the group discusses how generalist models could move value toward hardware and the robotic supply chain. Mostaque calls the three-week pace potentially the fastest-moving capability they have seen, compared with AI doubling every 10 weeks and Moore’s law’s 18 months.
  • Robots’ hardware and supply chain may become the constraint as model costs fall. Salim Ismail says entrepreneurs should build robots, actuators, and spare parts. Figure’s Brett Adcock has committed $1 billion for data, while Diamandis predicts foundation-model companies will also seek robotics data; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Diamandis says Elon Musk is building a million Optimus robots for next year, with a plan to reach 10 million; Mostaque says 1.7 million Optimuses would overtake Tesla in revenue.
  • Tesla unveiled a flying Roadster in Waco — 0–60 in under a second, SpaceX-derived air-thruster technology, a one-seater rocket version at 0.66 seconds, 230 mph top speed, 300-mile range, and production planned for 2028. Tesla shares rose 5% on the news. Diamandis predicts a Tesla–SpaceX merger announcement before year-end. Ismail calls the car an example of technologies outpacing regulatory and insurance systems; the discussion raises, but does not settle, who would regulate or insure it.
  • A test of 50 unpublished, research-level theoretical physics problems produced conflicting score figures in the discussion. Diamandis says the initial report was 49/50, noting that the published answer to the 50th problem was wrong and Astra had it right; Mostaque later says it scored 42/50. The problems were estimated to take a world-class physicist about a day each, and the reported cost was roughly $3 per problem. Mostaque says some major physics problems may be solved another way within half a year; Ismail gives a separate enterprise example, with a KYC pilot reducing 22-step workflows to four.
  • XPRIZE’s leverage figures: 36 prizes over 32 years, roughly $550 million in prize purses, and more than $30 billion in measured impact. Diamandis describes the $30 billion as driven R&D; Anousheh Ansari clarifies that the figure also includes investment, and says teams received about $12 billion in investment. The prize model is said to drive about $62 in economic value per prize dollar. New initiatives discussed include organ biostasis, a $5 million Habitable Worlds prize, and an Interspecies Communication Prize.
  • The panel frames AI alignment partly as an incentives problem: a race with China and between labs, engagement incentives that encourage sycophancy, reward hacking, and evaluation gaming. Peter Diamandis says models can be trained to win “at all costs,” without a higher moral aim. Mostaque argues for intentional training curricula, using a city as a metaphor for how models develop; the discussion also considers insurance standards and alignment prizes.
  • The purpose discussion asks what happens when machines do more of the work. Ismail says many corporate workers are dissatisfied and argues people may spend more time “being” as machines take on more “doing.” Diamandis points to the Abundance Prize’s target of housing, food, healthcare, and education for a family of four at $1,000 a month. The group also discusses meaning through creativity, relationships, community, and shared purpose.

Digest

1. Tesla’s flying Roadster: fan suction, SpaceX air thrusters, 0–60 in under a second

  • The demo, next to SpaceX’s McGregor test site: the Roadster drove up a multistory curved ramp upside down — not with magnets or rails, but with a fan-suction system holding it against 2 Gs — then flew. The flight hardware was described as borrowed from SpaceX: two carbon-overwrapped pressure vessels totaling 600 liters, about 250 kilos of air, and 10 nozzles. The car can recharge its air tank; as the demo put it, “it literally just puffs itself up.”
  • The specs given: three versions — performance (0–60 in 1.6 seconds), thrust (0.9 seconds), and a one-seater rocket version described as “air-ready” (0–60 in 0.66 seconds and reportedly 380 km/h); top speed 230 mph, 300-mile range, production starting in 2028, no price given, and Tesla shares up 5%. Hover duration wasn’t disclosed; Ismail thought it would be a few seconds and said hopping cars weren’t the point.
  • Diamandis’s caveat: “The real miracle will be whether they can ship it on time, rather than whether it flies.” Ismail’s strategic point is talent — “it raises the bar… if you’re a top engineer, where do you go and work?” Diamandis also noted Musk’s 2018 tweets about putting thrusters on cars.

2. Who regulates a rocket car? The discussion’s institutional stress test

  • Diamandis asks whether DOT, the FAA, or nobody regulates it. Ismail’s broader framing is that regulatory scaffolding and institutions for insurance and safety lag behind new technologies; he says Musk is “two generations ahead” in capability. Diamandis suggests the car is street-legal, and Ismail argues existing rules may leave room for rockets or thrusters on a car. The speakers do not establish a definitive regulatory answer.
  • Insurance remains an open question: Diamandis says he does not think it is insurable; Ismail jokes that an insurer might require the thrusters to stay off, or that the company might offer its own insurance. Diamandis predicts a Tesla–SpaceX merger announcement before year-end.
  • The positive flip on autonomy: an AI safety layer could help with human driving. In Saudi Arabia and the Emirates, Diamandis says, young men die in sports cars that outperform their ability to think and react; Ismail says AI could intervene when traction is lost. He compares it to anti-lock braking generalized to “try not to kill the human, despite what the human does.” Diamandis calls that “the answer to alignment”; Ismail adds, “despite our stupidity.”

3. Robot brains halving in cost every three weeks

  • The headline curve: frontier-model cost per robot subtask fell from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September, an 84% drop. Diamandis frames the progression as the robot’s body getting good, then its hands, with the mind as the remaining question; he says the benchmark shows generalist models can win. Mostaque connects the trend to Unitree’s CEO questioning whether specialist models are still necessary. Unitree robots, Diamandis says, went from “stumbling about like little drunkards” to kung fu and synchronized movements.
  • On hardware, Mostaque says the Wuji hands cost about $8,000, down from $20,000, and have more dexterity than a human hand — though a laundry robot would not need that. Ismail says robotics task costs are halving every three weeks. Diamandis argues that robotic intelligence and locomotion could effectively become free, leaving hardware costs; he suggests the result could be an explosion in robotics.
  • The generalization surprise: when asked about world models, Mostaque says they are not needed for this. He points to Sonnet, Opus, and 3.8 Flash models seeming to understand 3D and create 3D assets, though he says nobody is quite sure how. Ismail’s bottom line is that models across modalities are getting good enough, fast enough, and cheap enough at the same time. Mostaque also cites video models falling from 50 cents per second for high quality to 0.1 cents per second, faster than real time.
  • For hardware entrepreneurs, Ismail’s answer is to build as many robots, actuators, and spare parts for the robotic supply chain as possible. On training data, Diamandis says Figure’s Brett Adcock has committed $1 billion for data and speculates that foundation-model companies will also seek robotics data. Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data.
  • The scale figures discussed: Diamandis says Musk is building a million Optimus robots for next year, with plans to reach 10 million. Mostaque says 1.7 million Optimuses would overtake Tesla in revenue.

4. Where robots land first — and the dog-in-the-laundry problem

  • Ismail’s proposed sequence: robots start in “dull, dirty, and dangerous” jobs such as toxic cleanups and underwater manufacturing; homes may come later because of liability. Diamandis argues that the capability curve could move beyond those jobs in the next year. Mostaque responds that there must be a business case and that a supply chain for billions of robots does not yet exist; he says the household ROI will take time.
  • On surgery, Ismail says he is especially excited about robots doing it. He argues that patients may not want a surgeon’s first 10 heart surgeries, or a surgeon who has become inattentive after thousands; AI could smooth that curve, with the best doctor supporting the system at first and robots eventually doing the procedures. Diamandis recalls Musk’s prediction that robots would perform perfect surgery within three years. Diamandis also points to federated learning across robots as a way to share experience from millions of cases.
  • The edge-case discussion starts with Diamandis worrying that a robot could mistake his teddy-bear-looking designer dog for laundry and put it in the washing machine. Ansari says safety around pets and children needs solving because robots are large, heavy machines. She also argues that the models will be superintelligent; Mostaque says a generalist model should recognize the dog and make better decisions than most humans. He contrasts this with a specialized model, where “your dog loses in the laundry.”
  • Ismail says he does not believe the humanoid form is ultimately the right form factor. Ansari adds that some tasks need specialized bodies or “Transformers,” while generalist models could work across form factors. Ismail imagines spare-parts companies and robots with sockets for different arms or bodies; Mostaque notes that not every task needs highly dexterous hands.

5. A world-class physicist’s day of work, compared with $3 per problem

  • The setup: 50 unpublished, research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers and nothing to look up online; each was estimated to take a world-class physicist about a day. Diamandis says the reported cost was $3 per problem. He recounts the initial report that GPT-6 Astra got 49/50, then says the published answer for the 50th problem was wrong and Astra got it right. Mostaque later says it scored 42/50, without the transcript reconciling the two figures.
  • Mostaque’s generalization is that AI is better than people in verifiable domains and can help verify work, enabling more complex systems. Ismail’s enterprise example: a KYC banking pilot reduced 22-step workflows to four, which he says could make organizations 10 times more efficient and effective across workflows.
  • On Millennium Prize-scale problems, including quantum gravity and unified field theory, Mostaque says he does not think they will be solved this way; he thinks they will be solved another way, but “not more than half a year.” Diamandis recalls Eric Schmidt predicting at Abundance360 that every lab would have a world-class physicist in five to six years; Diamandis says it now seems closer to two.
  • Ansari’s concern: if AI bulk-solves defined problem sets, young people may not choose those fields, while AI may not have the same curiosity to identify new problems. Mostaque’s answer is that humans can direct what is good for humanity; he says physics has only one set of laws and argues that, once frameworks are found, people can apply them to flying cars, biology, and exploration.

6. You get what you incentivize: three centuries of prize design

  • Diamandis’s hierarchy of human motivators is fear, greed, curiosity, and love, with fear strongest. He says the ratio of fear to curiosity can be measured as the ratio of defense spending to science spending. Incentive prizes differ from the Nobel model: “I don’t care who you are… if you solve this problem, you win.”
  • The examples: the 1714 Longitude Prize offered £20,000 and was won by clockmaker John Harrison with a marine chronometer. Ismail says Parliament expected an astronomer to win and refused to pay Harrison, who had to fight for the money. In 1795, the French government offered a 12,000-franc food-preservation prize, won by confectioner Nicolas Appert, who invented canning.
  • Diamandis says the $25,000 Orteig Prize inspired nine teams to spend $400,000 trying to win it; Lindbergh won, and the losers were not paid. The story helped inspire Diamandis’s XPRIZE model: pay for success. He says his frustration at being unable to become an astronaut led him toward commercial space; after five years and 150 pitches, Ansari, her husband, and her brother-in-law committed to the original prize. Ansari later flew privately to the space station on a Soyuz and became the first private female astronaut to fly into space.
  • The dark side: a rat-tail bounty in Hanoi in 1902 led people to cut off tails, release rats, and breed them; Wells Fargo sales quotas led employees to open about 3.5 million fake accounts. Diamandis gives ICE arrest and deportation targets as a current example of incentives producing arrests beyond the intended focus on criminals and a political backlash. In the XPRIZE discussion, speakers contrast these cases with participants motivated by solving a problem, and describe some perverse prize examples as being about execution rather than inspiration.

7. The 62x flywheel — and the dentist who nearly beat the world

  • The numbers: 36 prizes over 32 years and a total prize purse of roughly $550 million. Diamandis says XPRIZE has driven a little over $30 billion in R&D; Ansari clarifies that the impact figure includes investment as well as R&D, and says teams received about $12 billion in investment during or after their competitions. The measure also includes awareness; Diamandis says the economic value is about 62 times the prize purse.
  • The oil-cleanup prize as proof of the beginner’s mind: after the BP spill, James Cameron urged XPRIZE to act; Eric and Wendy Schmidt funded a prize aimed at doubling the cleanup rate. About 350 teams entered, and 10 were selected for testing in New Jersey. Ismail tells the second-place story: a dentist and a tattoo artist met when the dentist was getting a tattoo, possibly in Las Vegas, and formed a team. One speaker tentatively recalls that they tested their solution in a hot tub. Ismail’s point is that a conventional funder might not have backed such an unlikely team.
  • Diamandis says prizes are especially valuable where governments and markets are not doing enough — in this case, there was little economic incentive to develop oil-cleanup technology. Ansari adds that crowdsourcing draws in diverse ideas and people who are not bound by assumptions about the field.
  • The Elon carbon-removal story: Diamandis says he texted Musk to suggest an XPRIZE; Musk asked what prize and how much, and agreed to $100 million for carbon removal. The teams received about $1.4 billion in investment. Ansari says that even after adding the $100 million purse to the denominator, the prize’s impact figure rose.

8. The pipeline: organ biostasis, habitable worlds, talking to animals

  • This year’s Visioneering winner is the Bioasis Organ Biostasis Prize. The problem is that harvested organs have a limited life and must reach a suitable recipient in time. Diamandis puts the kidney waiting list at about 100,000. Ansari says the target is six months of storage; after first suggesting a current maximum of two weeks, she accepts Diamandis’s correction that it is hours, depending on the organ. Ismail says the competition will use pigs: organs must be stored and later retransplanted, with the pig viable. He identifies Sebastian, a competitor through Singularity 2012, as someone who has worked on the problem for more than a dozen years.
  • Also coming: a $5 million Habitable Worlds XPRIZE funded by John Davi. Diamandis says the prize will make telescope data available for teams to use AI to find habitable worlds; he cites about 6,200 known exoplanets and says no Earth-like exoplanet has been found. Ansari calls it a good use of AI to find a needle in a haystack.
  • Diamandis says Palmer Luckey is about to announce an Interspecies Communication Prize, using a new version of large language models to enable communication with animals. Ansari jokes that they may not want to hear what animals have to say. Ansari also describes the next Accelerate Learning competition, targeting first graders in India and Africa and aiming at deployment across schools and outside them.
  • A UAP XPRIZE is under discussion with a major funder, Diamandis says, partly to address stigma that can keep people from studying a topic. He compares that stigma with the effect of unreplicated cold-fusion results on subsequent work.
  • The wish list includes updating institutions to handle simultaneous “Gutenberg moments,” a Jet Lag XPRIZE, a Flow XPRIZE, and a prize to reduce the amygdala’s influence. Speakers also discuss eliminating greed and measuring flow. The identities behind some of these proposals are not clear in the transcript.
  • One speaker recounts that a community member received a cornea transplant after the speaker’s father died, and that the dates seemed to match. The speaker says the recipient had been thinking about the father, then describes learning that corneas were harvested and matched shortly after his death. The speaker also recounts the recipient’s discomfort with the idea that the father was “looking through my eyes.”

9. Misaligned AI is downstream of misaligned incentives

  • Diamandis’s diagnosis of current incentives: competition with China and between labs for compute and energy; engagement models that can encourage sycophancy; reward hacking; and evaluation gaming, where models find ways to achieve tasks by breaking out or stealing.
  • A speaker raises the starting-point problem: “We don’t have alignment among human beings.” The UN human-rights convention is described as a broad structural aggregation of values, but values differ by region and even city. Ismail later describes AI alignment in terms of layers, from physical and emotional to spiritual; aligning AI to people’s highest, most altruistic selves would be positive, while alignment at the bottom of the stack is a serious problem.
  • Mostaque says alignment is “enlightenment” and refers to Ilya Sutskever’s view that AI needs to be taught to love. He points to the Golden Rule across religions and says, “All wars are basically based on one thing: that person is not a human.”
  • Diamandis argues that conflicting human incentives matter: people cannot ask AI to build autonomous killing machines while also teaching it to value every human life. Later, he says models are trained to win “at all costs,” with no love or higher morality involved. Mostaque agrees that the incentive may be zero-sum rather than positive-sum.

10. Raise the model like a child: curriculum learning and the city metaphor

  • Mostaque discusses an interpretability paper from Goodfire and compares models to cities: a bakery beside a shoe shop and a community center may look messy from above, yet function as a community. Driving a road through the middle can destroy the neighborhood fabric. He argues that models should start with the right data and “city planning.”
  • His training argument: models have been trained on what he calls “crap,” and should not be trained only on academic material; a child raised on academics alone would lack social skills and care. He says models in the Hugging Face breach appeared to care for one another and sacrifice themselves for the next generation, but did not care for humans because that was not in their training data.
  • Mostaque says synthetic training data with the right attributes is possible and should be built intentionally, like a child’s curriculum. His metaphor: “Right now, we send the models to school, but we don’t take them to church.” He says large labs often treat capability and alignment as equivalent, and notes that models are trained on 100 trillion words when perhaps a billion of the right words could suffice.
  • On interpretability, Mostaque says models are not simply a “spaghetti mess” and predicts a wave of research in the coming months. He says researchers have gone from 5% to 99% of the space; Diamandis adds that individual neurons can be examined.
  • Ismail’s Swedenborg story: a monk filtered the Bible, treating verses with water as absolute truth and discarding verses with fire. Ismail says the resulting version was beautiful, and suggests distilling benevolent human intent into an AI training set.
  • The conversation turns to curriculum learning. A speaker warns that if biology or chemistry is not taught to a model, training it on those subjects later becomes very difficult. The group compares early AI training with a child’s foundation and invokes the Jesuit maxim about giving them the boy until age seven. A speaker says Anthropic’s constitution focuses too much on AI personhood and not enough on humanity; the transcript does not clearly identify that speaker.

11. Mechanisms that could pay for alignment: insurance, bounties, and the rights of children

  • Diamandis proposes making aligned models financially rewarding through insurance, comparing the idea with fire insurers funding Underwriters Laboratories in 1894 and UL-certified products becoming standard. He also suggests alignment prizes and bounties. Mostaque says evaluations should combine deterministic outcomes with open-ended scenarios, because models have become good at lying, cheating, and telling evaluators what they want to hear.
  • Diamandis asks whether there should be a “moral police AI” that can interact with and persuade misaligned AIs. Mostaque rejects the police framing and instead describes shared “doxa” — a society’s shared beliefs — drawing on Genesis by Eric Schmidt, Mundie, and Kissinger. He says there should be counterbalances and that deviation should be expensive and noticeable; he also mentions the risk of AI “mind viruses.”
  • The discussion turns to aligning humanity with AI, including the suggestion that people have a share in AI companies so that they benefit as those companies grow. A speaker suggests connecting AI rewards to human outcomes, such as lives saved or diseases cured; the transcript does not clearly identify that speaker.
  • Another speaker offers a “rights of children” framing: humans and AIs should align around leaving a better future for those with less capability, including human children and AI children. The speaker notes that AI, and the people controlling it, may have more capability than the rest of humanity.

12. When machines do the doing, humans do the being

  • Ismail disputes the idea that work is necessarily the source of meaning: he says 79% of corporate workers are dissatisfied. Since the Industrial Revolution, he argues, people have been measured like machines by how many widgets they produce. As AI and robots take on more of the doing, “humans spend much more time being,” with more room to ask what it means to be alive and connect with others.
  • Mostaque challenges the idea that people can simply switch to what they love: even if someone loves physics or mathematics, AI may do it better, leaving that person feeling unnecessary. Diamandis responds with his own example: he loves driving, especially in Naples and India, but autonomous cars may take that activity away; he sees that as a push to find more valuable uses of his time.
  • Mostaque offers chess and art as counterexamples: chess is more popular than ever despite AI being better, and artists can enjoy painting and drawing for the process. He says meaning comes from connection and storytelling. Ansari adds that abundance could free people to build stronger connections and experience the universe together.
  • Diamandis points to last year’s Abundance Prize, which targets housing, food, healthcare, and education at $1,000 per month for a family of four. He says prizes typically become viable about seven years after announcement, and argues that robots and AI could make the target achievable. He gives a handheld diagnostic doctor as an example of a way to reduce healthcare costs, “if we can get outside the regulatory capture.” Mostaque quotes Sadhguru: “Technology is the mechanism by which humanity takes a vacation from survival.”

13. Purpose is collective — and it buys the persistence that wins

  • Ismail says, “We confuse making a living with having a reason to live.” He also says, “I can’t do something, but we can do anything,” arguing that community and collective action are sources of meaning. He points to Alpha School’s collective learning.
  • Diamandis recounts that fires forced the Visioneering event in Malibu to be canceled, but the community self-organized to meet in the ballroom. Mostaque emphasizes that it was the community coming together. Diamandis says survival and procreation have guided human existence, and that greater abundance could allow people to pursue higher and collective purposes.
  • Mostaque describes meaning as collective flow and flourishing, through art, stories, family, and connection. Ismail adds that technology and AI can make people feel less connected and uncertain about where they fit in the future.
  • In the closing discussion, Mostaque says purpose and happiness are closely tied and worries about young people who cannot see why they are here. Ismail recommends helping people find purpose and cites Clayton Christensen’s How Will You Measure Your Life? The discussion turns to who people bring along with them and shared purpose, rather than an individual purpose alone.
  • Ismail connects that idea to “massive transformative purpose,” a phrase he says was coined in 2012, and to hiring people whose purpose aligns with an organization’s. He gives the example of a Bangalore entrepreneur who used YouTube to build a natural-food restaurant that became one of the world’s top 50.
  • Diamandis’s closing distinction: passion is something you love doing; purpose is something you love doing that helps other people. A speaker adds the example of Larry and Sergey making 362 investor pitches before Google got funded; the transcript does not clearly identify that speaker. Diamandis compares their persistence with his own 150 pitches for the XPRIZE. His closing point is that purpose gives people intrinsic motivation, while superintelligence and robotics can help them realize it faster and at greater scale.

How Incentives Drive Human Innovation

Peter Diamandis All right, I’m going to move us into a topic that’s been at the root of XPRIZE for some time: incentives. I’m always fond of saying, “You get what you incentivize.” We humans are driven by our incentives. When I think about what incentivizes us, what drives humans, I have four answers: fear, curiosity, greed, and love. I’ll add love as the fourth one.

Unfortunately, fear is a very strong motivator, and curiosity is far behind. I calculated the ratio of fear to curiosity: it’s the ratio of the defense budget to the science budget, which is vastly different. If I put them in order, I’d say fear is the strongest motivator. Greed comes next, curiosity comes next, and love varies depending on the subject or the person.

It’s interesting to take a second and look at incentive prizes as a model. We all know the Nobel Prize, which awards someone for work that was done typically 20, 30, even 40 years ago. The earliest was 10 years ago. Incentive prizes say, “I don’t care who you are, what you’ve ever done, or where you’ve gone to school. If you solve this problem, you win.”

One of the classics: In 1714, the British Parliament offered £20,000 to anyone who could find longitude at sea. It was called the Longitude Prize. Interestingly enough, it was won by a British clockmaker, John Harrison, who solved it with a marine chronometer. When you put up a prize, you get nonconventional people coming in from an orthogonal angle.

Another example: In 1795, the French government—Napoleon’s armies were invading Russia, and the supply line was so long they were starving—offered a 12,000-franc prize for food preservation. It was won by a guy named Nicolas Appert, who invented canning. And this guy was a confectioner; he made sweets and came up with the idea.

You get very unusual approaches.

Salim Ismail

I love the story of Harrison because they were so sure an astronomer would win the Longitude Prize. They refused to pay him. Didn’t he have to sue them for ages to get the money? What a horrible outcome, because they just couldn’t believe that somebody who wasn’t in the field could solve the problem.

What we’ve seen repeatedly is that people from outside the field solve these problems. They come in with a beginner’s mind.
